pack: Week 40 — Psych I (Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders)
author: Alkarim Billawala / alkarim.billawala.ca
weeks: Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders

questions.stem: A family physician asks what proportion of her practice encounters are likely to involve a mental health condition. Which figure is correct?
options: 1 in 3
1 in 9
1 in 20
1 in 50
questions.explain: Why: 1 in 9 primary-care encounters involve a mental health condition, with other estimates as high as 30% of family-practice visits. Not the others: 1 in 3 is the lifetime prevalence of any mental illness or substance use disorder among Canadians, not an encounter rate.

questions.stem: Which statement about suicide in Canada is correct?
options: Women die by suicide about three times as often as men
Suicide is the leading cause of death in all age groups
About 12 Canadians die by suicide each day, and suicide is the second leading cause of death at ages 15 to 34
Fewer than 1,000 Canadians die by suicide each year
questions.explain: Why: about 12 deaths a day, 4,500 a year, the rate about 3 times higher in men, and suicide the second leading cause of death among youth and young adults aged 15 to 34. Not the others: the sex ratio is reversed; suicide is second, not first; the annual figure is thousands.

questions.stem: A student states that because women self-harm more often than men, women must also die by suicide more often. What is wrong with this?
options: Women neither self-harm nor die by suicide more often
Men self-harm more but women die more
Women self-harm more, but men die by suicide more; self-harm means non-suicidal self-injury
Self-harm and suicide are the same phenomenon
questions.explain: Why: men die by suicide more; women self-harm more, and self-harm is non-suicidal self-injury, a different behaviour from suicide. Not the others: each reverses or collapses the two facts.

questions.stem: A parent asks how common mental health disorders are at age 13 and which is the most common. Which answer is correct?
options: About 5%; ADHD
About 10%; adjustment disorder
About 20%; anxiety disorder
About 40%; depression
questions.explain: Why: 1 in 5 youth meet criteria for a mental health disorder, including anxiety, ADHD and depression, and anxiety disorders are the most prevalent in children and teens, often unrecognized, with early intervention improving outcomes. Not the others: the prevalence is 20% and the commonest diagnosis is anxiety, not ADHD or depression.

questions.stem: A nurse with depression delays seeking help because her employer offers no leave for mental health and she fears her colleagues would think less of her. Which levels of stigma are described, in order?
options: Individual, then interpersonal
Structural, then interpersonal
Interpersonal, then individual
Structural, then individual
questions.explain: Why: the absence of leave is a systemic barrier, structural stigma (the same level as racism); fear of colleagues' judgment is interpersonal stigma. Not the others: individual stigma is internalized shame ("I shouldn't be this way"), which is not described.

questions.stem: Which consequence of high internalized stigma is correct?
options: Earlier discontinuation of antidepressants
Higher rates of treatment adherence
Lower symptom severity
Increased help-seeking
questions.explain: Why: internalized stigma produces worse symptoms, lower self-esteem, hope and empowerment, and poorer treatment adherence; stigma can be measured, and when it is high antidepressants are discontinued earlier. Not the others: each states the opposite effect.

questions.stem: After a television series depicting a teenager's suicide in detail, deaths by suicide among adolescents rise for several months. Which phenomenon is this, and what does its counterpart describe?
options: Papageno effect; its counterpart is the rise in suicide after celebrity deaths
Werther effect; its counterpart, the Papageno effect, is a fall in suicidal ideation after recovery-focused portrayals
Social contagion; its counterpart is structural stigma
Werther effect; its counterpart is the media ban on reporting suicide
questions.explain: Why: a rise in suicidal behaviour after detailed, sensationalized or romanticized coverage is the Werther effect (about 195 extra deaths among US youth after 13 Reasons Why); the Papageno effect is the fall in suicidal ideation when media focus on coping and recovery. Not the others: the names are swapped in the first; the media ban is a consequence of the Werther effect, not its counterpart.

questions.stem: A patient says a viral video taught him to recognize depression by the shape of the eyebrows and chin. Which response reflects the evidence on mental-health content online?
options: Most popular mental-health videos are made by licensed professionals and are reliable
About a third of top mental-health videos are misleading, roughly half of popular ADHD videos are misleading, and none of those signs is a diagnostic criterion
Facial features are minor DSM-5 criteria for depression
Social media has no effect on stigma or help-seeking
questions.explain: Why: of the top 1,000 #MentalHealth videos, 19.1% were made by a licensed professional and one third were misleading; a 2022 UBC study found 52% of popular ADHD videos misleading; and no facial feature is a DSM-5 criterion. Not the others: social media does reduce stigma and increase help-seeking, but reliability is the problem.

questions.stem: Which assumption underlies degeneration theory?
options: Evolution is an iterative process responding to different stressors over time
Evolution acts on populations rather than individuals
Some humans have inherited traits that make them less suited to modern society
Mental illness is a treatable condition
questions.explain: Why: degeneration posited inherited defects that made individuals unfit for contemporary society, identifiable by physical features, with mental illness as the result and therefore no role for treatment. Not the others: the first two describe evolution accurately, which degeneration misread as a one-way path to an ideal; treatability contradicts degenerationist thinking.

questions.stem: Which statement about military psychiatrists in the world wars is correct?
options: Their main focus was the long-term quality of life of affected soldiers
They used hypnosis among their interventions
They established that shell shock was a form of hysteria
They abandoned talk therapy as ineffective
questions.explain: Why: Menninger and colleagues used talk therapy and hypnosis for shell shock. Not the others: the primary role was rapid return to duty, not quality of life; the hysteria explanation was thrown out rather than confirmed, because hysteria was constructed as a feminine disease; talk therapy was adopted, not abandoned.

questions.stem: Which edition of the DSM is considered the paradigm shift in psychiatric nosology, and why?
options: DSM-I, because it was the first compendium of mental illness
DSM-II, because it distinguished brain tissue diseases from psychogenic ones
DSM-III, because it introduced operationalized criteria and an atheoretical, descriptive approach
DSM-IV, because it was the first to require functional impairment
questions.explain: Why: DSM-III (1980) required distress or impairment, replaced expert opinion with statistically validated checklists, and admitted only reliably identifiable disorders. Not the others: DSM-I was a hospital census tool and DSM-II a neo-Freudian narrative manual; DSM-IV was an update, not a paradigm shift.

questions.stem: Of the somatic therapies of the 1930s, which survived properly conducted research, and what indication drift did it show?
options: Insulin coma; developed for mood, best for psychosis
Fever therapy; developed for syphilis, best for depression
Electroconvulsive therapy; developed for psychosis, most helpful for mood symptoms
Lobotomy; developed for agitation, best for anxiety
questions.explain: Why: research was consistently negative for cold baths, fever induction, insulin coma and psychosurgery; only ECT held up, and although developed to treat psychosis it proved most helpful for mood symptoms. Not the others: each names a therapy that failed.

questions.stem: Which factor was one of the four main problems of deinstitutionalization, and what was a stated consequence?
options: Community programmes were over-funded; consequence, a fall in homelessness
Stigma meant the most severely and disruptively ill were least likely to be seen at community clinics; consequence, homelessness, repeat brief admissions and more severe mental illness in prisons
Antipsychotics were unavailable; consequence, asylums reopened
Hospitals and community programmes were too tightly integrated; consequence, loss of privacy
questions.explain: Why: the four problems were insufficient scale, inflexible one-size-fits-all programmes, poor integration between hospitals and community programmes, and stigma excluding the sickest; the results were a surge in homelessness, repeat brief hospitalizations, and probably more people with severe and persistent mental illness in the carceral system. Not the others: each inverts a real problem.

questions.stem: A CBL question asks what the DSM has historically said about homosexuality and how that changed. Which account is correct?
options: It was never listed as a disorder

It was listed in DSM-I and DSM-II, Evelyn Hooker's 1950s study found no difference between 30 gay men and 30 matched controls on projective tests, and it was removed by APA vote in 1973 after the 1972 meeting
It was added in DSM-III and removed in DSM-5
It was removed because pharmaceutical companies requested it
questions.explain: Why: DSM-I (1952) and DSM-II (1968) listed it; Hooker's comparison of 30 gay men and 30 age-matched controls found no difference; a gay psychiatrist addressed the 1972 APA meeting in disguise; it was removed in 1973, with residual categories dropped by DSM-III-R in 1987. Not the others: the chronology and the driver are wrong in each.

questions.stem: What finding by social scientists in the 1970s most directly drove the move to operationalized diagnostic criteria?
options: Asylum mortality rates
Inter-rater reliability of psychiatric diagnosis as low as 30%
The failure of lobotomy
The success of chlorpromazine
questions.explain: Why: when social scientists examined psychiatric practice they found inter-rater reliability as low as 30%, diagnoses based on deviance rather than suffering, and neo-Freudians uninterested in diagnosis; St. Louis psychiatrists answered with statistically validated checklists by 1972, and DSM-III followed. Not the others: each belongs to a different era's disappointment or hope.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had persistent sadness, insomnia and poor concentration for six weeks. She lost her job recently but felt hopeless before the layoff, is struggling at work and in relationships, and has intermittent suicidal thoughts. Which feature best indicates that her symptoms qualify as a mental disorder?
options: Her sadness follows a recent life stressor
Her low mood affects her interpersonal functioning
A past history of social anxiety
The duration of her symptoms
questions.explain: Why: a mental disorder is a clinically significant disturbance with functional impairment, the feature that separates disorder from a normal emotional response. Not the others: a precipitating stressor, a comorbid history and duration do not by themselves establish disorder.

questions.stem: Two weeks after a flood destroyed his home, a man meets all nine criteria for a major depressive episode. Which statement about diagnosis is most accurate?
options: He must be diagnosed with major depressive disorder because he meets all nine criteria
The culturally expectable-response exclusion is one of the DSM criteria for major depressive disorder and rules it out automatically
The expectable-response exclusion is part of the general definition of a mental disorder rather than the MDD criteria, and a clinician might instead understand the picture as an adjustment reaction
Duration is irrelevant once symptoms are this severe
questions.explain: Why: the exclusion for an expectable response to a stressor belongs to the definition of a mental disorder, not to the MDD criterion list; a psychiatrist might not diagnose depression after a calamitous stressor and might use adjustment disorder instead, while the two-week persistence requirement still applies. Not the others: meeting criteria does not compel the diagnosis; the exclusion is not in the MDD criteria; duration still matters.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts categorical and dimensional models of diagnosis?
options: Categorical models treat disorders as continua; dimensional models treat them as discrete

Categorical models hold that disorders are qualitatively distinct and either present or absent; dimensional models hold that disorders are exaggerated, inflexible versions of normally distributed traits
Dimensional models are the current standard in clinical practice through DSM-5-TR
HiTOP and RDoC are categorical systems published by the WHO
questions.explain: Why: the categorical premise is discrete, qualitative distinctness (DSM-5-TR, ICD-11); the dimensional premise is a continuum with quantitative differences (HiTOP, RDoC), used in research rather than practice. Not the others: the first swaps the models; the current standard is categorical; HiTOP and RDoC are dimensional research frameworks, and RDoC is from the US NIH.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has low mood, poor appetite and lack of motivation with significant impairment at work and socially, but meets only four of nine criteria, so no major depressive episode is diagnosed. Which limitation of the diagnostic system does this illustrate?
options: Dimensional models are too rigid
Categorical systems fail to define symptom clusters
Arbitrary cutoffs can exclude clinically significant cases
Comorbidity is uncommon in mood disorders
questions.explain: Why: the categorical approach misses meaningful distress and impairment when the symptom count falls just below threshold: 4 of 9 is not an MDE, 5 of 9 is. Not the others: categorical, not dimensional, systems are the rigid ones; categorical systems do define symptom clusters; comorbidity is common.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old has had daily attacks of chest pain, sweating, dyspnoea, tremor and a sense of doom for nine months, avoids crowds and will not leave home alone. Which criteria set does he satisfy for panic disorder?
options: At least 2 of 13 panic symptoms and one week of worry
At least 4 of 13 symptoms peaking within minutes, plus at least one month of worry about further attacks or a maladaptive behaviour change
At least 5 of 9 symptoms over two weeks
Any panic attack with avoidance, regardless of duration
questions.explain: Why: criterion A is recurrent unexpected panic attacks with at least 4 of 13 symptoms peaking within minutes; criterion B is at least one month of persistent worry and/or maladaptive behaviour change after at least one attack; C and D exclude substances, medical conditions and other disorders. Not the others: 5 of 9 over two weeks is the depressive episode rule; the other thresholds are invented.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old store manager has lifelong low self-esteem, binge drinks, and has intense sadness lasting up to an hour once or twice a week; she misses no work or social events. Why does she not meet criteria for a major depressive episode, and what does a dimensional reading offer?
options: She meets criteria; the dimensional reading adds nothing

She lacks functional impairment and her episodes fail the two-week, most-of-the-day requirement; dimensionally, low self-worth, hopelessness and alcohol misuse still generate a plan of targeted psychotherapy and alcohol psychoeducation
She fails only because she does not have suicidal ideation; dimensionally she has no treatable traits
She fails because binge drinking excludes depression; dimensionally she needs an antidepressant
questions.explain: Why: a major depressive episode needs five of nine symptoms in the same two-week period, most of the day nearly every day, with impairment; hour-long episodes with intact functioning do not qualify. Described by traits, she has low self-worth, hopelessness and alcohol misuse, clinically significant suffering with a plan. Not the others: each misstates the criteria or the dimensional consequence.

guide.s: low self-worth, hopelessness and alcohol misuse

questions.stem: One patient with major depressive disorder has anhedonia, insomnia, 50 lb of weight loss and catatonia; another binge-eats and sleeps 14 hours a day. Which limitation of categorical diagnosis does the pair illustrate?
options: Arbitrary thresholds
Comorbidity
Heterogeneity: the same label covers very different patients
Subthreshold illness
questions.explain: Why: with five of nine symptoms required, hundreds of presentations share one label, so the same diagnosis can describe patients who look nothing alike and may not need the same treatment. Not the others: thresholds concern the cutoff, comorbidity concerns multiple labels on one process, and subthreshold illness concerns impairment without a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A supervisor is unsure whether a refugee with trauma symptoms meets full PTSD criteria or fits an 'other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder'. Which statement best reflects what a DSM label gains and costs?
options: A label is always harmful and should be avoided in trauma

A label gives reliable communication and access to treatment and services, at the cost of arbitrary thresholds, heterogeneity, stigma and saying what rather than why; the 'other specified' category exists for the subthreshold case
A label removes all stigma and fully explains the presentation
Trauma always produces a DSM diagnosis, so the question does not arise
questions.explain: Why: DSM-III made diagnosis reliable and communicable and it unlocks treatment and coverage, while the four limitations and stigma are its costs; 'other specified' categories capture impairment below threshold, and trauma affects identity and relationships with or without a diagnosis. Not the others: each takes an absolute position the material does not support.

guide.t: 6 · The pros and cons of a label

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with chronic anxiety and low mood asks why her brother, raised in the same home, is doing well. Which explanation is most consistent with the diathesis-stress model?
options: Her brother must have had a more secure attachment
Diathesis-stress interactions vary between individuals: siblings are not genetic copies and did not experience the same environment
She has a mental disorder and he does not, so the model does not apply to him
The same stressors always produce the same outcome within a family
questions.explain: Why: predisposition is a sliding scale set by genetics and early development, and both the diathesis and the stressors differ between siblings (an in-lecture poll answer). Not the others: attachment may differ but is not the general explanation; the model applies to everyone, ill or well; identical stressors do not give identical outcomes.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes temperament?
options: A stable pattern of behaviour developed through experience
Innate, biologically based traits present from infancy that shape early interaction with the world
Enduring traits that deviate from social norms
The emotional bond formed with a caregiver
questions.explain: Why: temperament is innate and biologically based, present from infancy and foundational to personality, established in the first few years of life. Not the others: the first describes learned behaviour, the third a personality disorder, the fourth attachment; temperament is distinct from both.

questions.stem: Two patients develop borderline personality disorder. Patient X was mildly emotionally sensitive and suffered severe childhood abuse. Patient Y was extremely sensitive and grew up in a loving family that often dismissed her feelings. Which principle do the two histories illustrate?
options: Trauma is required for borderline personality disorder
Emotional sensitivity alone causes the disorder
The more biological vulnerability a person has, the less environmental invalidation is needed, and vice versa
Invalidation only matters after age five
questions.explain: Why: Person A on the reactivity curve (about two SD above the mean) needs trauma-level invalidation; Person B at the extreme tail develops BPD with subtle invalidation. This is the diathesis-stress equation in BPD terms. Not the others: trauma is a severe form of invalidation but not required; sensitivity is a risk factor, not a cause on its own; maternal separation before five is one example, not a boundary.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with four adverse childhood experiences asks what that means for his health. Which statement reflects the ACE study?
options: About 12% of adults have four or more ACEs, and at that level the risk of major depression is roughly four-fold and of a suicide attempt up to twelve-fold, with physical illnesses such as heart disease and COPD also more likely
ACEs predict mental illness but not physical illness
Fewer than a quarter of adults report any ACE
Four or more ACEs make later illness inevitable
questions.explain: Why: the 1995 Kaiser-CDC study found about 64% of adults with at least one ACE and about 12% with four or more, with a dose-response rise in depression (4.4 times), anxiety (3.7), drug-use disorder (over 10), suicide attempt (up to 12), and in ischemic heart disease, COPD, cancer and obesity. Not the others: physical outcomes are central to the study; most adults have at least one ACE; not all high-ACE children develop illness, and positive experiences reduce the risk.

questions.stem: A mother of a highly sensitive 8-year-old describes what she does when he is upset. Which response is protective rather than a risk factor for later borderline personality disorder?
options: Telling him firmly that things are not so bad and he is overreacting
Giving him extra treats and attention whenever he has an outburst
Losing her temper, then later sitting down with him to talk about what happened and repair the rupture
Leaving the room until he calms down on his own
questions.explain: Why: invalidation followed by talking about it and repairing is protective; some invalidation is inevitable, and repair is what matters. Not the others: reassurance that minimizes the feeling is invalidation (Victoria's mother); reinforcement of emotional outbursts is a risk factor; turning away is a listed poor-fit response.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder says his parents never showed affection or encouraged emotional expression. He finds it hard to trust others and prefers to handle problems alone. Which attachment pattern is most consistent, and which cascade follows from it?
options: Anxious: hypervigilance to rejection
Avoidant: deactivation, alexithymia and compulsive self-sufficiency, associated with substance misuse
Disorganized: fragmented self-concept and dissociation
Secure: trust and exploration
questions.explain: Why: emotionally unavailable or rejecting care produces avoidant attachment, whose cascade is deactivation, alexithymia and self-sufficiency, with substance misuse, restricting eating disorders and schizoid traits as the typical phenotypes; the vignette pairs avoidance with alcohol use exactly as the table predicts. Not the others: an anxiously attached person seeks constant reassurance; disorganized attachment follows maltreatment or a frightening caregiver.

questions.stem: In Harlow's studies, infant rhesus monkeys were raised with a wire surrogate that provided milk and a cloth surrogate that provided none. What did the monkeys do, and what does it show?
options: They stayed on the wire mother because it fed them, showing that attachment follows feeding
They spent most of their time on the cloth mother and visited the wire mother only to feed, showing that contact comfort drives attachment
They avoided both surrogates, showing that attachment requires a live caregiver
They alternated equally, showing attachment is learned by reinforcement
questions.explain: Why: the hypothesis was that the monkeys would prefer the milk mother; instead they clung to the cloth mother as a secure base, returning to the wire mother briefly to feed. Not the others: each contradicts the observed preference for comfort over food.

questions.stem: Parents of a child with a high ACE score ask what could reduce his later risk. Which advice matches the week's teaching?
options: Protect him from every source of stress or frustration from now on
Add positive childhood experiences and provide good-enough, not perfect, care, accepting that some frustration is part of building resilience
Nothing changes the risk once ACEs have accumulated
Avoid discussing his feelings so as not to re-traumatize him
questions.explain: Why: each additional positive childhood experience lowers adult depression risk by 26%; Winnicott's good-enough parent provides ordinary, non-ideal care; and optimal frustration means some adversity is actively needed; being able to talk about emotions is protective. Not the others: shielding from all adversity removes the frustration that resilience needs; not all high-ACE children become ill; avoiding emotion is invalidation.

questions.stem: A student asks why the brain would evolve to be vulnerable to anxiety disorders. Which answer reflects the evolutionary view taught this week?
options: Anxiety is a modern invention with no ancestral function
Anxiety was once adaptive for avoiding danger; modern stressors activate the same systems without physical threat, and dysregulation produces disorder
Evolution selects for happiness, so anxiety is a failure of selection
Anxiety disorders are caused only by learned behaviour
questions.explain: Why: traits that seem maladaptive today were possibly adaptive ancestrally, evolution selects for reproductive fitness rather than health, and adaptive systems can become excessive or contextually mismatched; being anxious increased survival by avoiding predators. Not the others: each denies the ancestral function or misstates what evolution selects for.

questions.stem: A refugee claimant who concealed his sexuality for years under threat of persecution presents after a violent attack and the death of his mother. In the 4 P's grid, where does the long history of concealment and persecution belong?
options: Precipitating, biological
Predisposing, psychological and social/cultural
Perpetuating, biological
Protective, social
questions.explain: Why: predisposing factors are areas of vulnerability that raise the risk of the presenting problem; longstanding fear from concealment is psychological and the longstanding threat of persecution is social and cultural. The attack and the bereavement are the precipitants. Not the others: chronic discrimination is a strain on the predisposition side, not a trigger, a maintainer or a strength.

questions.stem: A psychiatrist opens every interview by reviewing the limits of confidentiality. Which set correctly lists the exceptions named?
options: Suicidal thoughts, substance use, unemployment
A threat to someone's life, concern for the care of a child, and driving safety
Any criminal activity, any drug use, any sexual history
Only situations the patient agrees to disclose
questions.explain: Why: the statutory safety exceptions placed on all doctors are threat to another's life, child safety and driving safety, stated before any disclosure so the patient knows what could follow; a patient describing impaired driving is then reported to the ministry. Not the others: substance use and employment are not exceptions; the exceptions are not at the patient's discretion.

questions.stem: A patient says, 'I think my marriage is falling apart.' Which response best fits the model of empathy taught?
options: 'At least you have a marriage.'
'Have you considered couples counselling?'
'I don't even know what to say right now. I'm just so glad you told me.'
'Many marriages go through rough patches.'
questions.explain: Why: empathy is feeling with the person, perspective taking, staying out of judgement, recognizing the emotion and communicating that; connection, not a fix, is what helps. Not the others: an 'at least' response is the silver-lining failure that is rarely if ever empathic; advice and normalizing keep the clinician at the top of the hole.

questions.stem: Which interviewing behaviour is correct according to the process checklist?
options: Interview from a checklist so nothing is missed
Leave sensitive topics such as suicide until the end so rapport is established first
Ask one concise question at a time, avoid leading questions, and raise emotionally loaded topics yourself when the patient hints at them
Fill silences quickly so the patient does not feel awkward
questions.explain: Why: the checklist calls for single, brief, non-leading questions, calm interest in loaded material, and raising such topics when there are verbal or non-verbal clues. Not the others: the checklist is used after the interview, not during; sensitive topics must not be left to the end; silence is left for the patient to think.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a severe depressive episode becomes unusually deferential toward a clinical clerk and repeatedly seeks reassurance; she later describes abandonment by paternal figures. Which phenomenon best explains her behaviour?
options: Countertransference
Identification
Transference
Therapeutic alliance
questions.explain: Why: the patient is unconsciously redirecting feelings from past relationships onto the clinician as an authority or parental figure: transference. Not the others: countertransference is the clinician's own reaction; identification is loss of objectivity; the therapeutic alliance is the collaborative clinical relationship.

questions.stem: A clerk notices she feels unusually irritated with a patient who reminds her of a critical older sibling and becomes dismissive during the assessment. What is happening, and what is the right first step?
options: Transference; confront the patient about their hostility
Countertransference; notice the reaction, debrief with a supervisor, keep boundaries and use it to understand the patient
Resistance; end the interview
Identification; take over the patient's care
questions.explain: Why: a clinician reacting to a patient on the basis of her own history is countertransference; the management is to notice the reaction, reflect or debrief, keep the professional role, and use it as a learning tool. It is normal, and the clue is a reaction that differs from one's usual. Not the others: the imported past here is the clinician's, not the patient's.

questions.stem: Asked gently about past relationships, a previously cooperative patient says, 'That's not relevant, let's talk about my medications, you're just a student.' Which response reflects the technique taught?
options: Apologize and move on to medications
Make a process comment: 'I notice you'd rather not talk about relationships; what's going on there?'
Insist that relationships are part of every history
End the interview and refer to a senior
questions.explain: Why: this is resistance, a process that interferes with the therapeutic objective, and it is not simply rolled with; the response is a process comment about what is happening in the interview rather than another content question. Not the others: capitulating, insisting and abandoning the interview each miss the phenomenon.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old refugee with hypervigilance, nightmares and avoidance is hesitant about Western psychiatric care and attributes his distress to ancestral spirits. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Challenge his cultural beliefs and provide psychoeducation
Refer him to a psychiatrist from his region and start an SSRI
Explore his explanatory model of illness and book a follow-up
Diagnose PTSD and reassure him the symptoms will pass
questions.explain: Why: understanding the patient's explanatory model builds trust and informs culturally sensitive care; eliciting the patient's perspective and collaborating are two of the six strategies against bias. Not the others: challenging beliefs is the opposite of eliciting them; referral and medication without engagement, or premature diagnosis and reassurance, do not build an alliance.

guide.t: 7 · Culture, hesitancy and the refugee patient

questions.stem: A woman with persistent low mood has had minimal benefit from three months of psychotherapy and is hesitant about medication because of side-effect worries. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Recommend neurostimulation because therapy has failed
Refer to inpatient psychiatry to start medication
Explore her concerns about pharmacological options and provide information
Continue psychotherapy unchanged
questions.explain: Why: medication hesitancy is met by exploring concerns and informing, which supports shared decision-making. Not the others: neurostimulation and admission are premature escalation or coercion; unchanged therapy ignores the inadequate response.

guide.t: 7 · Culture, hesitancy and the refugee patient

questions.stem: Which four domains are screened at essentially every psychiatric assessment?
options: Depression, mania or hypomania, psychosis, anxiety
Cognition, eating, sexual function, dissociation
Sleep, appetite, energy, concentration
Substance use, legal history, housing, finances
questions.explain: Why: the review of systems screens depression, mania/hypomania, psychosis and anxiety in every assessment other than an acutely agitated psychotic patient being treated in the emergency room. Not the others: cognitive, eating, sexual and dissociative symptoms are added when relevant; the third set is part of the depression screen; the fourth is history, not a symptom screen.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man three days after stopping heavy drinking reports feeling insects crawling under his skin. Which hallucination modality is this, and what is it most in keeping with?
options: Auditory; schizophrenia
Visual; delirium
Tactile; alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
Olfactory; temporal lobe epilepsy
questions.explain: Why: feeling bugs crawling or being touched is a tactile (somatic) hallucination, most in keeping with alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Not the others: auditory hallucinations point to schizophrenia, visual to delirium and medical causes, olfactory (burning smells) to temporal lobe epilepsy.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with profound low mood tells his doctor that his body no longer exists and the world has already ended. Which delusion type is this, and with which condition does it typically occur?
options: Referential; schizophrenia
Nihilistic; severe psychotic depression
Grandiose; mania
Erotomanic; delusional disorder
questions.explain: Why: the belief that one is dead, does not exist or the world has ended is a nihilistic delusion, which accompanies very severe depression; in depression with psychosis delusions are mood-congruent, nihilistic, somatic or guilty. Not the others: referential delusions concern messages from unrelated events; grandiose and erotomanic content is absent.

questions.stem: Which feature in a history most specifically distinguishes a manic period from a depressive one?
options: Poor sleep
Needing less sleep than usual while still feeling full of energy
Difficulty concentrating
Irritability
questions.explain: Why: decreased need for sleep with preserved energy is the S of GST PAID and is the opposite of the insomnia-with-fatigue of depression. Not the others: poor sleep, poor concentration and irritability occur in both.

questions.stem: Which statement about withdrawal is correct?
options: Opioid withdrawal is the most lethal and requires admission
Alcohol, benzodiazepine and phenobarbital withdrawal can cause seizures, delirium tremens and death; opioid withdrawal is severe but not lethal
Cannabis withdrawal commonly causes seizures
Benzodiazepine withdrawal is safely managed at home without medication
questions.explain: Why: withdrawal from central nervous system depressants can kill, and is managed by admission with diazepam and thiamine and intravenous treatment; opioid withdrawal is very uncomfortable but not lethal and can be medically managed. Not the others: each reverses the depressant-versus-opioid rule or invents a risk.

guide.s: Withdrawal from central nervous system depressants

questions.stem: A 20-year-old university student is admitted with sudden-onset psychosis and marked paranoia. Screening bloodwork shows a very high TSH. He also has hypercholesterolaemia and hypertension. What is the most likely explanation and the treatment?
options: First-episode schizophrenia; start an antipsychotic long term
Myxedema psychosis from untreated hypothyroidism; replace thyroid hormone
Substance-induced psychosis; observe
Bipolar disorder with psychotic features; start lithium
questions.explain: Why: untreated hypothyroidism can produce psychosis, and the very high TSH with lipid and blood-pressure abnormalities in an otherwise healthy young person points to myxedema psychosis, treated by thyroid replacement. Not the others: the medical history and screening labs are what prevent a schizophrenia label; nothing suggests substances or mania.

questions.stem: A patient's father has bipolar disorder. What is her approximate risk of bipolar disorder?
questions.explain: Why: a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder gives about a 10% chance of bipolar disorder. Not the others: the other figures overstate or understate the heritable risk.

questions.stem: Which item belongs to the six risk headings of the psychiatric history but is commonly forgotten, and what does the interview template add?
options: Suicide; the template adds nothing
Neglect of dependents; the template adds safe driving and cooking
Financial risk; the template adds gambling
Violence; the template adds legal charges
questions.explain: Why: the six headings are suicide, other self-harm, violence toward others, inability to look after oneself, self-neglect and neglect of dependents, and the template adds safe driving and cooking, items students routinely omit. Not the others: financial and legal history sit under personal circumstances, not risk.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man reports two months of feeling 'really sad', cannot get out of bed, has stopped working and playing guitar, has no appetite, and thinks his family would be better off without him. Which MSE finding is most likely?
options: Broad affect
Grandiose delusions
Slowed speech
Intact concentration
questions.explain: Why: depression shows on the MSE as poor eye contact, psychomotor slowing and reduced, slowed speech with increased latency. Not the others: affect would be restricted, not broad; grandiose delusions belong to mania or psychosis, and any depressive delusions would be nihilistic, somatic or guilty; concentration would be impaired.

questions.stem: A patient says her mood is 'terrible, the worst it has been' but laughs and jokes throughout the interview. How is this documented?
options: Mood depressed, affect congruent
Mood depressed by report, affect elevated and incongruent with stated mood
Mood elevated, affect depressed
Affect cannot be assessed when it conflicts with mood
questions.explain: Why: mood is the patient's subjective report and affect is what the examiner observes; when they disagree the affect is documented as incongruent with the stated mood, and the discrepancy is itself informative. Not the others: each collapses or reverses the two.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought by his family for social withdrawal, delusions and poor hygiene; he avoids eye contact and shows minimal emotional reactivity throughout. Which term describes his affect, and which axis does it belong to?
options: Labile; stability
Restricted; quality
Flat; quality
Broad; range
questions.explain: Why: minimal emotional reactivity is a flat affect, and flat describes quality; restricted describes range, and fixed or labile describe stability. Not the others: restricted is a range term; labile and broad describe the opposite of what is seen.

questions.stem: One patient hears her name called every time the phone rings; another hears a voice speaking to him while the room is silent. Which terms apply?
options: Both are hallucinations
The first is an illusion, the second a hallucination
The first is a hallucination, the second an illusion
Both are illusions
questions.explain: Why: an illusion is the misperception of a real stimulus (the ringing phone); a hallucination is a perception with no external stimulus (a voice in silence). Not the others: the presence or absence of a real stimulus is the discriminator.

questions.stem: Asked about his sleep, a patient describes his mattress, the store he bought it in, the clerk's accent and the drive home, and after several minutes says he sleeps about four hours. Which term describes this thought process?
options: Tangential
Circumstantial
Flight of ideas
Loose associations
questions.explain: Why: circumstantial thought eventually answers the question after excessive detail; tangential thought moves away and never answers. Not the others: flight of ideas is rapid shifting with discernible links, and loose associations are connections too weak to follow.

questions.stem: A patient says, 'I know I've been much sadder than usual, I think it's my depression coming back, and I know the antidepressant helped last time, so I'll book an appointment to restart it.' Which statement is correct?
options: She shows insight but not judgement
She shows all three tasks of insight and intact judgement, the combination required for capacity to make decisions about her care
She shows judgement but lacks insight
Insight and judgement cannot be assessed from a single statement
questions.explain: Why: insight is three tasks, recognizing new symptoms, attributing them to a pathological process, and recognizing the benefit of treatment; judgement is using that insight to act in one's own interest; both are required for capacity. Her statement contains all of it. Not the others: the two constructs can dissociate, but here both are present.

questions.stem: Police bring in a man who believes he is Jesus reincarnated; he is calm, polite and cooperative and has been caring for himself adequately. How are insight and judgement graded?
options: Both intact
Insight absent; judgement may be intact because it is read from behaviour
Insight intact; judgement impaired
Both cannot be graded in psychosis
questions.explain: Why: he cannot tell that his experience is not true, so insight is absent, but judgement is based on behaviour and decisions, which are appropriate, so it may be intact. The two are scored separately and can move in opposite directions. Not the others: each fuses the constructs.

questions.stem: A patient speaks rapidly and the interviewer cannot get a word in. Which MSE term applies and what does it suggest?
options: Verbose speech; anxiety
Pressured speech; a cardinal sign of mania
Circumstantial thought; personality disorder
Speech latency; depression
questions.explain: Why: fast speech that is hard to interrupt is pressured speech, a cardinal symptom of mania, and with distractibility and affect lability makes a manic picture. Not the others: latency is the long pause of depression; verbose describes quantity without the pressure.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a diagnosis from a formulation?
options: A diagnosis explains why the patient is ill now; a formulation lists the criteria met
A diagnosis describes what the patient has; a formulation is a hypothesis with a 'because' that explains why now and what to do
They are the same thing expressed in different words
A formulation is only used in research
questions.explain: Why: a diagnosis is a structured classification of symptom clusters that may not explain why they occur in this person; a formulation is a hypothesis answering why this patient fell ill now and what should be done, and it contains a 'because'. Not the others: the first reverses the two; formulation guides holistic treatment planning as well as research.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations, but is also disoriented to time and place and fluctuates in alertness. Where does the diagnostic hierarchy direct the assessment?
options: Toward schizophrenia, because delusions and hallucinations are present
Toward depression, because it is the commonest disorder
Upward, toward a physical or drug-induced cause, because confusion is the hallmark of the top rung and psychoses are unlikely to show it
Nowhere; the hierarchy applies only to prognosis
questions.explain: Why: higher rungs show the features of lower ones, but lower rungs rarely show the hallmarks of higher ones; confusion marks physical and drug-induced conditions, and psychoses are unlikely to feature it, so delusions with confusion point up the ladder. Not the others: the psychotic features alone do not settle the level; the hierarchy is a diagnostic approach.

questions.stem: In the model of sickness used by the clinical-skills course, what are the three components of a working diagnosis?
options: Symptoms, signs, investigations
Illness (classified symptoms and signs), predicament (context), disease (pathophysiology)
Biological, psychological, social
Predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating
questions.explain: Why: a working diagnosis classifies the symptoms and signs (illness), discerns the context (predicament), and where possible discovers the underlying pathophysiology (disease). Not the others: the third and fourth are the columns and rows of the formulation grid, not the components of diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with persistent low mood feels isolated and struggles to maintain close relationships; her parents were emotionally unavailable; she recently lost her job; she sleeps poorly and has passive thoughts of death. Which is the most appropriate psychological predisposing factor?
options: Recent unemployment
Sleep disturbance
Insecure attachment arising from emotionally unavailable parents
Passive suicidal ideation
questions.explain: Why: predisposing factors are vulnerabilities that raise the risk of the presenting problem, and the emotionally unavailable parents produce the insecure attachment that is both psychological and predisposing. Not the others: unemployment is precipitating, sleep disturbance perpetuating, and passive suicidal ideation is a symptom of the depression, not a factor.

questions.stem: In the formulation of a depressed 25-year-old with type 1 diabetes whose mother had severe depression and was often hospitalized, why does the mother's depression appear in two columns?
options: It is an error in the grid
It is heritability in the biological column and parental absence, producing insecure attachment, in the social column
It counts twice to increase the severity score
It belongs only in the psychological column
questions.explain: Why: the same fact carries two different mechanisms: genetic risk (biological, predisposing) and a mother who was away from him as an infant, so no secure base (social, predisposing), from which the psychological factors of insecure attachment and 'I am not good enough' are derived. Not the others: the grid has no scoring; the entry is deliberate.

questions.stem: For the same 25-year-old, what plan follows from the formulation, and how does it map onto the grid?
options: Prescribe fluoxetine only, because he is depressed
Improve glycaemic control and restart fluoxetine (biological), psychotherapy for self-esteem (psychological), and engage the healthcare team and address isolation (social)
Admit for neurostimulation
Refer to social work only
questions.explain: Why: the plan maps one to one onto the columns: better blood-sugar control and the SSRI he previously responded to, therapy for the self-esteem and trust conflict, and the team and supports for the isolation; that is different from 'he's depressed, give him Prozac'. Not the others: each addresses one column or none.

questions.stem: In Stanley's four-column formulation, which entry is a precipitating social factor?
options: Longstanding threat of persecution for same-sex relationships
The violent attack and forced migration
Housing instability
A supportive cousin
questions.explain: Why: the attack, the forced migration, the loss of home and occupation and the coming hearing are the precipitating social events. Not the others: the longstanding threat is predisposing, housing instability perpetuating, and the cousin protective.

questions.stem: Which set correctly describes the clerkship psychiatric case write-up?
options: History only, any length, no deadline
History, mental state examination, diagnostic impression and management plan, with a two-to-three-sentence summary naming the pertinent historical and mental-state findings
Mental state examination and a drug list
A formulation grid without a history
questions.explain: Why: the write-up consists of the history, the MSE, a diagnostic impression and a plan; the summary must be two to three sentences covering both history and mental state; a satisfactory score is required to pass. Not the others: each omits required parts.

guide.t: 5 · The management plan and the case report

questions.stem: A 40-year-old is described by colleagues as suspicious and quick to take offence, but he has a stable marriage, close friends and a successful career and reports no distress. Does he have a personality disorder?
options: Yes, paranoid personality disorder, because the traits are present
No, because a personality disorder requires the traits to cause distress or functional impairment
Yes, because suspiciousness is always pathological
Only if he also has delusions
questions.explain: Why: a personality trait is an enduring pattern across contexts; it becomes a disorder only when it causes distress or impairs functioning, and the general criteria require clinically significant distress or impairment. Not the others: the trait alone is never the diagnosis; delusions would point to a psychotic disorder, not a personality disorder.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old develops marked suspiciousness and grudge-holding six months after a traumatic brain injury, with no earlier history. Which general criteria exclude a personality disorder?
options: A and B
C only
D (onset by adolescence or early adulthood) and F (not attributable to another medical condition)
E only
questions.explain: Why: the pattern must be stable and long-standing with onset traceable to adolescence or early adulthood (D), and must not be attributable to a substance or another medical condition such as head trauma (F). Not the others: A, B and C concern the domains, pervasiveness and impairment; E concerns another mental disorder.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old software tester lives alone, eats lunch by himself, declines every invitation including family events, says he does not see the point of relationships, and is unaffected by praise or criticism. Affect is flat; no hallucinations or delusions. Most likely diagnosis?
options: Avoidant personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder
Schizotypal personality disorder
Major depressive disorder
questions.explain: Why: no desire for relationships, solitary activities, indifference to praise or criticism and flat affect are schizoid, which resembles the negative symptoms of schizophrenia without psychosis. Not the others: avoidant patients want relationships but fear rejection; schizotypal requires odd beliefs, perceptual distortions or eccentric speech; depression is an episode, not an enduring trait pattern.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman senses people's intentions through 'energy fields', wears mismatched layered clothing, speaks in vague metaphor, has no friends outside her family, and after two years in a book club still feels members are 'up to something'. No fixed delusions. Which feature most specifically distinguishes her diagnosis from avoidant personality disorder?
options: Lack of close friends
Social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity and is driven by paranoid fears rather than fear of rejection
Unusual clothing
Absence of delusions
questions.explain: Why: the schizotypal criterion is excessive social anxiety that persists despite familiarity and is tied to paranoid fears; avoidant anxiety is about criticism, rejection and inadequacy. Not the others: lack of friends occurs in both clusters; odd appearance supports schizotypal but is not the avoidant discriminator; absence of delusions distinguishes her from schizophrenia, not from avoidant PD.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old is brought in after a third arrest for fraud; he lies easily, shows no remorse and has never held a job. Which additional finding is required to diagnose antisocial personality disorder?
options: A score above threshold on the Hare Psychopathy Checklist
Evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15
A family history of antisocial behaviour
At least five of seven criteria
questions.explain: Why: antisocial personality disorder requires 3 of 7 criteria, age at least 18, and conduct disorder with onset before 15; he meets the age requirement, so the conduct-disorder history is what remains. Not the others: psychopathy is not a DSM diagnosis and the checklist is not a criterion; family history is not required; the threshold is 3 of 7.

questions.stem: At a party a woman is loud and flirtatious, changes emotional tone moment to moment, describes a new acquaintance as her 'best friend', and cannot give specifics when asked about a 'terrible' week. Which diagnosis fits, and which feature distinguishes it from narcissistic personality disorder?
options: Narcissistic; she seeks admiration
Histrionic; she seeks attention of any kind with shallow emotion, whereas the narcissist seeks admiration that confirms superiority and lacks empathy
Borderline; she fears abandonment
Dependent; she cannot be alone
questions.explain: Why: discomfort when not the centre of attention, seductive behaviour, rapidly shifting shallow emotion, overestimated intimacy and impressionistic speech are histrionic; the discriminator is why attention is sought. Not the others: no grandiosity or entitlement; no instability of self or fear of abandonment; no reliance on others for decisions.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old accountant misses deadlines because he redoes spreadsheets until they are perfect, refuses to delegate, works weekends although well paid, keeps decades of broken electronics, and sees nothing wrong with any of it. He has no intrusive, unwanted thoughts. Which diagnosis?
options: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
Hoarding disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder
questions.explain: Why: perfectionism that prevents completion, refusal to delegate, work devotion not due to economic need, inability to discard worthless objects, rigidity, and an ego-syntonic stance with no true obsessions or compulsions is the personality disorder (4 of 8). Not the others: OCD is ego-dystonic with intrusive obsessions and resisted compulsions; hoarding is one criterion here, not the whole picture; there is no generalized worry.

questions.stem: Which statement about the management of personality disorders is correct?
options: SSRIs are approved as first-line treatment for personality disorders
Antipsychotics are approved for cluster A disorders
Psychotherapy is the mainstay; medications may target comorbidities or specific symptoms
Personality disorders are primarily environmental in origin, so social intervention is the mainstay
questions.explain: Why: no medication is approved to treat a personality disorder directly; psychotherapy is the mainstay, and drugs are used for comorbid conditions or specific symptoms. Not the others: the etiology is a gene-environment interaction, and no drug class is approved for any cluster.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder says at times that her boyfriend is 'the best person in the world' and at other times 'the worst person ever'. Which criterion does this illustrate?
options: Anger outbursts
Unstable sense of self
Unstable relationships
Unstable mood
questions.explain: Why: extreme fluctuation in the perception of another person, idealization alternating with devaluation, is the unstable and intense relationships criterion (splitting). Not the others: anger, identity disturbance and affective instability are real criteria but the vignette describes her view of someone else, not her self-image or her mood.

questions.stem: Which description is most in keeping with the criteria for borderline personality disorder?
options: Affective instability, suicidal behaviour, inappropriate anger, relationship instability, unstable sense of self, fear of abandonment, impulsivity, dissociation or paranoia, feelings of emptiness
Affective instability, shallow expression of emotions, inappropriate anger, relationship instability, unstable sense of self, reckless disregard for safety, envy of others, interpersonal exploitation
Affective instability, suicidal behaviour, shallow emotions, reckless disregard for safety, envy, exploitation, considers relationships more intimate than they are
Affective instability, suicidal behaviour, reckless disregard for safety, relationship instability, shallow emotions, envy, exploitation
questions.explain: Why: the nine BPD criteria, five of which are required, are exactly the first list. Not the others: they mix in histrionic traits (shallow emotion, overestimated intimacy), narcissistic traits (envy, exploitation) and antisocial traits (reckless disregard for safety).

questions.stem: A 24-year-old reports shoplifting, frequent binge eating and cutting her forearms. How many BPD criteria do these behaviours satisfy?
options: One
Two
Three
None until suicidal intent is established
questions.explain: Why: shoplifting and binge eating are impulsivity in two self-damaging areas (criterion 4); cutting is recurrent self-harm (criterion 5). Self-harm cannot also count toward impulsivity, so the total is two. Not the others: the exclusion rule is what prevents a count of three; self-harm counts regardless of suicidal intent.

questions.stem: During stressful arguments a patient briefly hears her name called and feels she is watching herself from above; between stresses she has no such experiences. Which is the best interpretation?
options: A primary psychotic disorder
BPD criterion 7: transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociation, including brief 'micropsychosis'
Schizotypal personality disorder
Temporal lobe epilepsy
questions.explain: Why: transient, stress-related dissociation (depersonalization) with brief hallucinations is the seventh BPD criterion and does not indicate a primary psychotic disorder. Not the others: the experiences are confined to stress and resolve; schizotypal features are pervasive; nothing suggests seizures.

questions.stem: A family physician starts a 22-year-old with newly diagnosed BPD on an SSRI, quetiapine and lamotrigine at the first visit 'to cover all bases'. What is the main concern?
options: The SSRI dose is too low
Polypharmacy: no medication specifically treats BPD, antipsychotics and mood stabilizers are controversial, and the priority is a psychotherapy referral
Lamotrigine should have been lithium
Medication is contraindicated in all personality disorders
questions.explain: Why: there is no specific drug for BPD; antidepressants are reasonable only for significant comorbid depression or anxiety, antipsychotics and mood stabilizers are best left to psychiatrists, and dangerous or unhelpful polypharmacy is the classic error. Psychotherapy is first line. Not the others: the problem is the number of drugs, not the choice among them; medication is not contraindicated, only non-specific.

questions.stem: Which is not one of the four required modes of dialectical behaviour therapy?
options: Individual therapy
Skills group
Family therapy
Weekly therapist team meeting
questions.explain: Why: the four modes are individual therapy, skills group, between-session phone coaching and the weekly therapist team meeting. Not the others: each is a required mode; family therapy is not.

questions.stem: Which statement is a mind-reading validation?
options: 'So you've been waiting three months.'
'You look like you're feeling humiliated and furious right now.'
'Anyone would be frustrated by that.'
'Given how hard you worked to get here, of course this stings.'
questions.explain: Why: a mind-reading statement is an educated guess at what the patient feels from what they said or how they look. Not the others: the first is reflection, the third normalizing, the fourth makes-sense-in-context.

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department is shouting about a long wait. The resident says, 'I understand, but everyone has to wait.' What went wrong, and what would a better statement be?
options: Nothing; the statement normalizes appropriately

The 'but' cancels the validation and normalizes the system rather than the patient's reaction; better: 'Waiting this long while you're in this much pain is awful, AND I'd like to help make the next while more bearable'
The resident should have offered admission
The resident should have said nothing until the patient calmed down
questions.explain: Why: both-and statements use AND, never but, and validation must address the patient's reaction, not defend the system; the sequence is validate, both-and, offer help, suggest a skill, suggest another. Not the others: admission and silence are not the response to distress in the room.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder presents with an acetaminophen overdose. After medical stabilization the emergency physician asks for a psychiatric admission. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Tell the emergency physician that patients with BPD do not benefit from admission
Admit her because of the overdose
Assess her current mental state and suicidality
Discharge with outpatient follow-up
questions.explain: Why: after stabilization the psychiatric assessment must determine current suicidality and mental state; automatically admitting, discharging, or dismissing admission are all inappropriate without assessment. Not the others: the claim that admission is unhelpful in chronic fluctuating suicidality is a half-truth that becomes an error when stated before assessing.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old burns her forearm with a lighter after an argument and says it 'makes the feelings stop'; she denies wanting to die. What is the best interpretation?
options: A suicide attempt that she is minimizing
Deliberate self-harm serving an affect-avoidance function; believe her account of intent, still assess suicide risk, screen for BPD and other disorders, and refer to therapy
Attention-seeking behaviour requiring no further assessment
Borderline personality disorder, established by the self-harm
questions.explain: Why: self-harm is tissue damage without suicidal intent, usually to escape intense affect, and patients who say so are most likely truthful; it still carries a 37-fold suicide risk and marks emotional dysregulation, so risk assessment, screening and therapy referral follow. Not the others: 'attention-seeking' is an unfair label; self-harm alone never establishes BPD, especially in adolescents.

questions.stem: Compared with the general population, what is the approximate one-year suicide rate after an episode of self-harm?
options: About 3 times higher
About 10 times higher
About 37 times higher
About 100 times higher
questions.explain: Why: 439.1 versus 11.8 per 100,000 person-years, a 37-fold increase, which is why self-harm is never unimportant even when suicidal intent is absent. Not the others: the other multiples are wrong.

questions.stem: While suturing a patient's self-inflicted cuts, a nurse says, 'Sweetheart, you poor thing, we'll take such good care of you.' Why might this be counterproductive, and what tone is recommended?
options: It is too hostile; a warmer tone is needed
Overly soothing responses can reinforce self-harm; a kind, neutral, matter-of-fact and civil tone is recommended
It is fine; warmth always reduces self-harm
It is counterproductive only if the patient has BPD
questions.explain: Why: self-harm is reinforced by internal relief and, for some, by soothing and attention that follow it; the right stance acutely is neutral and matter-of-fact, no less civil than for any patient, and neither infantilizing nor hostile, because contempt is also attention. Not the others: the reinforcement principle applies regardless of diagnosis.

questions.stem: Victoria, assessed after five superficial wrist cuts, has suicidal thoughts she says she will not act on, no current intent, and plans to attend a party this weekend. Which set of actions is correct?
options: Certify and admit; warmly invite her back whenever upset
Discharge, refer to therapy, encourage crisis lines and distress-tolerance skills, and offer psychoeducation to her partner
Discharge with no follow-up because self-harm is not suicidal
Admit for observation and increase her appointment frequency during the crisis
questions.explain: Why: she is low risk (no intent, future-oriented), so admission and certification are unnecessary; therapy is the best intervention, crisis lines validate, skills build independent coping, and an informed partner helps. Not the others: 'come back whenever upset' drives unnecessary visits (the department is for emergencies); no follow-up ignores the dysregulation; escalating visit frequency in a crisis can reinforce crisis behaviour.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with chronic fluctuating passive suicidal ideation and weekly cutting asks to be admitted 'to get away from it all'; there is no plan or intent. Which consideration is most relevant?
options: Admission is mandatory whenever suicidal ideation is present
Admission often does not help chronic fluctuating suicidality and can become an escape behaviour that reinforces suicidal thinking; the decision is usually the psychiatrist's
Weekly cutting alone requires certification
Admission should be offered whenever a patient requests it
questions.explain: Why: hospitalization can interfere with coping in regular life and act as a potent reinforcer of suicidal communication and behaviour in chronic fluctuating ideation, so the call is made by psychiatry after assessment. Not the others: ideation alone does not mandate admission; self-harm is not an admission criterion; patient request is not the deciding factor.

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged after an intentional overdose. Which means-restriction steps apply?
options: Prescribe a three-month supply to avoid running out

Prescribe one to two weeks' supply, ask about stockpiling and adherence, ask about insulin, opiates, bulk acetaminophen and family members' cardiac medications, and address firearms, sharps and balcony access
Advise the family to hide all medications without telling the patient
Means restriction is unnecessary once the patient denies intent
questions.explain: Why: restricting means is one of the best ways to reduce risk, because a person who must wait, think or problem-solve may let the urge pass; the specific measures are small supplies, stockpiling and adherence questions, the named dangerous drugs, and firearms removed or locked with the key inaccessible and ammunition separate. Not the others: large supplies and secrecy are wrong; denial of intent does not remove the need.

questions.stem: A patient in clinic says life has felt so stressful that she has thought about death. Which sequence of questions follows?
options: Ask about protective factors, then about her childhood
Ask about method, means, intent and past attempts, classify acute versus chronic and active versus passive, then ask about reasons for staying alive
Refer to psychiatry without further questions
Ask whether she has a family history of suicide and end there
questions.explain: Why: the suicide screen runs ideation, method, means, intent, past attempts, then acute versus chronic and active (plans) versus passive (thoughts of death), and ends on protective factors; previous attempts are among the most powerful predictors at any age, and asking does not increase risk. Not the others: each stops short of the ladder.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man starts pharmacological treatment for moderate major depressive disorder; his physician explains the drug adjusts brain chemicals involved in mood. Which neurotransmitters are most likely affected?
options: Dopamine and glutamate
GABA and acetylcholine
Norepinephrine and serotonin
Oxytocin and endorphins
questions.explain: Why: most first-line antidepressants target serotonin and/or norepinephrine, monoamines involved in mood regulation. Not the others: glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, oxytocin and endorphins are not standard antidepressant mechanisms; dopamine is the antipsychotic and stimulant axis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old using methamphetamine develops paranoia and auditory hallucinations. Which statement about the mechanism is correct?
options: Amphetamines lower dopamine, producing psychosis
Amphetamines rapidly raise dopamine, and high dopamine produces psychosis; antipsychotics generally lower dopamine
The hallucinations reflect low serotonin
Psychosis arises from excess norepinephrine in the locus coeruleus
questions.explain: Why: high dopamine equals psychosis: an amphetamine raises dopamine rapidly and at high enough levels produces paranoia and hallucinations, and in schizophrenia there is too much dopamine in certain pathways, which antipsychotics lower. Not the others: low dopamine produces amotivation and anhedonia, not psychosis; serotonin and norepinephrine are not the psychosis axis.

questions.stem: Which pairing of mood stabilizer and indication is correct?
options: Valproic acid: bipolar depression
Lamotrigine: acute mania
Lithium: mania, depression and suicide prevention
Carbamazepine: suicide prevention
questions.explain: Why: lithium is listed for mania, depression and suicide prevention, the only agent with that indication. Not the others: valproic acid is for acute mania; lamotrigine is more effective for bipolar depression; carbamazepine is listed alongside lamotrigine without a suicide-prevention claim.

questions.stem: A musician with disabling tremor and palpitations only before performances asks for medication. Which agent is listed for this indication, and what caution applies to benzodiazepines?
options: Lorazepam long term; no caution
Propranolol for performance anxiety; benzodiazepines are short-term only because of dependence
Haloperidol; benzodiazepines cause psychosis
Clozapine; benzodiazepines are first line
questions.explain: Why: propranolol, a beta-blocker, is listed for performance anxiety and its physical symptoms; benzodiazepines such as lorazepam and clonazepam are for short-term use only because of dependence, and SSRIs or SNRIs are the antidepressant options for anxiety disorders. Not the others: antipsychotics are not anxiety agents.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with severe major depression has not responded to multiple medications, psychotherapies and psychedelic therapy. He is preparing for a psychiatric treatment that requires general anaesthesia. Which treatment is this, and what is its place?
options: Deep brain stimulation, first line for depression
Electroconvulsive therapy, the most effective antidepressant treatment, reserved for resistant cases
Transcranial magnetic stimulation, requiring anaesthesia
Ketamine infusion under anaesthesia
questions.explain: Why: ECT induces a seizure under general anaesthesia with muscle relaxants, typically 8 to 12 treatments three times a week, and is the most effective antidepressant treatment while being reserved for resistant cases. Not the others: DBS electrode placement can be done awake because the brain has no pain receptors, and neither DBS nor rTMS is first line; ketamine does not require general anaesthesia.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with low mood, anhedonia and early-morning waking has had minimal improvement after three months of psychotherapy and is hesitant about medication because of side-effect concerns. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Recommend neurostimulation because therapy has failed
Encourage continued psychotherapy unchanged
Refer to inpatient psychiatry to start medication
Explore her concerns about pharmacological options
questions.explain: Why: when a patient is hesitant, the clinician explores the concerns and provides information, supporting shared decision-making. Not the others: neurostimulation and inpatient care are premature escalation or coercion; unchanged therapy ignores the inadequate response.

questions.stem: Which statement about the mechanism and evidence for psychedelic therapy is correct?
options: Psychedelics are dopamine antagonists that suppress neuroplasticity

Psychedelics are 5-HT2A agonists that disrupt the default mode network, which is hyperactive in depression and experienced as rumination, and increase neuroplasticity and BDNF; MDMA-assisted therapy left 67% of PTSD patients no longer meeting criteria at 2 months versus 32% on placebo
Ketamine is a classical psychedelic acting at 5-HT2A
Psilocybin has no evidence in depression
questions.explain: Why: the mechanism is 5-HT2A agonism disrupting the ruminating default mode network with increased neuroplasticity and BDNF; the MDMA phase 3 figures are 67% versus 32%, and psilocybin has trial evidence in depression, end-of-life anxiety and alcohol use disorder. Not the others: ketamine is pharmacologically distinct, an NMDA antagonist; dopamine antagonism describes antipsychotics.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old with alcohol use disorder is admitted for withdrawal and mentions he takes omega-3 supplements for his mood without having told his doctor. Which statements are correct?
options: Naltrexone treats the withdrawal; omega-3 use is rare
Diazepam with thiamine covers the withdrawal, naltrexone and acamprosate treat craving afterward, and 30 to 50% of psychiatric patients use complementary medicine, often without telling clinicians
Acamprosate prevents seizures; complementary medicine has no evidence
Withdrawal needs no medication; omega-3 replaces antidepressants
questions.explain: Why: withdrawal from a CNS depressant can cause seizures, delirium tremens and death and is covered with diazepam and thiamine; naltrexone and acamprosate are anticraving agents, a different problem; and 30 to 50% of psychiatric patients use CAM, with omega-3 having reasonable evidence in mild depression. Not the others: each confuses withdrawal cover with craving management or dismisses CAM.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man starts therapy for persistent insecurity and conflict in relationships; the sessions focus on his childhood and early relationships. Which approach is this?
options: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Dialectical behaviour therapy
Psychodynamic psychotherapy
Acceptance and commitment therapy
questions.explain: Why: the idea that unconscious conflicts and early relationships shape current patterns, explored through the therapeutic relationship, defences and transference, is psychodynamic; CBT does not go back into childhood. Not the others: CBT tracks and tests thoughts; DBT teaches skills; ACT works on acceptance and values.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman in therapy for depression has thoughts such as 'I can't do anything right, I always mess things up'; her therapist tracks her thoughts and evaluates their accuracy using worksheets. Which approach is this, and which distortion is illustrated?
options: Psychodynamic; projection
Cognitive behavioural therapy; over-generalizing
DBT; mental filter
ACT; denial
questions.explain: Why: thought records and testing accuracy are cognitive restructuring, the core of CBT; 'I always mess things up' draws a sweeping rule from events, over-generalizing. Not the others: the technique is not exploratory, skills-based or acceptance-based, and projection and denial are defences, not distortions.

questions.stem: A clerk criticized harshly by an attending says nothing at work, then goes home and snaps at her partner. Which defence mechanism is this?
options: Projection
Sublimation
Displacement
Regression
questions.explain: Why: displacement redirects an emotion to a safer target. Not the others: projection attributes one's own feeling to another; sublimation channels the impulse into an acceptable outlet such as a long run; regression reverts to earlier behaviour.

questions.stem: A student thinks, 'If I fail this exam I'll be expelled, then I won't be able to pay rent, then I'll be homeless.' Which cognitive distortion is this?
options: Mental filter
Disqualifying the positive
Magnification (catastrophizing)
Mind reading
questions.explain: Why: blowing an event out of proportion into a chain of escalating disasters is catastrophizing, the magnification half of magnification and minimization; the chain is the giveaway. Not the others: mental filter attends only to negative evidence; disqualifying the positive discounts good things; mind reading assumes what others think.

questions.stem: A patient asks why a slow exhale calms her. Which chain is correct?
options: Exhaling raises blood pressure, which stimulates the amygdala

A slow exhale lowers intrathoracic pressure and alters venous return, reducing heart rate and blood pressure; the brainstem relays this to limbic structures as 'all is well', and the prefrontal cortex comes back online so cognitive techniques work
Exhaling increases sympathetic tone, which suppresses rumination
Breathing has only a placebo effect
questions.explain: Why: anxiety is sympathetic overdrive; the physiological sigh (two nasal inhales, one long exhale of at least ten seconds) settles the body first, then the thinking; three repetitions can drop heart rate 15 to 20 beats per minute, enough that syncope has occurred. Not the others: each reverses the physiology.

questions.stem: Why does holding an ice pack to the face or neck help an overwhelmed patient?
options: Cold is distracting only
It triggers the bradycardic diving reflex, lowering heart rate, which signals the limbic system that the danger is over; it is the T of DBT's TIPP skills
Cold raises blood pressure, improving alertness
It has no physiological basis
questions.explain: Why: TIPP (temperature, intense exercise, progressive muscle relaxation, paced breathing) tips body chemistry from sympathetic to parasympathetic, and each letter lowers heart rate; temperature works through the diving reflex. Not the others: the effect is physiological and lowers, not raises, arousal.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with schizophrenia lives alone, is inconsistent with follow-up, has missed his last two prescriptions, and recently ran out of food and electricity. Which social intervention is most likely to improve his outcomes?
options: More frequent clinic appointments
