The heterogeneity problem has a number attached: with five of nine required, the possible symptom combinations run to over 250, which is why two patients with the same label can need different plans.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Adversity does not exclude depression; extent of response and loss of normative function decide. Libido is an early anhedonia probe.
  • Impairment makes a disorder, not the stressor, the history or the duration on its own.
  • Expectable response is in the definition of disorder, not in the depression criteria; adjustment disorder is the alternative.
  • Categorical = discrete, qualitative, DSM-5-TR and ICD-11. Dimensional = continuum, quantitative, HiTOP and RDoC, research only.
  • Panic disorder: 4 of 13, minutes to peak, one month of worry or behaviour change. MDE: 5 of 9, two weeks, one of them depressed mood or anhedonia.
  • Four limitations by name: arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity, subthreshold illness.
  • DSM-5-TR is APA; ICD-11 is WHO.
  • A diagnosis says what; a formulation says why now.
A mental disorder is a clinically significant, impairing disturbance of cognition, emotion or behaviour arising from dysfunction, not an expected response to a stressor. The categorical system that operationalizes this, built on DSM-III's rules, gives reliable, discrete diagnoses and four known failures: arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity and subthreshold illness. The dimensional alternative treats disorder as the extreme of normally distributed traits and can generate a plan where the categories generate nothing.

guides.title: Week 40 · 4 Why People Become Ill: Vulnerability, Stress and Early Experience
guides.html:
Byrne L1 · PD Module 2 · L2 formulation · CBL 40 · WFQ

Why People Become Ill: Vulnerability, Stress and Early Experience

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The diathesis-stress equation and its three columns, the biological, social and attachment sources of vulnerability, what protects, and how the same logic fills the predisposing row for the depressed 25-year-old, Victoria and Stanley.

The equation

Mental illness = predisposition (diathesis) + stressor. Diathesis is a sliding scale, not a binary switch: everyone carries some risk, set by their biological, psychological and social history, and the same stressor crosses the threshold in a person with high predisposition but not in a person with low predisposition. A person with high diathesis needs very little stress to develop symptoms; a person with low diathesis may weather major stress and stay well. On the diagram, predisposition runs along the x-axis, stress up the y-axis, and a diagonal line divides "disorder not manifested" from "disorder manifested": any point above and to the right of the line manifests, and the line is a threshold across both axes, not a point on either.

The stressor side is "acute events and chronic strains": bereavement, job loss, divorce, academic pressure, physical illness, substance use, chronic discrimination. The predisposition side splits three ways, biological, psychological, social/environmental, which is the biopsychosocial model of George Engel (1977), to which the course always adds culture.

The same principle applies to borderline personality disorder under another name. On the bell curve of emotional reactivity, Person A, about two standard deviations above the mean, develops BPD only after severe invalidation such as trauma; Person B, at the extreme tail, develops it with subtle invalidation. The more biological vulnerability, the less environmental insult is needed, and vice versa. Dandelion children (easy temperament) grow in most environments and need a large insult to fail; orchid children (spirited, intense) flourish in the right environment and wither in the wrong one.

Two people in the same household do not share a diathesis or a stressor. Siblings are not genetic copies, and what happened to each at school and at recess differed; when one sibling is ill and the other is well, the explanation is that diathesis-stress interactions vary between individuals. The risk factors the model names are what a psychiatric interview looks for, because they are what treatment addresses.

Where vulnerability sits in the formulation

The three columns of the diathesis (bio, psycho, social) become the columns of the 4 P's formulation grid, and vulnerability is its first row. Predisposing factors are "areas of vulnerability that increase the risk for the presenting problem": genetics, life events, temperament, attachment insecurities, ACEs. The stressor of the equation becomes the precipitating row; what keeps the problem going (avoidance in panic disorder, poor glucose control) is perpetuating; and strengths that counteract the first three are protective. The formulation grid is the diathesis-stress model with time added. The CBL case adds a fourth column, cultural, otherwise folded into social.

Predisposing rowBiologicalPsychologicalSocial / cultural
Lecture case: 25-year-old man, depression after a breakupFamily history of depression; type 1 diabetesInsecure attachment, difficulties with trust (mother depressed and often hospitalized)Parents divorced at 7; unavailable parent
Victoria, 18, self-harm (PD module)Emotionally intense temperament: colic, inconsolable crying, tantrumsLearned that her inner experience "must be wrong"Invalidating fit: mother reassured her, called her overreacting, felt helpless and confused
Stanley, refugee claimant (CBL 40)No clear biological vulnerability identifiedLongstanding fear from concealing his sexualityLongstanding threat of persecution for same-sex relationships; cultural context of that persecution

Biological vulnerability

FactorDetail
HeritabilityAunts and uncles with anxiety make anxiety more likely. BPD carries a family history of substance use (especially alcohol), anger problems and other impulsive behaviour.
TemperamentInnate traits influencing early interaction with the world: present from infancy, biologically based, foundational to personality, and distinct from learned behaviour and from attachment. A relaxed temperament lowers risk; a neurotic one raises it. Temperament is established in the first few years of life and probably genetic, and emotional reactivity is normally distributed (mean about 100, SD about 13): extreme sensitivity is a tail position, not an illness. The interview asks about it in the early-childhood block of the personal history.
The emotionally sensitive temperament (BPD)Three features: high sensitivity (low threshold, easily triggered), emotional intensity, and slow return to baseline. Being sensitive or intense is not a problem in itself.
ImpulsivityA separate inherited trait, heritability 20 to 62%, one of the most heritable personality traits; it is what turns the drive to escape emotional pain into impulsive behaviour.
EpigeneticsDNA methylation from early life stress can change how genes are expressed and raise long-term risk (this literature is debated).
Neurodevelopmental abnormalities"Things that happen to you in childhood" acting on brain development.
Methylation is epigenetic; the serotonin transporter short allele is not. The short versus long allele of the serotonin transporter gene conferring higher risk is an inherited sequence variant, not an epigenetic change. Keep the two apart: methylation = epigenetic change from experience; short allele = heritability.

Social and environmental vulnerability

Early adversity: the ACE study

Early adversity is an important risk factor for later physical and mental illness. In 1995 a Kaiser-CDC team mailed a retrospective questionnaire to over 17,000 insured adults after routine check-ups, tallied childhood adversities (each "yes" = 1 point = the ACE score), and then followed their medical records prospectively. The ten questions, all "before your 18th birthday": not enough to eat, dirty clothes or no one to protect you; losing a parent to divorce, abandonment or death; living with someone depressed, mentally ill or suicidal; living with someone with a drinking or drug problem; adults in the home hitting or threatening each other; living with someone who went to prison; being sworn at, insulted or put down; being hit, beaten or kicked; feeling no one in the family loved you; unwanted sexual contact.

FindingFigure
Adults with at least one ACEAbout 64%
Adults with four or moreAbout 12%
Four or more ACEs: major depressionAbout 4.4 times
Four or more ACEs: anxiety disordersAbout 3.7 times
Four or more ACEs: drug-use disorderOver 10 times
Four or more ACEs: suicide attemptUp to 12 times
Four or more ACEs: ischemic heart disease, COPD, cancer, adult obesityAbout 2.2, 3.9, 1.9 and 1.5 to 2 times; diabetes also raised

The relationship is dose-response: the higher the score, the worse the outcomes, physical as much as mental. The questionnaire is a clinical instrument, offered as an invitation rather than a classroom exercise.

The invalidating environment

At the level of the family, the environmental half of vulnerability is the invalidating environment. Validation is showing you understand someone's experience; invalidation is not understanding it, shown by dismissing, ignoring, not responding, being confused, criticizing. Not everyone who is emotionally intense develops BPD: the traits are risk factors, not causes on their own. A sensitive child experiences emotions as overwhelming, confusing and painful, and even well-intentioned parents find it hard to stay attuned; feeling helpless and frustrated, they lose empathy and respond by giving up, turning away or criticizing. That is the "poor fit".

  • Invalidating environments named: not understanding why the child reacts; getting angry at the child for being emotional; maternal separation for about 4 months before age 5; neglect and all forms of abuse. Trauma is a severe form of invalidation: childhood sexual abuse is 10 to 20% in the general population and 40 to 70% in inpatient BPD samples.
  • Social risk factors for BPD: maternal separation, neglect, lack of caregiver attunement, reinforcement of emotional outbursts, dismissal of a child's emotions, needs or identity, trauma. Not risk factors: a caregiver suggesting healthy coping strategies, being able to talk about emotions, and invalidation followed by talking about it and repairing.
  • What repeated invalidation does to an intense child: emotions intensify, the sense of self becomes confused, emotions become hard to interpret (alexithymia), and they become so overwhelming that the person looks for ways to escape. With inherited impulsivity, escape becomes alcohol and drugs, self-harm or suicide attempts, binge eating, overspending, gambling, shoplifting.
  • Example: a child cries when her grandparents leave and is told "stop that crying or I'll give you something to cry about"; she learns that her inner experience must be wrong.

The stressor list's chronic discrimination is the adult form of the same insult, and it is Stanley's predisposing social factor: years of concealment under threat of persecution, before any single precipitating event.

Well-meant reassurance is invalidation. Victoria's mother telling her "things aren't so bad" and that she was overreacting is a social risk factor, not support. And reinforcing outbursts with attention is a risk factor while repair after invalidation is protective; some invalidation is inevitable and is not the problem.

Psychological vulnerability: attachment

Insecure attachment and adverse early caregiving are associated with increased risk of psychopathology across diagnostic categories. John Bowlby (1958 to 1980s): the human infant is biologically wired to seek proximity to a caregiver who provides food and protection. Harlow's rhesus monkeys (1950s to 1960s): raised with a wire surrogate that gave milk and a cloth surrogate that gave none, the infants spent most of their time on the cloth mother, returning to the wire mother only to feed. Contact comfort, not feeding, drives attachment; the cloth mother is the secure base.

The evolutionary argument for why humans are wired this way: a large brain and bipedal hips cannot both be had with a fully developed newborn, so humans are born very immature, and an infant whose parents did not care for it died. Seeking closeness, security and safety is survival machinery. Securely attached children feel safe to explore because they know there is a base to return to; they trust more, connect to others and do better in life. Insecurely attached children are afraid to explore, mistrust others, lack social skills and struggle to form relationships. Two thirds of people are securely attached; one third are insecure, in three subtypes.

CaregivingAttachmentDevelopmental cascadeClinical phenotypes often seen
Prolonged inconsistent or intrusive careAnxiousHypervigilance to rejection, chronic worryGeneralized anxiety disorder, panic, somatic symptom disorder
Emotionally unavailable or rejecting careAvoidantDeactivation, alexithymia, compulsive self-sufficiencySubstance misuse, restricting eating disorders, schizoid traits
Maltreatment or a frightening caregiverDisorganizedFragmented self-concept, dissociation, affect labilityBorderline personality disorder, complex PTSD, self-harm

The bottom row is the biosocial theory of BPD from the attachment side: maltreatment and invalidation, a fragmented sense of self, affect lability and self-harm are the same cascade as invalidation, confused sense of self, alexithymia and escape. Two in-lecture polls apply the table. A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder whose parents never showed affection, who finds it hard to trust and wants to handle problems alone, is avoidant; an anxiously attached person would be texting friends constantly for reassurance. A 5-year-old who hides behind furniture when upset and rarely seeks comfort, with a caregiver who ignores her crying, is showing an adaptation, not a deficit: children learn to hide the feeling that makes the parent angrier, because for an infant abandonment is death.

Protective factors and resilience

  • Not all high-ACE children develop illness. Each additional positive childhood experience reduces adult depression risk by 26%; positive experiences can counter early adversity.
  • The "good enough" parent (Winnicott): ordinary, non-ideal care is enough for healthy development; perfection is unnecessary and unrealistic. Add optimal frustration: some adversity or challenge in childhood is actively necessary to develop resilience. "Shield the child from all adversity" is therefore not a protective factor.
  • In the family: invalidation followed by repair; being able to talk about emotions; a caregiver suggesting healthy coping strategies. Some invalidation is a normal part of life, and everyone develops best with an optimal amount of it.
  • In the grid: the protective row for Stanley reads future orientation, help-seeking, perseverance, a supportive cousin, employment and education; for the depressed 25-year-old, a previous good response to fluoxetine and the capacity to attend clinic.

Why the brain is vulnerable at all

Traits that look maladaptive today were possibly adaptive in ancestral environments; evolution selects for reproductive fitness, not for happiness or health; and some emotional responses are normally adaptive systems that have become excessive, persistent or contextually mismatched. Anxiety once increased survival by avoiding predators; modern stressors such as academic pressure activate the same systems without any physical threat, and when the response becomes dysregulated the result is an anxiety disorder. A line to use with patients: "Your brain didn't evolve to keep you happy or even at peace. This is a survival machine." Worry, rumination and constant problem-solving were selected for, and each trait sits on a spectrum where some people cross into the unhelpful range. A 26-year-old with excessive, hard-to-control fear of being evaluated has an evolved threat-detection and social-evaluation system that was useful ancestrally and is now mismatched.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Temperament, attachment, learned behaviour, personality disorder are four different things: innate traits from infancy; the bond with a caregiver; a pattern developed through experience; enduring traits that deviate from social norms.
  • Diathesis is a scale. "Same house, different outcome" is explained by varying diathesis-stress interactions, not by one sibling being weaker.
  • Person A needed more. The less sensitive person on the curve needed trauma-level invalidation; the very sensitive one needed only subtle invalidation.
  • 64% and 12%; 4.4, 3.7, over 10, up to 12. ACE prevalence and the four mental-health risk multipliers at four or more ACEs.
  • Contact comfort, not milk, is what Harlow's monkeys chose.
  • Avoidant pairs with substance misuse; disorganized with BPD, complex PTSD and self-harm; anxious with GAD and panic.
  • Reassurance can invalidate; repair protects; reinforcing outbursts is a risk factor.
  • Good enough, not perfect, and some frustration is required.
  • A child hiding distress is adapting to a rejecting caregiver, not showing a deficit.
Illness appears when a person's predisposition and their stress together cross a threshold. Predisposition is built from heritability, temperament and impulsivity; from early adversity, whether counted as ACEs or lived as an invalidating family or chronic persecution; and from the attachment pattern that early caregiving produced. Positive experiences, good-enough care with some frustration, and repair pull the threshold back. The same three columns and the same logic fill the predisposing row of every formulation, for the depressed 25-year-old, for Victoria, and for Stanley.

guides.title: Week 40 · 5 The Psychiatric Interview: Process, Rapport and the Difficult Encounter
guides.html:
Byrne L2 · CS2 guide · L1 · WFQ · CBL 40

The Psychiatric Interview: Process, Rapport and the Difficult Encounter

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Goals and safety, the opening and confidentiality, alliance and observable empathy, the process checklist, resistance, transference and countertransference, and engaging the hesitant or culturally distant patient, with Stanley as the case.

The same assessment as the rest of medicine

Psychiatry uses the same approach as every other medical assessment: identifying data, chief complaint, history of present illness, past history, examination. What differs is the depth of the personal and developmental history, a routine safety screen, and the mental status examination standing in for the physical examination. Interviewing is a technique to be acquired, not a talent: it needs interest, attention, willingness to practise and the gradual accretion of experience, no more and no less than suturing or auscultation. Techniques break into observable behavioural steps, which is why the course uses standardized checklists for self-evaluation and peer feedback. An emergency psychiatric interview can take seven minutes; an outpatient assessment can take more than an hour.

The interview has four goals: understand the concern, build an alliance, assess diagnosis and safety, develop a shared plan. Alliance matters more here than elsewhere because patients are asked to share very difficult things, and they share them when they trust the interviewer. Safety is asked about at every psychiatric interview: suicidal thoughts, violent thoughts toward others, driving safety, child safety.

Before beginning: safety for both people

  • In hospital or the emergency room other staff or security may be present and the door is left ajar; the interviewer keeps a clear exit path and sits closest to the door.
  • A person with psychosis carries about twice the general population's risk of violence. Clerks are not sent alone to agitated patients. If a patient becomes agitated, stop the interview, de-escalate and seek help.
  • Attend to the patient's comfort throughout: tissues, water, a comfortable seat, while they describe very difficult things.

Opening the interview

Three openers: introduce yourself; review the nature of the interaction and the time available; review the limits of confidentiality. The confidentiality statement is given before anything is disclosed, every time: everything discussed is confidential, with the exceptions the law places on all doctors around safety, a threat to someone's life, concern about the care of a child, and driving safety. A patient in the emergency department with cocaine use disorder who then describes driving impaired has been warned, and the report to the ministry follows. The warning has to come before the disclosure, not after.

The process checklist adds the student-specific steps: greet the patient and obtain their name; give your name and the fact that you are a medical student; ask the patient's understanding of the reason for the interview and explain it if they do not know; say how much time is available; then start with open questions so the patient tells the story in their own words.

Alliance and empathy

For an alliance the patient must feel the evaluation is a joint effort, that the physician is genuinely interested, and that the physician cares. Four behaviours: listen without interrupting, acknowledge distress, explain questions, agree on priorities. Talk like a human being, not a clinically distant robot; patients about to describe trauma or childhood need to feel the interviewer cares.

Empathy is understanding what the patient is thinking and feeling, putting oneself in the patient's place while maintaining objectivity. Verbally: "that must have been very difficult for you." Nonverbally: raised eyebrows, leaning toward the patient, nodding, passing a tissue. The objectivity clause guards against over-identification; the aim is to feel enough that empathic statements come naturally without losing the clinician's role. When a mother describes the death of one of her twins in a collision, the response is "I'm so sorry that happened to you, that's horrible", not a grief checklist typed into a screen.

Four qualities of empathy (Wiseman)
Perspective taking (recognizing another's perspective as their truth) · staying out of judgement · recognizing emotion in others · communicating that recognition. Empathy fuels connection; sympathy drives disconnection. Empathy climbs into the hole ("I know what it's like down here, and you're not alone"); sympathy calls down from the top. Rarely, if ever, does an empathic response begin with "at least." "I had a miscarriage" answered with "at least you know you can get pregnant" is the silver-lining failure; "I don't even know what to say, I'm just so glad you told me" is the alternative. Rarely does a response make something better; connection does.

In the clinical-skills course empathy is behavioural and observable: paying attention is the first step, showing that you are paying attention is the second. The opening behaviours demonstrate that the interviewer is attending to this patient in particular, not to a routine specimen already figured out. A medical student's role, before they can solve anything, is to gather the history and hold the space: to sit with someone's suffering without rushing to fix it. Empathy takes a little more vulnerability than sympathy.

Running the interview: the process

The core loop is stop, look and listen: slow down and think; look and notice; listen; prompt for more; probe for clarification; repeat. Do not rush to talk, ask or explain: it is more efficient to let a patient disclose and explain than to poke with question after question, which signals that asking is what the interviewer wants to do rather than listening. A clinical interview should not feel like an interrogation; a patient who feels misunderstood, judged or patronized clams up. Never interview from a checklist, because it sounds like an agenda; use the checklist at the end to make sense of what was seen and heard.

PhaseSteps
Eliciting the spontaneous accountListen attentively; allow the patient to complete statements without interruption; leave space to think without filling the silence too quickly; after the chief complaint, ask whether there is anything more or anything else; repeat or paraphrase to prompt; notice and respond to hints at unexplored problems and to non-verbal clues (body language, tone, facial expression, affect) that reinforce, supplement or contradict what is said, and explore their meaning; encourage feelings and thoughts.
Getting the information neededContinue with open questions while productive; move from open to closed to resolve ambiguities; encourage precision, especially where it can be dated or quantified; ask the patient to explain their own technical or obscure words; use concise single questions, never stacked; avoid leading questions; avoid jargon; show calm interest in emotionally loaded material (suicide, domestic abuse, money, sex, death and dying) and raise such topics yourself when there are clues.
Managing timeKeep track of time; avoid repetition; keep flexibly on task with a logic clear to the patient too; allow full responses but redirect tactfully when the information is unnecessary or repetitious.
ClosingDo not wait until the end to raise sensitive topics; summarize the main points briefly; thank the patient.
Language. Replace words with a negative connotation: "die by suicide" or "complete suicide", not "commit suicide"; "drug use", not "drug abuse". And the items most often omitted are the ones in the middle of the interview, not the greeting: asking the patient's understanding of the reason, stating the time available, allowing statements to finish, tolerating silence, noticing hints, moving from open to closed, avoiding stacked and leading questions, raising loaded topics, keeping time, summarizing.

Feedback guides score three global qualities by definition. Self-assurance: appears confident, open and relaxed; no confusion, hesitancy, shyness or embarrassment. Empathy: shows by questions and responses an understanding of the nature of the illness, its effect on the patient's life, and how the patient perceives the problem. Warmth: by smiling, sitting attentively and facilitating responses, shows regard and concern. Key phrases from the interview template: "Help me to understand", "Let's work together to", "You're doing well, let's keep going", "In the interest of time, I may ask questions more quickly", "I apologize if I interrupt you", "What you're talking about is important." End the interview by conveying your understanding of the concerns, validation, and where appropriate hope.

Difficult moments

SituationResponse
Question about your qualifications ("are you old enough to be my doctor?")Answer directly and truthfully.
Sarcastic commentAddress the underlying issue: "Are you worried I won't be able to help you? I'll be reviewing everything with the senior resident."
Surface-level personal question ("Do you watch football?")Answer directly and briefly, without elaboration, then return to the patient.
Persistent pushing"Let's keep this assessment about you. Tell me again, how is your mood?"

The pattern: answer briefly and factually, redirect, and treat a hostile question as data about the patient rather than an attack.

Resistance

Resistances are the processes, conscious or unconscious, that interfere with the therapeutic objectives of treatment. A patient comes for help but avoids emotionally difficult material: asked gently about past relationships, "I don't see how that's relevant; let's just talk about my medications. You're just a student." A previously cooperative 60-year-old who suddenly says "that's none of your business" when asked about her childhood is resisting. Resistance is not simply rolled with. The tool is the process comment: instead of a content question ("How do you feel?"), a comment on what is happening in the interview itself, "I notice when I ask about your relationships you look at the ground; what's going on there?" Acting out is different: the material is discharged into unrelated behaviour, starting to sing or do something else, rather than blocked.

Transference

The patient unconsciously transfers feelings and behaviour from past relationships, often childhood, onto the clinician, usually an authority figure; the patient may be angry, demanding or obsequious because of former patterns. A clerk's patient who is very deferential, keeps calling the student "doctor" despite correction, seeks constant reassurance about decisions, and mentions never feeling supported by his father is showing transference; so is a 58-year-old woman with severe depression who becomes unusually deferential and reassurance-seeking and later reveals abandonment by paternal figures. Naming it prevents misunderstanding the behaviour and reacting personally. The tell is a funny feeling of "what is going on here?"

Countertransference

The clinician unconsciously reacts to a patient based on their own history and the current interaction. Signs: feeling unusually angry, protective or emotional with a patient; dreading or overly looking forward to seeing someone; feeling bored, sleepy or distracted; acting out of character, too distant or too involved. A clerk who feels an overwhelming urge to comfort a tearful patient after a suicide attempt, becomes overly emotional, and later realizes the patient resembles a cousin with depression; a clerk who becomes irritated and dismissive with a patient who reminds her of a critical older sibling. Management: notice your reactions; reflect or debrief with a supervisor or peer; keep boundaries; use it as a learning tool. The signal is a reaction different from your usual, not any particular emotion, and countertransference is normal. Used well it deepens understanding: a patient who leaves an experienced clinician doubting herself after one meeting is having that effect on everyone in his life.

Transference = the patient's past imported onto the clinician. Countertransference = the clinician's own reaction. Identification = loss of objectivity. Therapeutic alliance = the collaborative clinical relationship. The discriminator is always whose past relationship is being imported.

Culture, hesitancy and the refugee patient

Clinicians misread culturally normative behaviour as pathology (spiritual experiences, voices during prayer, mistaken for psychosis) and interpret behaviour differently across racial groups: Black patients in North America are more likely to receive a schizophrenia diagnosis than a mood-disorder diagnosis with similar symptom profiles. Six strategies against bias: cultural humility (ongoing self-reflection); structured tools such as the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview; elicit the patient's perspective ("What does this experience mean to you?"); collaborate with interpreters, cultural liaisons or community healers, as with Indigenous healers on an inpatient unit; education in local idioms of distress and culture-bound syndromes; avoid assumptions about pathology versus accepted practice. A refugee with hypervigilance, nightmares and avoidance who attributes his distress to ancestral spirits is engaged by exploring his explanatory model of illness and booking follow-up, not by challenging his beliefs, referring him elsewhere, or diagnosing and reassuring. Use trained interpreters, never family.

The same principle governs medication hesitancy: a woman with persistent depression who has not improved after three months of psychotherapy and fears side effects is met by exploring her concerns and providing information, shared decision-making, not by escalation to neurostimulation or inpatient admission. The interview's content items include the patient's own opinion about the nature and cause of the problem and their hopes for treatment; a plan must be feasible.

Stanley, a refugee claimant with trauma, is the week's case. Before meeting him: a possible language barrier, trauma-informed care, and cultural differences without assumptions. When he seems closed off: reassurance, confidentiality, a safe environment, attention to body language, tone and attitude. When he discloses an extremely traumatic past: thank him for sharing and trusting you; acknowledge and validate; "I'm very sorry. You went through something terrifying, and you lost your mother in the middle of it. Thank you for trusting me enough to tell me. How are you feeling talking about this now? Is there anything you need from me right now before we continue?" History-taking with a refugee still asks about symptoms the same way, a full history of present illness, and adds the facts of his refugee status: support networks, health coverage, the stage of the claim and hearing, legal representation, work status, family here and abroad, and safety if returned.

The first clinical-skills session: process lessons

The Week 40 session put the checklist to work on a real patient and a standardized patient, and its lessons were about process rather than content.

  • Feel comfortable being useless in the moment. When a patient mentions a medication the student does not know, the useful response is to say so and gather: "I don't know that medication. How do you spell it? When do you take it, and how much? I'm going to review it with my supervisor." Forfeiting ignorance at the outset yields better information and sounds better to the supervisor than improvised advice.
  • The standardized-patient encounter simulates a medical student working with a supervisor, not a psychiatrist in independent practice. Saying so ("I'm the medical student working with the psychiatrist; I'll take down your concerns and we'll come back to you") frees the interviewer to not know things.
  • Ground the interview in demographics first when nothing is known about the patient: who they live with, what they do, how they support themselves. With real patients, read the chart first, because someone who has told their story to thirteen people is exhausted and annoyed by a fourteenth who knows nothing.
  • When something important surfaces mid-thread, signpost or summarize and pivot. "That seems important; do you mind if we come back to it once I finish this?" keeps the structure; a one-sentence summary of what has been heard is a graceful way to change direction, and it reads as skill rather than rescue.
  • One question at a time. A follow-up stacked on the first before the patient answers narrows the reply; open questions give the patient room, which patients notice and value.
  • Sensitive questions asked late are still worth asking. A clumsy late question about suicidality is better than a smooth omission; looping back is part of learning.
  • In the impression, name what was missed. "I did not establish prior psychiatric history or substance use, and I would go back for both" is what a supervisor wants to hear; there is almost always another chance to ask, to get collateral, or to bring the patient back.
  • How broad to screen depends on confidence in the working diagnosis. Two quick screens serve when the story is low-risk: "Has there ever been a time when you saw or heard things other people could not explain?" and "Has there ever been a time when you could not sleep at all and had tons of energy?" Anyone who is depressed is screened for mania, because most of the time spent ill in bipolar disorder is spent depressed, and for psychotic depression when the episode is severe.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Admit what you do not know, gather, and review with the supervisor; the SP encounter is a student-with-supervisor simulation.
  • Signpost or summarize to pivot; one question at a time; name what was missed in the impression.
  • Four goals: concern, alliance, diagnosis and safety, shared plan. Four safety items: suicide, violence, driving, children. Three confidentiality exceptions: threat to life, child safety, driving.
  • Empathy keeps objectivity; sympathy stays outside the hole; "at least" is never empathic.
  • Resistance blocks; acting out discharges; the process comment is the response.
  • Transference is the patient's; countertransference is the clinician's; a change from the clinician's own baseline is the clue.
  • Explore the explanatory model; explore medication concerns; both are engagement, not escalation.
  • Sensitive topics go in the middle, not the end; language is "die by suicide" and "drug use".
  • Interview technique is assessed in every OSCE station, not only psychiatry stations.
The psychiatric interview follows medicine's ordinary structure with three additions: safety for both people, an alliance built on observable empathy, and attention to what happens in the room, resistance, transference and the clinician's own reactions. Cultural engagement and shared decision-making are the same skill applied to belief and to treatment: ask what the patient thinks is happening, and what they hope for, before doing anything else.

guides.title: Week 40 · 6 The Psychiatric History and the Symptom Screens
guides.html:
Byrne L2 · CS2 guide · CBL 40

The Psychiatric History and the Symptom Screens

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The fifteen headings and the five-item minimum, identifying data and the HPI, MSIGECAPS and GST PAID, hallucinations and delusions with their likely causes, the anxiety screen, substances and lethal withdrawal, the rest of the history, and risk assessment.

The structure

The psychiatric history has the same skeleton as any medical history, in fifteen headings: identifying data; chief complaint and reason for referral; history of present illness; review of systems; risk assessment; substance use history; past psychiatric history; past medical history; medications; allergies; family history; developmental and social history; mental status examination; physical examination; collateral. The order of the written presentation is not the order of information-gathering. At a minimum the interview must establish five things: why the patient is here (problems and expectations); the development and course of the problems including prior illness and treatment; severity, meaning effect on day-to-day function and on safety; factors plausibly involved in causation; and factors that affect management and prognosis. The course of the sickness is discovered entirely from the history, and cross-sectional findings do not carry the same significance as longitudinal ones.

Identifying data and the chief complaint

Psychiatry is unusually thorough with identifying data because it contextualizes the history of present illness and feeds the social column of the formulation: full name, age, sex, gender identity and pronouns; ethnicity and cultural background; relationship status, gender of partner, children; occupation, education, source of income; living situation (alone, with family, shelter); referral source (self, emergency, family, physician, court); inpatient or outpatient, voluntary or involuntary; date and setting. The chief complaint is the main reason for presenting, in the patient's own words, brief and focused: "What has brought you in today?" "Please tell me about the concerns you've had recently." Record the symptom and its duration.

History of present illness

ElementDetail
Onset, duration, progressionIntensity; fluctuation with the day, the reproductive cycle and the season; "describe for me what that's like; how do you experience it?"
Context: precipitating stressorsRelationship, work, trauma, losses, changes; social determinants
Symptom clustersMood, anxiety, psychosis, sleep, appetite, cognition
Functional impactActivities of daily living and instrumental activities; personal care and survival; occupational, academic, social, family and sexual functioning
SafetySuicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, intent, behaviour; driving and child safety
Insight, coping, help-seekingSupports, treatments tried, coping strategies; the reason for seeking help now
Longitudinal courseSimilar past episodes: first onset, worst episode, typical duration and frequency; the last period of wellness; any change in usual personality when unwell
The patient's viewOpinion about the cause and nature of the problem, willingness to engage, hopes and expectations of treatment

The history of present illness for a refugee claimant is taken the same way as for anyone else, a full account of symptoms, with the refugee-specific facts added.

Review of systems: the four screens

At every psychiatric assessment, other than an acutely psychotic patient in the emergency room being treated for agitation, four domains are screened: depression, mania or hypomania, psychosis, anxiety. Cognitive, eating, sexual, somatic and dissociative symptoms are added when relevant.

Depression: MSIGECAPS

LetterDomainScreening question
MMood"Have you felt sad, down or hopeless lately?"
SSleep"Sleeping too much, trouble falling or staying asleep?"
IInterest"Have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?"
GGuilt"Do you feel guilty or blame yourself unnecessarily?"
EEnergy"How is your energy level through the day?"
CConcentration"How is your concentration?"
AAppetite"How has your appetite changed?"
PPsychomotor"Slowed down in movement or thinking, or restless and unable to sit still?"
SSuicidality"Have you had thoughts that life isn't worth living?"

The nine letters map one to one onto the nine criteria for a major depressive episode: five or more in the same two-week period, most of the day nearly every day, a change from previous functioning. The template's gate questions: "Have you ever had two weeks or more when you felt sad or low, for most of the day, nearly every day?" and the same for loss of interest; then anchor an episode (worst, most recent, first, longest) and ask "during that period, did you have…" each item.

Mania: GST PAID

Mania is a distinct period of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy or activity. Gate: "Have you had an unusually high mood for many days in a row? How many? Did you have increased energy?"

LetterItemScreening question
GGrandiosity"Unusually confident, or special abilities or powers?"
SSleep, decreased need"Needed less sleep than usual but still felt full of energy?"
TTalkativeness, pressured speech"Talking much more than usual?"
PPleasurable but risky activities"Overspending, reckless driving, impulsive behaviour?"
AActivity increase"Unusually active, lots of new projects?"
IIdeas racing"Thoughts racing so fast they are hard to keep up with?"
DDistractibility"More easily distracted than usual?"
Decreased need for sleep with preserved energy is mania; insomnia with fatigue is depression. Pressured, hard-to-interrupt speech is manic; slowed speech with latency is depressive.

Psychosis

Hallucinations are perceptual disturbances without external stimuli.

ModalityQuestionMost in keeping with
Auditory"Do you hear voices when no one is around, that are not your own voice?" How many; recognizable; commenting on your actions; commanding you to hurt yourself or others; inside or outside the headSchizophrenia (the commonest primary psychiatric modality)
Visual"Have you seen things others don't see?"Delirium and medical causes
Olfactory"Do you smell things others don't, like smoke or chemicals?"Medical cause, classically temporal lobe epilepsy
Tactile or somatic"Felt things on or under your skin that weren't there?" (bugs crawling, being touched)Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal

Delusions are fixed false beliefs. Stem: "Has it ever seemed that…"

TypeBeliefQuestion
PersecutoryHarassed, followed, spied on, harmed"…people are after you or doing bad things to you?"
GrandioseExceptional abilities, fame, wealth, a special mission"…you have special traits or abilities?"
ReferentialUnrelated events, television, radio carry special meaning directed at the person"…things on TV or the internet are sending you messages?" A woman with schizophrenia who believes commercials speak directly to her
ErotomanicAnother person, often of higher status or a stranger, is in love with the individual"…someone famous was in love with you or sending secret signals?"
NihilisticOne is dead, does not exist, or the world has ended"…you or parts of you don't exist, or the world has already ended?" Accompanies severe psychotic depression
Control, thought insertion, thought withdrawal, somatic, mind readingAn outside force controls actions or thoughts; thoughts inserted or removed; a change in the body"…some outside force is controlling your actions?" "…your thoughts are taken out of your head?"

In depression with psychosis, delusions are mood-congruent: nihilistic, somatic, guilty. When psychotic symptoms are present, always ask about concurrent substance use and the intensity of symptoms when abstinent.

Anxiety

ConditionScreening question
Generalized anxiety"Do you worry excessively about many things and find it hard to control?"
Panic"A sudden rush of fear peaking in minutes with racing heart and shortness of breath?"
Agoraphobia"Do you avoid situations like being in public?"
Social anxiety"Very anxious in social situations or speaking in front of others, to the point of avoiding them?"
Specific phobia"Especially afraid of flying, heights, animals, needles, and avoid them at all costs?"
OCD"Unwanted thoughts or images that keep coming back? A need to check or follow routines?" (tapping, counting, checking)
PTSD"Anything traumatic that still affects you today? Flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive memories?"

Post-traumatic symptoms are the norm after trauma: being jumpy, looking over one's shoulder, sleeping badly. In about 90% they have resolved a year later; the 10% who continue with nightmares, flashbacks, hyperarousal and sitting with their back to the wall have PTSD. OCD and PTSD are screened under anxiety for convenience, although DSM-5 places them in their own categories.

Substance use

Always ask: alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, opioids, stimulants, hallucinogens, sedatives, and in the template also caffeine, prescriptions, gambling and online use. Six probes: route, frequency, quantity, duration; first, typical and last use, periods of abstinence; withdrawal symptoms (including seizures and delirium tremens), tolerance, cravings; impact on functioning and on symptoms; past treatments (detox, rehab, 12-step, residential); screening tools (CAGE, AUDIT); motivation to change.

Withdrawal from central nervous system depressants can kill. Alcohol, benzodiazepines and phenobarbital withdrawal cause seizures, delirium tremens and death; management is admission with diazepam and thiamine and intravenous treatment. Opioid withdrawal is very uncomfortable but not lethal, and can be medically managed. About a quarter of an emergency psychiatrist's shift can be admissions for safe withdrawal.

The remaining history

SectionContent
Past psychiatric historyPrevious diagnoses and mental-health contacts (counselling, case manager); emergency visits; hospitalizations (approximate total, last discharge); suicide attempts (number, severity, medical intervention, most recent); self-harm (cutting, burning, hitting); aggression, violence, charges; treatments, pharmacological and not, with effectiveness and side effects. The four questions: admitted before? suicide attempts? medications? psychotherapy?
Past medical historyChronic conditions, especially endocrine and neurological (diabetes, epilepsy, HIV, seizures, head injury); surgeries; pregnancies; relevant labs and imaging. Medical and psychiatric comorbidity worsen each other's outcomes, and medical conditions produce psychiatric pictures: a university student admitted with sudden psychosis and paranoia whose screening TSH was very high had myxedema psychosis, treated by replacing thyroid hormone, not as schizophrenia; hypercholesterolaemia and hypertension in a healthy young person were the other clues.
Medications and allergiesGeneric name, dose, frequency; contraceptives; over-the-counter, herbal and naturopathic products; recent changes; adherence, effectiveness, side effects; anaphylactic reactions.
Family history"Does anyone in your family have mental health concerns?" Depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, suicide, substance use, hospitalizations, legal problems; relevant medical history such as epilepsy. A first-degree relative with bipolar disorder gives a 10% chance of bipolar disorder.
Personal and developmental historyFour domains: early life, current circumstances, relationships and supports, identity and culture. The template: birthplace, time in current location, heritage, religion; family members and the quality of relationships; trauma (verbal, physical, sexual abuse, neglect, domestic violence); prenatal and perinatal complications; early childhood milestones, temperament, caregivers, home stability; school (academics, socializing, bullying, inattention, behaviour); sexuality and identity; adult education, occupation, relationships; hobbies, meaning, strengths, accomplishments, hopes. Look for emotional development in early life, major themes, recurring patterns, identity formation, experience of failure and loss, and the effect of experience on beliefs about self, others and the world, and on trust, intimacy, anger and self-esteem. Depth is titrated to relevance: not in the emergency room, in full for the panic patient whose "why" needs explaining. Students first secure the basic problem, its immediate context and its impact; the earlier-life detail can wait for a later interview.
CollateralInformation from someone other than the patient (family, friends, carers, other professionals) on physical and mental health, social circumstances and function in the period before assessment. Essential in emergency psychiatry, especially with suicidal thoughts.

Risk assessment

Six risk headings: suicide; other deliberate self-harm; violence toward others; inability to look after oneself; self-neglect; neglect of dependents; the template adds safe driving and cooking. Four functional-impact domains: personal care and survival; family functioning; occupational functioning; broad social functioning. The suicide screen runs as a ladder: ideation ("Has life seemed so stressful that you think about death or suicide?"), method ("ways you would end your life?"), means ("prepared or acquired the means?"), intent, past attempts and when, then acute versus chronic, active (plans) versus passive (thoughts of death), and protective factors ("reasons for staying alive?"). Assessment after self-harm and the full risk-factor framework are in the self-harm and suicide guide.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Fifteen headings; presentation order is not gathering order; five minimum items; four screens at every assessment.
  • MSIGECAPS = the nine MDE criteria; GST PAID needs a distinct period of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy.
  • Auditory: schizophrenia. Visual: delirium. Olfactory: temporal lobe epilepsy. Tactile: withdrawal.
  • Nihilistic delusions belong to psychotic depression, with somatic and guilty delusions; referential delusions are messages from unrelated events.
  • Post-traumatic symptoms resolve in 90% by a year; PTSD is the 10%.
  • CNS depressant withdrawal kills; opioid withdrawal does not. Diazepam and thiamine.
  • High TSH plus new psychosis is myxedema psychosis; think of medical causes and of endocrine and neurological history.
  • 10% bipolar risk with a first-degree relative.
  • Six risk headings, plus driving and cooking; the suicide ladder ends on protective factors.
The psychiatric history is a medical history with more identifying data, a longer developmental history, a routine screen for depression, mania, psychosis and anxiety, an always-asked substance history, and a risk assessment. The screens carry the diagnostic vocabulary of the whole block: the nine depressive criteria, the seven manic features, the four hallucination modalities with their likely causes, the delusion types, and the anxiety syndromes.

guides.title: Week 40 · 7 The Mental Status Examination
guides.html:
PW01 · Byrne L2 · CS2 guide · WFQ

The Mental Status Examination

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Psychiatry's physical examination: ASEPTIC with its descriptor vocabulary, mood versus affect on three axes, perception and thought terms, insight, judgement and capacity, cognition, and the patterns of depression, mania and psychosis.

Psychiatry's physical examination

The physical examination has been the identifying act of the physician since the sarcophagi of ancient doctors; in psychiatry the mental status examination is its equivalent. It is a formalized, organized way of reading verbal and non-verbal cues, a skill everyone has practised since infancy, and it is a summary of observations that, paired with the history, leads to a diagnosis. The data are gathered throughout the interview, tracked and evaluated while the patient is talking, not collected in a separate block at the end. The MSE is a snapshot of someone's mental status at that moment, and its purpose is to transmit an abnormal picture to another clinician: a written MSE lets a clerk convey a case to staff who were not in the room. Not every descriptor is reported for every patient; the tables are a vocabulary, not a checklist. Psychiatrists also examine physically when indicated: a neurological examination for delirium, signs of intoxication, withdrawal, malnutrition or medication side effects, tremor and extrapyramidal signs, catatonia, and weight and blood pressure as a baseline for psychotropics.

The history and the examination cover the same ground from two sides: the history is what the patient reports, the mental state is what the examiner observes.

Asked about in the historyObserved in the mental state
Behaviour and adaptive functioningOvert behaviour
Physical manifestations of mental disorderAppearance
EmotionsMood and affect
Consciousness, orientation, memory, intellectSensorium or alertness, memory
Speech, thinking, perception, self-experienceSpeech and thought process, thought content, perception

ASEPTIC

The domains, with the descriptor vocabulary used to document them.

DomainDescriptors
A: Appearance and behaviourAge (stated, younger, older); dress (casual, formal, inappropriate to weather or setting); grooming and hygiene (good, unkempt); gait (brisk, slow, intoxicated, ataxic, rigid, shuffling, staggering); psychomotor activity (normal, reduced, excessive); level of consciousness (alert, confused, lethargic, stuporous); abnormal movements (grimaces, tics, tardive dyskinesia, foot tapping, compulsions, tremor, dystonia, catatonia); eye contact; attitude (cooperative, belligerent, oppositional, submissive, guarded, evasive, hostile); reliability and ease of rapport
S: SpeechRate (rapid, pressured, slowed); rhythm (hesitant, rambling, halting, stuttering, jerky, long pauses); tone; volume (loud, soft, whispered, yelling, inaudible); accent; clarity; quantity (responds only to questions, offers information, repetitive, verbose); spontaneity; latency
E: Emotion, mood and affectMood is the patient's subjective state, what they say when asked "How is your mood?", rated 0 to 10 with 0 the worst. Affect is the observed state. Quality (euthymic, elevated, depressed, anxious, irritable), intensity, range (broad or full, restricted, flat, blunted), stability (fixed or labile), congruence with mood and thought content, appropriateness to the situation
P: Perceptual disturbancesHallucinations, auditory, visual, olfactory (burning smells, classically temporal lobe epilepsy), tactile or somatic; illusions, distortions of real images or sensations; depersonalization, the self is not real; derealization, the world is not real; observed "responding to internal stimuli" or "internally preoccupied"
T: Thought process and contentProcess: linear, goal-directed; circumstantial (answers eventually, after excessive detail); tangential (moves away and never answers); flight of ideas (rapid shifts with discernible connections); loose associations (connections weak or hard to follow); word salad; thought blocking (halted); repetition. Content: themes and preoccupations, over-valued ideas, delusions, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal ideation with intent and plan
I: Insight and judgementInsight is the patient's understanding of what is happening to them, the ability to realize they have a mental-health concern and appreciate its implications. Judgement is the ability to use facts and make reasonable decisions, judged from recent behaviour about safety, social functioning and treatment. Each graded none or impaired, partial, intact or full
C: CognitionOrientation in three spheres (name, place, time); attention and concentration; memory, short-term (recent events) and long-term (distant events); intellect; MoCA or MMSE if applicable. Without formal testing: "Cognition not formally assessed, but grossly intact."

The clinical-skills guide distils the same content into thirteen categories, appearance, attitude, behaviour, sensorium or alertness, speech, form of thought, cognition, mood, affect, thought content, perception, insight, judgement; the case-report form scores them, including attitude, in the same order. Learn the domains, not a count.

Mood and affect

Mood is subjective, reported; affect is objective, observed. A patient who says they are very sad while laughing has an incongruent affect, and the discrepancy is itself informative. Three separate axes describe affect, and questions turn on which axis a word belongs to: quality (euthymic, elevated, depressed, flat), range (broad or restricted), stability (fixed or labile). A person whose feeling visibly shifts from embarrassment to excitement within a conversation has a normal range; someone in prodromal schizophrenia may have a range that does not move. Flat is the quality; restricted is the range. A 26-year-old brought by his family for social withdrawal, delusions and poor hygiene, who avoids eye contact and shows minimal emotional reactivity, has a flat affect.

Perception

  • Hallucination: a perception with no external stimulus ("I am seeing someone standing right here"; hearing a voice "that is not your own voice", while there is no auditory input). Illusion: misperception of a real stimulus (hearing one's name called when the phone rings; a real object in the room seen as a ghost). Commonest in psychosis, also in mood disorders, delirium and temporal lobe epilepsy.
  • Depersonalization and derealization are forms of dissociation: disconnection from oneself or from reality, seen in PTSD and in psychosis.
  • A patient who breaks off to attend to something no one else can perceive is documented as internally preoccupied, attending to internal stimuli.

Thought

Ordinary thought is goal-directed and logical. In mania or psychosis it can be all over the place: "I see ketchup on the floor, my mom loves…", an unrelated sequence that is tangential or loosely associated. The pairs to keep straight: circumstantial gets there eventually; tangential never does. Flight of ideas keeps discernible links; loose associations lose them. Content is what the person is thinking about: delusions (persecutory, grandiose, referential, erotomanic, nihilistic), obsessions, and thoughts of self-harm, suicide or harm to others. Beyond discrete symptoms, the examiner notes trends that speak to risk: a depressed patient with a poor sense of the future and hopelessness, or paranoid delusions focused on a specific person such as a spouse or boss; both raise the risk of harm to self or others.

Insight, judgement and capacity

Insight is three tasks: accurately recognizing that new or unusual symptoms are present ("I feel much more sad and hopeless than usual"); accurately attributing them to a pathological process ("I am having a depressive episode"); and accurately recognizing the benefit of treatment ("restarting my antidepressant would help"). Judgement is the ability to use insight to make decisions in one's own interest ("I need to book an appointment to restart my antidepressant"). Both insight and judgement are required for capacity to make decisions about one's own medical care. The two dissociate: a man brought in by police believing he is Jesus reincarnated has no insight, but if his behaviour is otherwise appropriate his judgement may be intact, because judgement is read from behaviour. Assessing either is hard, and clinician bias makes it harder.

Why dress is a real finding
A patient with schizophrenia held involuntarily in a 35-degree summer, wearing multiple jackets and at risk of overheating, was presented to the Consent and Capacity Board as evidence of impaired judgement, and the lawyer's cross-examination asked what material the jackets were. Sometimes how someone dresses does not matter; sometimes it does. The descriptor is "inappropriate to weather or setting", and the observation has to be tied to a consequence.

Cognition

Cognitive impairment shapes every other finding, so a thorough interview often includes a brief bedside screen: the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) or the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), which is better known but perhaps less reliable. Orientation is asked in three spheres, attention and concentration are observed, and memory is split into short-term (recent events) and long-term (distant events). When nothing formal has been done the phrase is "cognition not formally assessed, but grossly intact".

Patterns

PresentationExpected MSE
DepressionPoor eye contact; psychomotor slowing; slowed speech with reduced quantity and increased latency, a long pause before answering; restricted or depressed affect; impaired concentration; hopeless or guilty content; may or may not be unkempt. A 36-year-old man two months "really sad", not getting out of bed, not working, no longer playing guitar, no appetite, feeling his family would be better off without him: the most likely finding is slowed speech, not broad affect, grandiose delusions or intact concentration
ManiaPressured speech that is hard to interrupt, a cardinal sign; distractibility; affect lability; grandiose content; excessive psychomotor activity. Fast speech becomes pressured speech when the listener cannot break in
PsychosisFlat or restricted affect; poor hygiene; avoidance of eye contact; delusions and hallucinations; internally preoccupied; disorganized thought process

A model MSE

Of a film clip of a man with schizophrenia talking to a roommate who is not there: "This is a middle-aged Caucasian male. He was dressed in hospital clothing. He was poorly kempt, and in restraints. His gait was not observed. He had excessive psychomotor activity; he was agitated, throwing himself off the chair. He was alert. He was non-cooperative. He was experiencing a visual hallucination, internally preoccupied, attending to internal stimuli." Two habits in it: what cannot be observed is stated as not observed rather than guessed, and observed responding to hallucinations is described in observational language. Of a second clip, a man ranting at 4 a.m. about a novel's ending: the fast, hard-to-interrupt speech is pressured speech, and that mental status would be suspicious for mania.

Vocabulary from the clinical-skills session

The mental status examination is observed, not asked; the one item elicited is mood, written in the patient's own words in quotation marks. Psychiatry calls objective what everyday language calls subjective: the examiner's description of affect is the objective finding. Every descriptor should lead the reader toward the impression; what is unremarkable is stated as such ("dressed in street clothes, nothing remarkable"), and what could not be observed is recorded as not observed.

DomainPoints to add
Appearance and behaviourDress inappropriate to the season in mania or psychosis; heavy make-up in histrionic presentations; a clutched object in a borderline crisis; cuts on the arms; a laceration from a suicide attempt; a certified patient in handcuffs with police at the bedside; a confused patient pulling at tubes. Gait and movement carry medication signs: antipsychotics can produce a parkinsonian shuffle and tremor, tardive dyskinesia, or catatonia (rigidity, purposeless movements, mannerisms), which is also a marker of severe illness. Eye contact is recorded separately: avoidant, absent, or an intense fixed gaze in anger or agitation.
SpeechLatency: the long blank pause before an answer in depression. Prosody: flat and unvarying in depression; stereotyped (the same melody for a question and a statement) in intellectual disability and autism spectrum; sing-song in mania. Very soft, hard-to-hear speech in severe social anxiety. Loud, fast speech becomes pressured only when the listener cannot interrupt.
AffectRestricted: the affect cannot be budged from one position across a long interview, the severe depression that does not lift at a lighter comment. Labile: crying one minute and laughing the next, in psychosis and in some neurological conditions. Incongruent requires a stated mood that clashes with the observed affect ("my mood is amazing" from a downcast, unreactive patient); a patient who simply shows no variation in expression is restricted, not incongruent. Inappropriate is affect that clashes with the content, chuckling about a death.
PerceptionHallucinations are the neon signs. Ask their modality, content and consequences: command hallucinations, benign or dangerous, and whether the patient would act on them or recognizes them as hallucinations. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic experiences at the edge of sleep are common and far less pathological. Formication, ants crawling on the skin, points to substance use; olfactory hallucinations to neurological disease. A guarded, paranoid patient may deny hallucinations while visibly scanning the room; that is documented as appearing to attend to internal stimuli. Depersonalization and derealization are non-psychotic perceptual disturbances, typical of panic and of severe distress in personality disorders.
Thought formThe path from A to B: linear, circumstantial, tangential, disorganized or incoherent. Over-inclusive, long-winded but eventually on target, is the anxious pattern. Clang associations (words linked only by sound) and neologisms (invented words) mark severe thought disorder, occasionally in mania. The normal line: linear, logical, coherent.
Thought contentThe examiner's summary of the salient themes: guilt, burden and hopelessness with little future orientation in depression; fear and a persecutor in paranoia; suicidal or homicidal ideation. A delusion is a fixed false belief; it is a thought, not a perception, and belongs here rather than under perception.
Insight and judgementInsight is best stated specifically, insight into the illness, into the danger of a substance, into the benefit of a medication, rather than as a bare adjective. Lack of insight is intrinsic to delusion and to mania, in which the patient feels well and the world is the problem. Judgement is read from behaviour: impulsive, risky action means impaired judgement.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Restricted needs no stated mood; incongruent needs a stated mood that clashes with the affect.
  • A delusion is a fixed false belief and is thought content, not perception; formication suggests substances, olfactory hallucinations neurology, hypnagogic images are benign.
  • Mood is subjective, affect is objective; quality, range and stability are three axes; flat is quality, restricted is range.
  • Hallucination has no stimulus; illusion distorts a real one. Depersonalization is self, derealization is world, both dissociation.
  • Circumstantial versus tangential; flight of ideas versus loose associations.
  • Insight is three tasks; judgement is behaviour; both are needed for capacity; they can dissociate.
  • Depression on the MSE is slowed speech; mania is pressured speech; psychosis is flat affect.
  • Olfactory hallucinations point to temporal lobe epilepsy.
  • MoCA versus MMSE: the MMSE is better known but maybe less reliable.
  • Documentation phrases: "cognition not formally assessed, but grossly intact"; "gait not observed"; "internally preoccupied".
The MSE is an observational snapshot organized as ASEPTIC, gathered throughout the interview and written to carry the picture to another clinician. Its highest-yield content is the vocabulary: the mood-affect distinction with its three axes, hallucination versus illusion, the thought-process pairs, the three tasks of insight and their link to capacity, and the speech findings that separate depression from mania.

guides.title: Week 40 · 8 Diagnosis, Formulation and the Case Report
guides.html:
Byrne L2 · CS2 guide · CBL 40

Diagnosis, Formulation and the Case Report

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What a diagnosis is and is not, the diagnostic hierarchy, the two questions a formulation answers, the 4 P's grid worked for the depressed 25-year-old and for Stanley, and how the case report is written and marked.

Diagnosis

A diagnosis is a structured classification based on established criteria, DSM-5-TR in North America. It assigns a label such as major depressive disorder or schizophrenia according to specific symptoms, duration and severity, and it outlines the cluster of symptoms present. It may not explain why those symptoms occur in that individual. The goal of diagnosis is a plan of management, and a working diagnosis has three components:

ComponentTaskWord
1Classify the symptoms and signs the patient bringsIllness
2Discern the context in which they are to be understoodPredicament
3Discover, if possible, the pathophysiological processes underneathDisease

The diagnostic hierarchy

The major psychiatric disorders can be imagined on a ladder, with no moral implication. Disorders higher on the ladder often show the features of those below; disorders lower on the ladder rarely show the hallmarks of those above.

RungCategoryHallmarkNotes
1, topPhysical disease and drug-induced conditionsConfusionMay show everything below; identifiable pathology; specific, sometimes life-saving treatment
2The psychoses: schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorderImpaired reality-testing: delusions and hallucinationsUnlikely to show confusion; reliably diagnosed across cultures; disabling, sometimes dangerous; good evidence for drug treatment
3, bottomDepression and anxiety, often togetherAffective symptoms without confusion or impaired reality-testingVery common; much distress and disability; often in stressful situations; medication plus psychological, environmental and behavioural treatment; less sinister prognosis
Delusions with confusion push the assessment up the ladder toward a physical or drug-induced cause, not down to a primary psychosis. A young man with sudden psychosis and a very high TSH has myxedema psychosis, not schizophrenia. Always ask about substances, and about symptom intensity when abstinent.

The course of the sickness is of vital importance and is discovered entirely from the history; cross-sectional signs do not carry the same significance as longitudinal ones. Accurate appraisal asks five questions: how dangerous is the condition, to the patient or anyone else; how great the functional impairment, in everyday activities, work, self-support, dependents, family and community; what is the immediate psychosocial context, including loss or change; what physical factors are at play, illness, medications, drugs, alcohol; and who is the person, their intelligence, capacity for enduring relationships, work and independence.

Formulation

A formulation is a hypothesis that answers two questions: why has this patient fallen ill now, and what should we do to help? Formulations have a "because" in them; they are ideas about causation, and they provide hypotheses about how present insults interact with the patient to create the problems needing treatment. Diagnosis describes what; formulation explains why now. Two patients meeting identical criteria for panic disorder, a 20-year-old whose panic is about social embarrassment and anxiety and a 70-year-old whose panic followed a stroke and serves to keep her warned of threat, are treated very differently once the driver is understood. Formulation is the detective work of psychiatry; in-depth formulation takes years to learn, and the basic model is the 4 P's grid.

The 4 P'sDefinitionExamples
PredisposingAreas of vulnerability that increase the risk of the presenting problemGenetics, temperament, life events, attachment insecurity, ACEs
PrecipitatingThe specific event or trigger for the onset of the current problemDeath of a loved one, abuse, a divorce, a car accident, stopping a medication
PerpetuatingWhat maintains the problem once establishedSubstance use, all-or-nothing thinking, avoidance in panic disorder, poor glucose control
ProtectiveStrengths that reduce severity, counteract the first three and promote adaptive functioningTreatment response, supports, psychological-mindedness

The rows are crossed with the three columns of the diathesis-stress model, biological, psychological, social, with cultural folded into social; the CBL template gives cultural its own column. The grid is the diathesis-stress model with time added, and the plan that follows maps onto the columns.

The worked formulation

A 25-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with three months of depression after a relationship breakup. His mother had severe depression, was often hospitalized and unavailable as a parent; his parents divorced when he was seven. He has poorly controlled type 1 diabetes with recurrent DKA that stops him keeping regular work. He responded well to fluoxetine at 16 and stopped it six months ago because of cost.

BiologicalSocialPsychological
PredisposingFamily history of depression; type 1 diabetesMother with severe depression, frequently in hospital and away from him as an infant; father left when he was sevenInsecure attachment, difficulty with trust; the belief "I am not good enough"
PrecipitatingStopped the antidepressant because of costGirlfriend cheated on him; breakupReactivates feelings of inadequacy and increases trust issues
PerpetuatingPoor blood-glucose controlLow income; social isolationConflict of trust and self-esteem
ProtectiveWilling to take medication, previously adherent, previous good response to an SSRIGood healthcare teamPsychologically minded, self-reflective

The reasoning inside the cells. Heritability predisposes him; type 1 diabetes is itself a risk factor for depression, through the inflammatory hypothesis, diabetes being an inflammatory condition. The mother's depression is entered twice on purpose: in the biological column as heritability, in the social column as absence, and a child whose mother was often in hospital and whose father left did not have a secure base. A child abandoned by a parent often blames himself, "I wasn't enough to keep my dad around", which is the derivation of "I am not good enough". Someone with insecure attachment hanging on to a girlfriend who then cheats has suffered a blow that reactivates exactly those beliefs. The arrows run from the social to the psychological column in each row.

The formulation is delivered to the patient as understanding: "Of course you have these abandonment issues; your self-esteem is really low; your blood sugar is all over the place; this is what has caused you to feel so terrible." It produces buy-in, and it produces a plan that maps onto the columns: better blood-sugar control and restart fluoxetine (biological); psychotherapy for self-esteem (psychological); the healthcare team and the isolation (social). That is different from "he's depressed, give him Prozac", and it takes about 45 minutes with the patient.

Placing a factor. A 36-year-old woman with persistent low mood, isolation and difficulty keeping relationships, whose parents were emotionally unavailable and who recently lost her job: the psychological predisposing factor is the insecure attachment from unavailable parents. Recent unemployment is precipitating; sleep disturbance is perpetuating; passive suicidal ideation is a symptom of the depression, not a factor at all. Watch for the option that is a feature of the disorder rather than a cause.

Stanley's formulation

The CBL applies the same grid to a refugee claimant with trauma, with four columns.

BiologicalPsychologicalSocialCultural
PredisposingNo clear biological vulnerability identifiedLongstanding fear from concealing his sexualityLongstanding threat of discovery and persecution for same-sex relationshipsPersecution of same-sex relationships in his country of origin
PrecipitatingShoulder injury and pain after the attackGrief after his mother's death; guilt and self-blame; fear of returnViolent attack; forced migration; loss of home and occupation; the coming refugee hearingDisplacement from his community and its norms
PerpetuatingPoor sleep; persistent shoulder painTrauma reminders; guilt; anticipatory fear about returnHousing instability; financial insecurity; occupational disruption; limited supportsLanguage barrier; isolation from a cultural community
ProtectiveNo significant medical comorbidity or substance useFuture orientation; help-seeking; perseverance; capacity to work and planA supportive cousin; employment; educationConnection to an affirming community, where available

The narrative: Stanley experienced severe interpersonal violence, the death of his mother and forced migration in the context of persecution for his sexual orientation; his current distress is the reactivation of years of concealed fear by an attack and a bereavement, maintained by pain, poor sleep, insecurity and the hearing ahead, and protected against by his own perseverance, his cousin and his work. Whether he meets full criteria for PTSD or for adjustment disorder is a separate question for psychiatry; the formulation stands either way, and the work-up for medical contributors, at minimum a CBC and TSH, proceeds in the meantime.

The management plan and the case report

A management plan is biopsychosocial, covering medication, therapy and lifestyle, it must be feasible, and it must mitigate safety concerns. The clerkship write-up, submitted within two weeks of the final session, consists of the history, the mental state examination, a diagnostic impression, and a plan of management; a satisfactory score is required to pass, and interview technique is also assessed in every OSCE station.

Formative checklistItems scored not done, inadequate, adequate
HistoryChief complaint and the patient's expectations; current problems; course; expectations of the doctor; active physical illness; medications; substance use; personal and social circumstances; recent losses or changes; impact on personal care, occupational, family and social functioning; risk of self-harm or suicide, self-neglect, neglect of dependents, aggression or violence; previous psychiatric problems; screens for cognitive impairment, psychosis, depression and mania, anxiety
Mental status examinationAppearance, attitude, behaviour, level of alertness, speech, thought form, cognition, mood, affect, thought content, perception, insight, judgement
