SummaryTwo to three sentences naming the most pertinent historical and mental-state findings; a diagnostic impression within current knowledge

The summative mark has four domains on a five-point scale with "meets expectations" as the pass point: data collection (sufficient to identify the major problem; outstanding adds the psychosocial context of the individual), language (appropriate use of terms; outstanding applies every term in the right category), approach to the problem (recognizes and describes the illness; outstanding is highly relevant and accurate), and global assessment (complete history and MSE, succinct; outstanding is synthesis and emerging application). The jump from meets to outstanding is the jump from completeness to synthesis, and the language domain rewards putting each observation in the right MSE category.

Depth of formulation at this stage, and a model impression

The clinical-skills preceptor set the expectation for second year plainly: hold a broad biopsychosocial conceptualization of why this person is unwell now, across culture, family, genetics and circumstance, without turning the note into a biography. The reason the exercise exists is the heterogeneity of categorical labels: two people who each meet five of nine criteria for depression can look nothing alike, so "depressed, therefore this plan" does not work the way "streptococcal pneumonia, therefore this plan" works. Formulation supplies the why. Its vocabulary applies to any diagnosis: in social anxiety disorder the classic perpetuating factor is avoidance, never going to the party, never ordering from a human being.

A first-encounter impression, of the kind the case report asks for, has a recognizable shape. For a standardized patient with six months of panic attacks:

A model impression, spoken to a supervisor
A young man who works in his family business and lives in the family home, with six months of worsening panic attacks, no medical history and no medical explanation after an emergency assessment cleared cardiac causes. The attacks are recurrent and out of the blue, with persistent fear of the next one and a measurable effect on his life, so he most likely meets criteria for panic disorder; the somatic symptom list was not run in full. Prior psychiatric history and substance use were not established and would be asked next; no depressive syndrome on review of symptoms; no suicidal ideation; psychosis not screened. He has been using a friend's benzodiazepine several times a week, which is not a treatment for panic disorder; first-line treatment is an antidepressant taken daily plus cognitive behavioural therapy, and he is open to both.

The structure is the point: an identifying line, the course, the medical exclusion, the working diagnosis with its criteria named, the negatives that matter for safety, what was missed and will be asked, and the direction of the plan. A history and mental status written this way leads the reader to the impression; that is what the case report's "approach to the problem" and "synthesis" descriptors reward.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Formulation answers why now because categorical labels are heterogeneous; in social anxiety the perpetuating factor is avoidance.
  • An impression names the working diagnosis with its criteria, the safety negatives, and what was missed.
  • Illness, predicament, disease: symptoms classified, context discerned, pathophysiology discovered.
  • Ladder: confusion at the top, impaired reality-testing in the middle, affective symptoms at the bottom; features flow downward, hallmarks do not flow upward.
  • Diagnosis says what; formulation says why now, with a "because".
  • Predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective crossed with bio, psycho, social; a symptom is not a factor.
  • Type 1 diabetes predisposes to depression through inflammation; the mother's depression is heritability in one column and absence in another.
  • Plan = biopsychosocial, feasible, safety-mitigating; summary = two to three sentences of history and mental state.
Diagnosis classifies; formulation explains and directs treatment. The 4 P's grid crossed with the biopsychosocial columns turns the vulnerability, the trigger, the maintainers and the strengths into a plan that names what to do in each domain, for the depressed 25-year-old and for Stanley alike. The case report is that reasoning written down: history, MSE, a two-to-three-sentence summary, a diagnostic impression, and a feasible, safe, biopsychosocial plan.

guides.title: Week 40 · 9 Personality and the Ten Personality Disorders
guides.html:
PD Module 1 · Byrne L1 · WFQ

Personality and the Ten Personality Disorders

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Trait, temperament and disorder, the general criteria, the three clusters with every disorder's core pattern and threshold, and the look-alike pairs that get tested.

Traits, temperament and disorder

A personality trait is an enduring pattern of perceiving and relating to the environment, exhibited across a wide range of contexts. Traits such as narcissism and neuroticism are normally distributed in populations, partly heritable and partly developmental, and a personality disorder is the point where an inflexible, exaggerated, extreme version of a trait that lies to some extent in everyone causes harm: a personality disorder is present when a person's traits cause them distress or impair their functioning. Having one does not mean having a bad personality; a person with a personality disorder can be kind, charismatic and engaging. Temperament is different again: innate, biologically based traits present from infancy that shape early interaction with the world and are foundational to personality, distinct from learned behaviour, from attachment, and from the enduring norm-deviating traits that define a disorder.

Personality disorders arise from an interaction of genetic predisposition and environmental influence. No medication is approved to treat a personality disorder directly; medications target comorbidities or specific symptoms, and psychotherapy is the mainstay. Patients with personality disorders present for medical care more often than people without them, which is why every physician meets them.

General criteria for any personality disorder

Criterion
AAn enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour deviating markedly from cultural expectations, in at least 2 of 4 areas: cognition (perceiving and interpreting self, others, events), affectivity (range, intensity, lability, appropriateness), interpersonal functioning, impulse control
BInflexible and pervasive across a broad range of situations
CClinically significant distress or impairment
DStable and long-standing, onset traceable to adolescence or early adulthood
ENot better explained by another mental disorder
FNot attributable to a substance or another medical condition such as head trauma

A pattern that began after a head injury or only during substance use fails E or F; a pattern confined to one setting fails pervasiveness; a first appearance in mid-adulthood fails D.

Three clusters, ten disorders

ClusterOne wordMembersUnifying idea
AEccentric (odd)Paranoid, schizoid, schizotypalResemble features of schizophrenia without true hallucinations or delusions
BIntense (dramatic)Antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissisticInstability, impulsivity, emotionality, disregard for others
CAnxiousAvoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsiveFear-driven: of rejection, of being alone, of loss of control

"Mad, bad and sad" is discouraged as derogatory and inaccurate; "eccentric, intense, anxious" is the set to use.

Cluster A

DisorderCore patternResemblesThresholdDistinctive criteria
ParanoidDistrust and suspiciousness; others' motives read as malevolentParanoid delusions4 of 7Suspects exploitation without basis; doubts loyalty of friends; reluctant to confide; reads hidden demeaning meanings into benign remarks; bears grudges; perceives attacks and counterattacks; suspects partner's fidelity
SchizoidDetachment from relationships; restricted emotional expressionNegative symptoms (detachment, flat affect, anhedonia, asociality)4 of 7Neither desires nor enjoys close relationships; solitary activities; little sexual interest; few pleasures; no confidants; indifferent to praise or criticism; emotional coldness
SchizotypalAcute discomfort in close relationships, cognitive or perceptual distortions, eccentricityPositive symptoms (odd beliefs, perceptual distortions, odd speech)5 of 9Ideas of reference; magical thinking; unusual perceptual experiences and bodily illusions; odd speech; suspiciousness; constricted or inappropriate affect; odd appearance; no close friends; social anxiety that does not diminish with familiarity and is tied to paranoid fears, not negative self-judgement
The wanting test. Schizoid people do not want relationships; avoidant people want them but fear rejection. Schizotypal social anxiety persists with familiarity and is paranoid in flavour; avoidant anxiety is about rejection and inadequacy. Ideas of reference and illusions without fixed delusions or true hallucinations are schizotypal, not schizophrenia.

Cluster B

DisorderCore patternThresholdDistinctive criteria
AntisocialDisregard for and violation of the rights of others3 of 7, plus age at least 18 and conduct disorder with onset before 15Unlawful acts; deceitfulness, aliases, conning; impulsivity; irritability and fights; reckless disregard for safety; irresponsibility at work and with money; lack of remorse
BorderlineInstability of relationships, self-image and affect, and marked impulsivity5 of 9Affective instability, inappropriate anger, emptiness, impulsivity in two areas, recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-harm, identity disturbance, transient paranoia or dissociation, idealization and devaluation, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment; the full account is in the borderline guide
HistrionicExcessive emotionality and attention seeking5 of 8Uncomfortable when not the centre of attention; seductive or provocative behaviour; rapidly shifting, shallow emotions; uses appearance to draw attention; impressionistic speech lacking detail; theatricality; suggestibility; considers relationships more intimate than they are
NarcissisticGrandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy5 of 9Grandiose self-importance; fantasies of unlimited success; believes self special; requires excessive admiration; entitlement; interpersonally exploitative; lacks empathy; often envious; arrogant

Psychopathy is not a DSM diagnosis; it is identified with the Hare Psychopathy Checklist-Revised. Most people with psychopathy probably have antisocial personality disorder, but many with antisocial personality disorder do not have psychopathy. A 16-year-old with repeated theft, lying and fights has conduct disorder, because antisocial personality disorder requires age 18; an adult with antisocial behaviour but no conduct disorder before 15 does not meet criteria.

Why they want attention
Histrionic: attention itself, by emotion, appearance or seduction, with shallow feeling. Narcissistic: admiration that confirms superiority, without empathy. Borderline: instability of self, relationships and affect with impulsivity and fear of abandonment. On a symptom-list question, "shallow expression of emotions" and "considers relationships more intimate than they are" are histrionic intruders, "often envious" and "interpersonal exploitation" are narcissistic, and "reckless disregard for safety" and "irritability and aggressiveness" are antisocial; the borderline list is the nine above.

Cluster C

DisorderCore patternThresholdDistinctive criteria
AvoidantSocial inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to negative evaluation4 of 7Avoids occupational contact for fear of criticism; unwilling to engage unless certain of being liked; restraint in intimacy for fear of ridicule; preoccupied with rejection; inhibited in new situations; views self as inept and inferior; reluctant to take risks that may embarrass
DependentExcessive need to be reassured and taken care of5 of 8Cannot make everyday decisions without reassurance; needs others to assume responsibility; difficulty disagreeing for fear of losing support (realistic fears of retribution do not count); cannot initiate projects from lack of confidence, not lack of energy; excessive lengths to obtain nurturance; helpless when alone; urgently seeks a new relationship when one ends; preoccupied with being left to care for self
Obsessive-compulsivePreoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control4 of 8Preoccupied with details and rules so that the point of the activity is lost; perfectionism that prevents completion; devotion to work not explained by economic necessity; inflexible morality not explained by culture or religion; cannot discard worthless objects; reluctant to delegate; miserly; rigid and stubborn
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is not OCD. The personality disorder is a pervasive, ego-syntonic style with no true obsessions or compulsions; OCD is ego-dystonic, with intrusive obsessions and compulsions the person resists. An accountant who redoes spreadsheets until perfect, refuses to delegate, hoards broken electronics and sees nothing wrong with it has the personality disorder. Avoidant fears rejection and avoids people; dependent fears being alone and clings to people. Poor initiation from low confidence is dependent; from low energy or motivation, think depression.

Thresholds and look-alikes

ThresholdDisorders
4 of 7Paranoid, schizoid, avoidant
5 of 9Schizotypal, narcissistic, borderline
5 of 8Histrionic, dependent
4 of 8Obsessive-compulsive
3 of 7Antisocial, the lowest, with the age and conduct-disorder requirements
PresentationThinkNot
Loner, flat affect, does not want friends, indifferent to praiseSchizoidAvoidant
Wants friends, avoids them for fear of rejectionAvoidantSchizoid
Magical thinking, odd speech, ideas of reference, no fixed delusionsSchizotypalSchizophrenia
Suspicious, grudges, insults in benign remarks, no fixed delusionsParanoid PDDelusional disorder
Seeks admiration, entitled, no empathyNarcissisticHistrionic
Loud, flirtatious, shifting emotions, calls a new acquaintance "best friend", cannot give detailsHistrionicBorderline
Rigid perfectionist who never finishes, will not delegate, ego-syntonicObsessive-compulsive PDOCD
Cannot decide without reassurance, cannot be alone, new partner within a weekDependentAvoidant
16-year-old with theft, fights, lyingConduct disorderAntisocial PD
Suspiciousness and grudges starting six months after a brain injuryNot a personality disorder (criteria D and F)Paranoid PD

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Distress or impairment turns a trait into a disorder; the trait alone never does.
  • 2 of 4 domains (cognition, affectivity, interpersonal, impulse control), inflexible and pervasive, onset by adolescence or early adulthood, not another disorder, substance or medical condition.
  • Antisocial needs 3 of 7, age 18, and conduct disorder before 15; psychopathy is not a diagnosis.
  • Cluster A maps to schizophrenia without psychosis: schizotypal to positive symptoms, schizoid to negative, paranoid to paranoid delusions.
  • No approved medication for any personality disorder; psychotherapy is the mainstay.
  • The threshold groups: three 4-of-7s, three 5-of-9s, two 5-of-8s, one 4-of-8, one 3-of-7.
Personality disorders are the extremes of normally distributed traits, diagnosed only when enduring, pervasive, early-onset and impairing, and grouped as eccentric, intense and anxious. The discriminations that get tested are desire versus fear in the schizoid-avoidant pair, paranoia versus rejection in schizotypal versus avoidant, attention versus admiration in histrionic versus narcissistic, style versus obsessions in the two obsessive-compulsive conditions, and age plus conduct disorder for antisocial.

guides.title: Week 40 · 10 Borderline Personality Disorder: Criteria, Management and Helping a Distressed Patient
guides.html:
PD Modules 2–4 · Byrne L3 · WFQ

Borderline Personality Disorder: Criteria, Management and Helping a Distressed Patient

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Why BPD is common, serious and treatable, the nine criteria in four domains with their counting rules, Victoria's case, DBT, and the validation, both-and and TIPP skills any physician can use.

Common, serious, treatable

SettingPrevalence of BPD
General population2 to 6%
Primary care6%
Psychiatry outpatients10%
Psychiatric inpatients20%

There is no sex difference in community samples. People who self-harm use emergency services more than people with other chronic conditions (232 visits per 100 person-years versus 117.6 for asthma), and BPD patients have higher health-care use than people with other personality disorders. It is serious: 8 to 10% die by suicide, similar to schizophrenia and depression; about three quarters self-harm (cutting, burning, overdosing) with real disfigurement and morbidity; quality of life is rated as low as in serious medical illness. And it is treatable: about 75% improve with dialectical behaviour therapy. Every physician meets these patients, whatever the specialty.

Where it comes from

BPD is the interaction of an emotionally sensitive temperament (biological) with an invalidating environment (social): the biosocial theory, which is the diathesis-stress model applied to one disorder and is set out in full in the vulnerability guide. The temperament has three features, low threshold, high intensity, slow return to baseline, with impulsivity as a separate heritable trait; the environment is one that dismisses, ignores, criticizes or reinforces outbursts, up to trauma and neglect. The more sensitive the child, the less invalidation is needed. Victoria, colicky and inconsolable as a baby, "so sensitive and moody" as a teen, told by a loving but overwhelmed mother that she was overreacting, is the case that runs through all four modules. Presented with the diagnosis at 18 she said, "I just thought I was a freak. What a relief!" Naming the diagnosis can bring relief rather than stigma.

The nine criteria

A pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affect, and marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts, shown by five or more of nine, grouped in four domains.

DomainCriterionDetail
Affect1. Affective instability from marked reactivity of moodIntense feelings lasting a few hours to a few days, "up and down" in response to events; not a sustained episode
2. Inappropriate intense angerDisplays of anger, recurrent fights
3. Chronic emptinessA physical sensation, often located in the chest or stomach; patients endorse or deny it
Behaviour4. Impulsivity in at least two self-damaging areasSpending, sex, substances, reckless driving, binge eating; does not include self-harm or suicidal behaviour
5. Recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-harmCounts once even when both are present
Cognition6. Identity disturbanceUnstable self-image: a different person with different friend groups; values and interests change with company
7. Transient, stress-related paranoia or severe dissociationDerealization, depersonalization (a spectator in one's own life, watching from the ceiling); "micropsychosis" with brief hallucinations is this criterion, not a psychotic disorder
Interpersonal8. Unstable, intense relationshipsAlternating idealization and devaluation: people are good or bad, not good and bad (splitting)
9. Frantic efforts to avoid abandonmentThreats, extreme accommodation, physically stopping someone leaving, begging; "leaving" can be leaving the room; self-harm does not count here

Two mnemonics: ARMS ASIDE (Anger, Relationships, Mood, Self, Abandonment, Suicide or self-harm, Impulsivity, Dissociation, Emptiness) and IMPULSIVE (Impulsive, Moody, Paranoid under stress, Unstable self-image, Labile relationships, Suicidal or self-harm, Inappropriate anger, Vulnerable to abandonment, Emptiness). With five of nine required there are 256 ways to meet criteria, so BPD is heterogeneous and self-harm alone never establishes it.

Counting traps. Impulsivity needs two areas and excludes self-harm. Suicidal thoughts and cutting are one criterion together. Frantic phoning to prevent a breakup is abandonment, not unstable relationships; calling the same person "the best thing that happened to me" and "the worst person alive" is unstable relationships, not unstable self or unstable mood. A two-week episode of low mood, anhedonia and early waking is a depressive episode, not reactive affective instability. A 19-year-old with self-harm, suicidal threats, impulsive spending and anger has only two confirmed criteria (self-harm counts once; spending is one area), so the rest must be screened.

Screening

Start with affective instability, a fairly sensitive and specific screen: "Do you have intense moods that change rapidly, from neutral to irritated to really anxious? How long do they last? Are they usually a reaction to something?" If several behavioural indicators are present, anger outbursts, self-harm or suicidality, impulsivity such as substances or an eating disorder, ask enough to see whether five criteria are met: "Do you often feel empty inside?" "Do you have a solid sense of who you are?" "When really stressed, do you go fuzzy or numb, lose time, feel unreal?" "Do you find yourself frantically trying to stop someone close to you from leaving?" "Stormy relationships where you run hot and cold?"

Victoria's criteria

First year at university: her boyfriend broke up with her in frosh week; she phones and texts him constantly and would drop out to follow him (abandonment); she has slept with three men she was not interested in and drinks most nights, missing classes (impulsivity); her mood is up and down, sad for hours or a day, and she rages at her roommate (mood, anger); Mark is "the best thing to happen to me" and "the worst person alive" (unstable relationships); suicidal thoughts on and off since 12 without plan or attempt, and cutting her thighs since 13, now daily (suicide and self-harm, one criterion). Six confirmed, longstanding and impairing: she meets criteria, with self, dissociation and emptiness not yet assessed. Her mental status examination is calm, cooperative, euthymic with full reactive affect, organized, without hallucinations, with passive suicidal ideation and no intent: reactive mood instability, not a sustained mood episode.

Management

OptionVerdict
NothingWrong. There are helpful treatments.
MedicationMaybe. No specific medication treats BPD. Antidepressants help significant comorbid depressive or anxiety symptoms; antipsychotics and mood stabilizers are sometimes used but are controversial and best left to psychiatrists; polypharmacy is common, dangerous or at least unhelpful, and must be avoided; some patients improve with no medication at all.
PsychotherapyCorrect. BPD-specific therapies or general therapeutic approaches.

Dialectical behaviour therapy

A structured psychotherapy rooted in CBT but focused less on thoughts and more on understanding behaviour, experiencing emotion and skilful coping; a third-wave therapy built from dialectical philosophy, Buddhism and behaviour therapy, especially effective in BPD and in emotion dysregulation generally. Typically 6 to 12 months at one hour of individual therapy and two hours of skills group a week. Four required modes: individual therapy, skills group, between-session phone coaching, weekly therapist team meeting. Four skill sets: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness. About 75% of patients have significant reductions in self-harm, emergency visits and admission days. The "D" is dialectics: two opposites can both be true at once, which is the basis of the both-and statement. Other evidence-based therapies include mentalization-based treatment, transference-focused psychotherapy, schema therapy and good psychiatric management.

Helping a distressed patient in the room

Told that therapy exists but there is a wait of months, Victoria speaks louder and faster, gestures bigger, slaps the arms of the chair. Treating BPD is beyond the undergraduate curriculum, but management is more than referral, and the techniques below are indispensable in any emergency department with any emotionally overwhelmed person.

Validation, six ways

WayExample
Show interestEye contact; not the computer screen
Reflective statement"You're really upset about the wait lists."
Mind-reading statement (an educated guess from what they said or how they look)"You're feeling hugely let down and disappointed, and angry, because of the waitlists."
Makes sense in context (knowledge of the individual)"Of course this is incredibly frustrating given how long you waited the last time."
Normalizing (most people would react this way)"Waiting is one of the biggest problems in our whole system; it IS frustrating."
Genuine, authentic, cheerleading"I wish this was a problem I could fix. I think you can get through this and I'll do my best to help."

Invalidating: "You're overreacting, please calm down." "A few months is nothing." "Wait lists are a normal part of the system" (this normalizes the system, not the patient's reaction). "I know it's frustrating, but it's not that bad." Validation works when it is sincere, insistent and emphatic; half-hearted validation does not. People tense when challenged or doubted and relax when understood. If validation calms them, skills are unnecessary; if it makes them more upset or they stay upset because they feel entitled to be, ask whether they would like to learn a coping skill. "If you don't know anything else about psychotherapy, validate, validate, validate. You cannot overdo it." Validation comes before problem-solving: "that sounds really hard" is the validating response; a rush to fix is not.

Both-and, then skills

A both-and statement links validation to something on offer: "I hear how hard it is to wait AND I believe you can get through it." Use "and", never "but", which cancels what came before. Then: validate and offer help ("I can't fix the wait list, and maybe I can help with how you're feeling right now; would you try something with me?"); make specific suggestions, hold something cold to the temples, breathe together with a longer exhalation, get exercise such as jumping jacks, squeeze something hard; praise the willingness; keep trying if the first do not work; repeat the validation. These are DBT's TIPP crisis-survival skills, temperature, intense exercise, progressive muscle relaxation, paced breathing, all of which lower heart rate; cold works through the bradycardic diving reflex, and a low heart rate tells the limbic system the danger is over. The sequence: validate, both-and, offer help, suggest a skill, suggest another. If she declines, back off respectfully, keep validating, give space. If she is still distraught and time is up, do a brief risk assessment to decide about the emergency department, end gently, and give handouts or websites.

The clinician's stance

Coach and cheerlead; do not do for patients what they can do themselves (help her plan and rehearse a call to the landlord rather than making it). Polite gestures are fine. In an unfamiliar boundary situation, being followed on social media, a run of personal questions, take time and consult a colleague. Frustration is common, because change is hard and patients can be hostile, demanding or withdrawn, and it has produced considerable stigma toward BPD among health professionals. The antidote is the dialectic: the lives of suicidal people are unbearable as currently lived; they are doing the best they can, they want to improve, and they need to try harder.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • 2 to 6, 6, 10, 20: population, primary care, outpatients, inpatients. 8 to 10% suicide; three quarters self-harm; 75% respond to DBT; no sex difference in the community.
  • Five of nine, four domains (3 affect, 2 behaviour, 2 cognition, 2 interpersonal), 256 combinations.
  • Idealization and devaluation of another person = unstable relationships, not unstable self or mood.
  • Micropsychosis is criterion 7, not schizophrenia; a two-week mood episode is not criterion 1.
  • No specific drug; avoid polypharmacy; psychotherapy first. DBT's fourth mode is phone coaching, not family therapy.
  • Mind-reading versus reflection versus normalizing versus makes-sense-in-context are four different validations; "but" undoes them.
Borderline personality disorder is common, lethal in one in ten, and responsive to psychotherapy. Its nine criteria are instability of affect, behaviour, cognition and relationships, five of which make the diagnosis with the counting rules that separate them. No drug treats it; DBT does, and its in-room skills, validation, the both-and statement and TIPP, are what any physician can offer an overwhelmed patient while the referral waits.

guides.title: Week 40 · 11 Self-Harm and Suicide Risk
guides.html:
PD Module 5 · CS2 guide · Byrne L1–L2 · WFQ · CBL 40

Self-Harm and Suicide Risk

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What deliberate self-harm is and does, why it is never unimportant, the assessment after self-harm and the suicide ladder, avoiding reinforcement, disposition, and managing the means.

Self-harm is not suicide, and is never unimportant

Deliberate self-harm is deliberately causing tissue damage in the absence of suicidal intent: superficial cutting, burning, hitting oneself, head banging, overdosing on prescribed or over-the-counter medication. It serves two functions: avoiding intense affect, by providing an intense stimulus that distracts or releases endorphins, and communicating distress, by people who find it hard to put pain into words, to ask for help, or who feel dismissed when they try. The goal of treatment is to learn to tolerate feelings without escaping, avoiding or distracting, which takes a lot of psychotherapy.

  • Self-harm is a BPD criterion but not pathognomonic. It also occurs in teens with depression and in neurodevelopmental disorders, and BPD itself has 256 ways of meeting criteria; self-harm alone never establishes it. Even outside BPD it signals difficulty regulating emotion, so referral to therapy is considered regardless.
  • A patient who says they cut to relieve emotion and were not trying to die is most likely telling the truth. Self-harm often occurs without imminent suicide risk.
  • But self-harm and suicidal ideation often co-occur, and the 1-year suicide rate after self-harm is 439.1 per 100,000 person-years, 37 times the general population's 11.8. Accidental death happens: too many pills, not knowing how dangerous they are, cutting deeper than intended and hitting an artery. Self-harm is never unimportant, because it marks emotional dysregulation needing treatment and possible suicide risk.

The wider picture: men die by suicide more often, women self-harm more often; more than ten Canadians die by suicide each day, suicide is the second leading cause of death from 15 to 34, and BPD carries an 8 to 10% lifetime suicide rate with three quarters of patients self-harming.

Assessing after self-harm

Victoria comes to the emergency department with her boyfriend after a fight, having made five superficial cuts to her wrist with a craft knife; he fears she was trying to kill herself. The question is whether to certify and hold her because she is at imminent risk, and answering it means separating self-harm from suicidal intent.

  1. ABCs and medical treatment first.
  2. Take the self-harm history: age started, methods, frequency, precipitants. Victoria: started at 13, cutting and scratching, two to three times a month, usually after fights with her boyfriend or when she feels rejected or alone.
  3. Ask explicitly about intent at the time. Victoria: relief from awful feelings, despair, fear, shame and worthlessness.
  4. Ask about suicidal ideation without presuming it. Victoria: sometimes, but not this time; while cutting she did not want to die.
  5. Do the suicide risk assessment, looking for intent and future orientation. Victoria has suicidal thoughts she will not act on, no current intent, and is planning to attend a friend's party: low risk.
  6. Screen for the other BPD criteria, remembering that not everyone who self-harms has BPD, especially adolescents, and get a diagnostic assessment and some form of therapy regardless.

The suicide screen itself is a ladder: "Has life seemed so stressful that you think about death or suicide?" then method ("ways you would end your life?"), means ("prepared or acquired the means?"), intent ("how would you describe your level of intent?"), past attempts and when; then classify acute versus chronic and active (plans) versus passive (thoughts of death); and end on protective factors ("what are some reasons for staying alive?"). The history's risk headings are suicide, other self-harm, violence toward others, inability to look after oneself, self-neglect and neglect of dependents, plus safe driving and cooking; and a history of previous attempts is one of the most powerful predictors of suicide at any age. When a patient reveals suicidal ideation, the most important next step is this assessment: what drives it, when it comes and goes, plan, intent, means and access, past attempts, protective factors and hope. Asking does not increase risk.

After an overdose, assess before deciding. A 24-year-old with BPD medically stabilized after an acetaminophen overdose is neither automatically admitted, nor discharged, nor dismissed with "patients with BPD do not benefit from admission": the next step is to assess her current mental state and suicidality. The claim about admission is a half-truth that becomes an error when stated before assessing.

Avoiding reinforcement

Reinforcement is a consequence that makes a behaviour more frequent. For most patients self-harm is reinforced by internal relief from painful emotion; for some it is also reinforced by soothing and caring from others. "Attention-seeking" is an unfair, judgmental label, because the intent is rarely to get attention, but attention that follows self-harm, positive or negative, can make it more frequent, and anger and contempt are still attention.

Too soothingToo hostileRight
"You poor thing, you must really be in pain to do this, I hope now you get the help you need.""What were you hoping this would accomplish?" "I don't know why I'm bothering, you'll do this again next week."Kind, respectful, neutral and matter-of-fact, no less civil than for any other patient; a friendly, light emergency physician who simply asks her to work on the self-harm

Longer term: the sooner warm, caring contact follows self-harm, the more it reinforces it. What helps is genuine warmth when the patient has not recently self-harmed, and genuine disappointment, not punitive anger, when they have. More frequent appointments during a crisis can reinforce crisis behaviour; keep the frequency, or increase it only if the patient can stay away from self-harm and suicide threats.

Management and disposition

ABCs and medical care, suicide risk assessment, encourage follow-up with mental-health resources, refer to psychiatry whenever unsure or for a second opinion. Many patients with chronic, fluctuating suicidal ideation do not benefit from admission: hospitalization can become an escape from ordinary life and a potent reinforcer of suicidal thinking, communication and behaviour. That call is usually the psychiatrist's.

For VictoriaVerdict
Discharge homeYes: not at imminent risk
Certify, or admitNo: unnecessary; she does not intend to act, and admission is not an intervention for self-harm
Refer to therapyYes: the best intervention for learning healthy coping
Tell her contemptuously to manage her feelingsNo: unprofessional, and hostility reinforces
Warmly invite her back to the emergency department whenever upsetNo: drives unnecessary visits; the department is available for emergencies, and the message is emotion-coping skills
Crisis lines and distress-tolerance skills for urgesYes: crisis lines validate; skills build independent coping
Psychoeducation for partner or family, if she agreesYes: a partner who is less panicked makes more helpful suggestions than insisting on hospital

Managing the means

One of the best ways to reduce risk, because if a person has to wait, think or problem-solve, the urge may pass before they act.

MeansAction
HeightsBalcony or high-rise access locked or blocked by someone
Medications at homeReduce supply as far as possible; nobody needs 100 acetaminophen tablets at home
SharpsSome knives are needed for cooking, but not ten
FirearmsIdeally removed; otherwise locked, key inaccessible, ammunition locked separately
PrescribingOne to two weeks' supply; ask about stockpiling and whether they are taking it
Dangerous drugsAsk specifically about insulin, opiates, bulk acetaminophen, and other people's medications such as cardiac drugs

Suicide without a diagnosis

Suicidal thinking is a symptom of many illnesses, one of the nine criteria for a major depressive episode among them, but suicide is not always the outcome of a psychiatric illness. There is the concept of rational suicide and the reality of medical assistance in dying; and many attempts happen while the person is intoxicated, when impulses are poorly managed, so an otherwise healthy person can make an impulsive attempt they would not have made sober. The assessment is the same either way: the attempt is taken seriously, the intent and the means are established, and the role of alcohol or drugs is named as a risk factor in its own right.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Intoxication turns ideation into action; an attempt without a psychiatric diagnosis still gets a full risk assessment.
  • Tissue damage without suicidal intent is the definition; believe the stated intent and assess anyway.
  • 439.1 versus 11.8 per 100,000; 37 times.
  • Assess before admitting, discharging or dismissing after an overdose.
  • Neutral, matter-of-fact, civil acutely; warmth when not self-harming; no escalation of visit frequency in a crisis; "for emergencies", never "whenever you're upset".
  • Admission can reinforce chronic fluctuating suicidality; the psychiatrist decides.
  • One to two weeks of medication, ask about insulin, opiates, acetaminophen and others' cardiac drugs; firearms locked with ammunition separate.
  • Self-harm in a 17-year-old is affect avoidance until proven otherwise, and not BPD by itself.
Self-harm is tissue damage without suicidal intent, usually to escape unbearable feeling, and the patient's account of intent is usually true; it still marks a 37-fold suicide risk and always earns a risk assessment. The response is neutral and civil, never soothing or hostile; the disposition for low risk is discharge with therapy, crisis lines, skills and family education; and the highest-yield intervention is restricting the means.

guides.title: Week 40 · 12 Biological Treatments: Psychotropics, Monoamines, Neurostimulation and Psychedelics
guides.html:
Byrne L3 · L2 · PD Module 4 · WFQ

Biological Treatments: Psychotropics, Monoamines, Neurostimulation and Psychedelics

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The seven classes and their crossover uses, the three monoamine systems and dopamine's pathways, every drug named by indication, ECT and the other neurostimulation techniques, complementary medicine, and psychedelics acting on the default mode network.

Treatment mirrors formulation

The formulation grid has biological, psychological and social columns; so does treatment. Biological treatments are medications, neurostimulation, complementary and alternative medicine, and the emerging psychedelic therapies; psychological and social, cultural and spiritual treatments are the subject of the next guide. Psychiatry is not a talking-only specialty: psychiatrists prescribe, deliver ECT, order investigations and examine patients, and almost nobody on an inpatient unit is not on a psychotropic. The frame for the whole subject: people's mental health can get better, and a doctor's job is largely to instil hope, because there is a great deal that helps people suffer less.

Seven classes, and what they are really used for

Psychotropic drugs are medications used to treat psychiatric disorders, commonly described by their primary clinical application. "Commonly described by" is not "only used for".

ClassPrimary applicationCrossover use
AntidepressantsDepressionAlso first line in anxiety disorders
AntipsychoticsPsychosisAlso mood disorders, and augmentation of antidepressants in depression
Mood stabilizersBipolar disorder
AnxiolyticsAnxiety
HypnoticsSedationAgitation in the emergency room, as in psychosis or methamphetamine intoxication
Cognitive enhancersDementia
StimulantsADHD

Monoamines

Serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine are key neurotransmitters in mood, cognition and behaviour, and many psychiatric medications modulate them. Their neurons arise in small brainstem nuclei, receive input from the spinal cord below and the cortex above, and project diffusely to executive (frontal lobes, striatum), limbic (cingulate, hippocampus) and sensory cortex: a few million monoamine neurons among about 100 billion, acting as switches for whole networks and running like main highways, which is why modulating them changes mood, cognition and behaviour at once and why side-effect profiles are broad.

MonoamineFunctionsNucleusTargeted by
Serotonin (5-HT)Mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite, painRaphe nucleiSSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics
NorepinephrineAttention, arousal, mood, stressLocus coeruleusSNRIs, tricyclics, bupropion, stimulants
DopamineReward, motivation, movement, psychosisMidbrainAntipsychotics, stimulants, bupropion

High dopamine produces psychosis: methamphetamine, an amphetamine, raises dopamine rapidly and at high enough levels causes paranoia and hallucinations; in schizophrenia there is too much dopamine in certain pathways, and antipsychotics generally lower it. Low dopamine produces amotivation and anhedonia, the state of depression and substance use disorders, which is the rationale for a dopamine-boosting antidepressant such as bupropion. Four pathways: mesolimbic (emotion, reward), mesocortical (cognition, motivation), nigrostriatal (movement), tuberoinfundibular (prolactin). Dopamine and norepinephrine differ by a single hydroxyl on the side chain; serotonin is an indole. An SNRI is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, hitting both transporters; SSRIs are selective for serotonin and are not norepinephrine agents.

Most first-line antidepressants target serotonin and/or norepinephrine, the monoamines of mood regulation. On a question about a newly prescribed antidepressant, the answer is norepinephrine and serotonin; dopamine paired with glutamate, GABA with acetylcholine, and oxytocin with endorphins are not standard antidepressant mechanisms.

Medications by disorder

IndicationClassAgents
DepressionSSRIsFluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline, escitalopram
SNRIsVenlafaxine, duloxetine
OthersBupropion, mirtazapine, tricyclics, MAOIs
Bipolar disorderMood stabilizersLithium: mania, depression and suicide prevention; valproic acid: acute mania; carbamazepine, lamotrigine: lamotrigine more effective for bipolar depression
Atypical antipsychoticsAcute episodes or maintenance
Anxiety disordersAntidepressantsSSRIs, SNRIs
BenzodiazepinesLorazepam (Ativan), clonazepam: short-term only, dependence
Beta-blockersPropranolol: performance anxiety, physical symptoms
Psychotic disordersFirst-generation (typical)Haloperidol (Haldol)
Second-generation (atypical)Risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine
Treatment-resistantClozapine
ADHDStimulantsMethylphenidate (Ritalin), amphetamine salts (Vyvanse, Adderall)
Non-stimulantsAtomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine
DementiaCholinesterase inhibitorsDonepezil
NMDA antagonistMemantine
Antipsychotics, cautiouslyFor agitation
Substance useAlcohol, anticravingNaltrexone, acamprosate
Alcohol, withdrawalDiazepam (Valium) with thiamine, admission with intravenous treatment; withdrawal cover and craving management are different problems
OpioidsMethadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist; Suboxone)
Personality disordersNo approved medication; antidepressants for comorbid depression or anxiety; antipsychotics and mood stabilizers controversial in BPD; avoid polypharmacy

The pairings that get asked: lithium for suicide prevention; lamotrigine for bipolar depression; valproate for acute mania; clozapine for treatment resistance; propranolol for performance anxiety; benzodiazepines short-term only; memantine the NMDA antagonist and donepezil the cholinesterase inhibitor; methadone full and buprenorphine partial agonist. The rule for memorization is to know the class of each drug; questions give clues. Withdrawal from central nervous system depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates) causes seizures, delirium tremens and death; opioid withdrawal does not kill.

Medication hesitancy. A woman with persistent depression, early-morning waking and minimal benefit from three months of psychotherapy who fears side effects is met by exploring her concerns and providing information, shared decision-making. Neurostimulation for "therapy failure" and inpatient referral to start medication are premature escalation or coercion.

Neurostimulation

Brain stimulation uses electrical currents or magnetic fields to alter neuronal firing. Transcranial, applied outside the skull: ECT, transcranial direct current stimulation, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, magnetic seizure therapy. Surgical: cortical brain stimulation, deep brain stimulation, vagus nerve stimulation. Neurostimulation is reserved for resistant cases.

  • Electroconvulsive therapy induces a seizure. Under general anaesthesia with an anaesthetist present, the psychiatrist applies electrodes to the head, the patient has a generalized seizure with muscle relaxants given to reduce its physical impact, and wakes after a few minutes. Typically 8 to 12 seizures, three times a week, over a few weeks. It is the most effective antidepressant treatment, and life-saving; a lawyer with a psychotic depression, nihilistic delusions, and no response to multiple medications, is the kind of patient who responds. Most effective is not first line: ECT comes after multiple failed medications and therapies.
  • Deep brain stimulation places an electrode in the brain connected to a pacemaker-like device under the skin, for very treatment-resistant depression; the surface of the brain has no pain receptors, so electrode placement can be done awake. Sunnybrook is a major centre.
The anaesthesia clue
A 63-year-old with severe depression unresponsive to multiple medications, psychotherapies and psychedelic therapy prepares for a treatment requiring general anaesthesia. It is ECT: a seizure cannot be induced in an awake patient, whereas DBS can be placed awake.

Complementary and alternative medicine

CAM comprises non-conventional approaches used alongside (complementary) or instead of (alternative) standard care; 30 to 50% of psychiatric patients use it, often without telling their clinician, and it aligns with holistic, mind-body-spirit principles and appears in mainstream guidelines. Named agents: omega-3 fatty acids, with reasonable evidence in mild depression, and chamomile; vitamin D and lavender also have some evidence in mild depression. The point is not the agents but that patients take them and will ask about them.

Psychedelics

Psychedelics alter perception, cognition and affect through 5-HT2A receptor agonism, which disrupts default mode network activity and increases neuroplasticity and BDNF expression. The classical compounds are psilocybin (magic mushrooms), LSD, DMT (ayahuasca) and mescaline (peyote); MDMA and ketamine are sometimes included although pharmacologically distinct, ketamine being an NMDA receptor antagonist with profound effects in depression. They have been used for thousands of years in spiritual and shamanic settings, were studied in the last century, shut down by the war on drugs, and are now re-emerging, with an active research programme at CAMH.

The brain runs on eight to twelve networks. The default mode network, a loop from frontal to lower structures, monitors the internal state during mind-wandering and is supposed to switch off for a task. In depression it is hyperactive and does not shut off, experienced as rumination. SSRIs reduce that hyperactivity; ketamine does too; psychedelics do it intensively, a reboot with a surge of neuroplasticity factors.

ConditionCompoundFinding
Major depressive disorderPsilocybinTwo doses gave rapid, sustained reduction in depression (NEJM 2021)
PTSDMDMA-assisted therapyPhase 3 trial: 67% no longer met criteria at 2 months versus 32% on placebo (Nature Medicine 2021)
End-of-life anxietyPsilocybinOne session reduced existential distress for months (J Psychopharmacology 2016)
Alcohol use disorderPsilocybinPilot trial: significant reduction in heavy drinking days (JAMA Psychiatry 2022)

"Psychedelics may act as a catalyst for psychotherapeutic processes rather than a standalone cure." The same compound in a dark room among frightened people is unlikely to help and with a guide in a supportive setting likely to; the biology is measurable, and set and setting, with the accompanying psychotherapy, still matter, which is the bridge to the psychological treatments.

The review lecture: scope, ECT, ketamine and psychedelics in practice

The scope for pharmacology: knowing the drugs in the medication table is sufficient, and exam stems will carry clues to the class (a patient with low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep and low energy who is prescribed fluoxetine is being treated with an antidepressant that acts on serotonin from the raphe nuclei). Trade names are not required. The list to know: antidepressants fluoxetine (SSRI), venlafaxine (SNRI), bupropion, mirtazapine; mood stabilizers lithium, valproate, lamotrigine; antipsychotics haloperidol (first generation), risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine (second); anxiolytics are the antidepressants again, with benzodiazepines such as lorazepam short-term and beta-blockers such as propranolol for performance anxiety; ADHD methylphenidate and the amphetamines (the two stimulant families) plus atomoxetine and guanfacine; substance use naltrexone and acamprosate (anti-craving) and methadone and buprenorphine (opioid agonists). Lithium is uniquely anti-suicidal, and mood stabilizers are also used to augment treatment in unipolar depression.

Question raisedAnswer
Are ECT and deep brain stimulation interchangeable?No. ECT is standard of care for treatment-resistant depression, acute suicidality and catatonia (in depression or schizophrenia); it is effective, and the patient is asleep for a few minutes. DBS is experimental, a last resort after standard treatments including ECT have failed.
What are the side effects of ECT?Mostly anaesthesia-related (death under general anaesthetic roughly 1 in 100,000) or seizure-related: post-ictal confusion; rare longer-term memory problems, with most patients' memory and cognition recovering completely; a sore jaw; rare cracked teeth or fractures, which muscle relaxants and restraints are given to prevent.
Are psychedelics available to patients in Canada?Only through Health Canada special access, granted rarely (end-of-life distress) and hard to obtain, or through research trials such as the psilocybin programme for treatment-resistant depression. Ketamine is not a psychedelic: an NMDA antagonist, available by prescription, inpatient or outpatient, for treatment-resistant depression and PTSD and for chronic pain; any physician can prescribe it.
Is a benzodiazepine a treatment for panic disorder?No. It can be used occasionally while definitive treatment takes hold if attacks are severe, but it carries tolerance and dependence, and first-line treatment is an antidepressant taken daily and standing, with cognitive behavioural therapy.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • ECT is standard of care (resistant depression, acute suicidality, catatonia); DBS is experimental. ECT risk is mostly anaesthetic, about 1 in 100,000.
  • Ketamine is prescribable and not a psychedelic; psilocybin is special access or research only. A benzodiazepine is not a treatment for panic disorder.
  • Antidepressants treat anxiety; antipsychotics treat mood disorders and augment antidepressants.
  • Serotonin from the raphe, norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus; antidepressants target both; dopamine up is psychosis, dopamine down is anhedonia.
  • Lithium prevents suicide; lamotrigine for bipolar depression; valproate for acute mania; clozapine for resistance.
  • ECT: general anaesthesia, 8 to 12 treatments three times a week, most effective antidepressant, reserved for resistant cases. DBS can be placed awake.
  • 30 to 50% use CAM, often undisclosed.
  • 5-HT2A agonism, default mode network, BDNF; ketamine is an NMDA antagonist; 67% versus 32% for MDMA in PTSD.
  • Explore concerns before escalating; benzodiazepines are short-term; diazepam plus thiamine for alcohol withdrawal.
Biological treatment modulates the monoamine highways from the brainstem, so the classes cross indications more than their names suggest. The drug-by-disorder table carries the pairings that get tested, neurostimulation begins with ECT and is reserved for resistant illness, a third to a half of patients use complementary agents without saying so, and psychedelics act on the ruminating default mode network as catalysts for psychotherapy rather than cures.

guides.title: Week 40 · 13 Psychological, Social, Cultural and Spiritual Treatments
guides.html:
Byrne L3 · L2 · PD Module 4 · WFQ · CBL 40

Psychological, Social, Cultural and Spiritual Treatments

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What psychotherapy is and why validation comes first, the three waves with their tools (defences, cognitive distortions, the physiological sigh, TIPP, the body scan), social interventions, and cultural and spiritual care.

What psychotherapy is

Psychotherapy is the informed and intentional application of clinical methods and interpersonal stances derived from established psychological principles, to help people modify their behaviours, cognitions, emotions or other characteristics in directions the participants deem desirable (Norcross, 1990). Two phrases carry the weight: it is derived from established principles, so it is not just talking, and the patient defines the goal. There are many types, each based on a model of psychological difficulty, and a year of psychiatry residency is spent learning to be a psychotherapist. Psychotherapy is not fluffy: it changes the brain measurably, in a pattern that differs from medication. In major depression, CBT increases hippocampal and dorsal cingulate activity and decreases dorsal, ventral and medial frontal activity, while recovery on paroxetine increases prefrontal and decreases hippocampal and subgenual cingulate activity, opposite directions in the same regions.

Validation is a central feature of psychotherapy. Physicians want to fix things, but in psychotherapy what the clinician thinks someone should do does not matter; it has to come from the patient's own experience and context. Before anything else, show the person that their suffering is understood. "That sounds really hard" is the validating response; a rush to point out the nail in their forehead is not. If nothing else about psychotherapy is known, validate, and keep validating; it cannot be overdone.

Three waves

PsychodynamicCognitive behavioural therapyThird wave: DBT and ACT
EraThe old school, from Freud, Anna Freud and JungTraditional, from the 1980s and 1990sNewer
Core ideaUnconscious conflicts and early relationships shape current patternsThoughts, feelings and behaviours all influence each other; identify and challenge automatic thoughtsAcceptance, mindfulness, values-driven behaviour; change the relationship with thoughts rather than the thoughts
MethodSelf-awareness, emotional insight, the therapeutic relationship; exploration of defences, transference and repetition of past relational patterns; less structured; short- or long-termCognitive restructuring, behavioural experiments, homework, goal setting, relaxation training, in vivo and interoceptive exposure; practical and time-limitedDBT: emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, mindfulness, from dialectical philosophy, Buddhism and behaviour therapy. ACT: accept painful experience while committing to actions aligned with values
IndicationsChronic mood disorders, personality disorders, relational difficultiesPanic disorder (with fluoxetine, the L1 case), anxiety disorders and depression as first lineDBT especially effective in borderline personality disorder and emotion dysregulation
How it looks in a vignetteA 37-year-old with insecurity and relationship conflict whose sessions focus on his childhoodA 30-year-old whose therapist tracks her thoughts and tests their accuracy with worksheetsSkills groups, crisis skills, mindfulness practice

A therapy is identified by what the sessions do, not by the diagnosis: childhood and early relationships point to psychodynamic work; thought records and worksheets to CBT.

Psychodynamic tools

A patient who feels abandoned in relationships explores how early parental neglect produces an intense fear of rejection in therapy. Transference, the patient's past relationships imported onto the clinician, and countertransference, the clinician's own reaction, are psychodynamic constructs used in every interview. Defence mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies that protect against anxiety, conflict or distress; there are dozens, and five are taught.

DefenceDefinitionExample
DenialRefusing to accept realityA patient insists they do not have cancer despite clear evidence
ProjectionAttributing one's own thoughts or feelings to othersAngry oneself, asking a partner "why are you so angry at me?"
SublimationChannelling impulses into socially acceptable outletsAnger after a breakup goes into a ten-mile run; aggression into competitive sport
DisplacementRedirecting emotion to a safer targetCriticized by the boss, yelling at family; upset by a harsh attending, ignoring the dog at home
RegressionReverting to earlier developmental behaviourAn adult's tantrum under stress; acting like one's twelve-year-old self at a family dinner

CBT tools

Cognitive distortions and restructuring

Distortions are thinking patterns that arise under stress as attempts to simplify reality and reduce anxiety, and that make things worse in the long run; helping people notice their own tendencies ("I do a lot of all-or-nothing thinking; this is not reality") is cognitive restructuring.

DistortionDefinitionExample
All-or-nothing thinkingBlack and white"If I'm not perfect I have failed"; "either I do it right or not at all"
Over-generalizingA pattern from a single event; overly broad conclusions"Nothing good ever happens"
Mental filterAttending only to certain evidenceNoticing failures but not successes
Disqualifying the positiveDiscounting good things that happened or that one did"That doesn't count"; "he only invited me to be nice"
Jumping to conclusionsMind reading (knowing what others think) and fortune telling (predicting the future)"None of the students liked the lecture, because nobody spoke to me after"; "I for sure failed the exam"
Magnification (catastrophizing) and minimizationBlowing things out of proportion, or shrinking them"If I fail the exam I'll be expelled, then I can't pay rent, then I'll be homeless"; the chain is the giveaway

The physiological sigh

Two inhales through the nose followed by an extended exhale through the mouth: the biggest inhale of the day, another sip of air at the top, then a slow exhale through pursed lips of at least ten seconds. It is what a child does recovering from a tantrum. The chain: anxiety is sympathetic overdrive; a slow exhale lowers intrathoracic pressure and alters venous return, lowering heart rate and blood pressure; the low heart rate and pressure are signalled up the brainstem to the limbic and midbrain emotion structures, "everything is OK"; and the prefrontal cortex comes back online, so cognitive techniques become usable. The body settles first, then the thinking works. Three repetitions can drop the heart rate by 15 to 20 beats per minute, and a participant in a meditation group fainted from the fall in blood pressure; it is best tried before an exam or a presentation, not somewhere fainting would matter. It is taught to the panic patient, and to the anxious patient in an emergency department waiting for an X-ray, on any rotation.

Third-wave tools

TIPP

DBT's crisis-survival skills reduce physical arousal, tipping body chemistry from sympathetic to parasympathetic; every letter lowers heart rate, and a low heart rate tells the limbic system the danger is over.

LetterSkillHow
TTemperatureIce pack on the back of the neck or temples, cold water on the face; the bradycardic diving reflex lowers heart rate as temperature drops
IIntense exerciseTen jumping jacks
PProgressive muscle relaxationSqueeze the fists for a five-count and release; shrug the shoulders and release; push the feet into the floor and release; then all together
PPaced breathingExhale longer than inhale; the physiological sigh

Mindfulness: the body scan

When distressed, people live in their heads and forget they have bodies; grounding in the body relaxes the mind. The seven steps: find a quiet place and get comfortable; warm up with deep breaths; slow down your thoughts; start at one end of the body; move to the next part; be mindful in all parts; come back into the room. In practice: settle with deep breaths, let the shoulders fall and the spine lengthen, set aside what came before and what comes next, sweep attention from the soles of the feet up through the legs, pelvis, spine, shoulders, arms, hands, abdomen, chest, neck, skull and face to the ears and to sound, noticing tension, tingling, temperature or nothing at all without trying to change it, and returning attention to the body each time it wanders. Validation, relaxation training and cognitive restructuring are the three psychotherapy skills every student practises.

Social interventions

Social determinants of health are strongly linked to psychiatric outcomes, and social interventions are not adjuncts but essential components of effective psychiatric care (Compton and Shim, 2015). The determinants: education access and quality, health-care access and quality, neighbourhood and built environment, social and community context, economic stability. Formulate someone, then intervene socially as well.

InterventionExamplesPurpose
Case managementAssertive Community Treatment, Intensive Case ManagementLink treatment with practical support
Supportive housingHousing First, rent subsidies, shelterStable housing and recovery
Income supportDisability benefits such as ODSP, medical leaveAddress financial strain and basic needs
Peer supportPeer mentors, lived-experience programmesConnection, hope, self-confidence

A 62-year-old man with schizophrenia who lives alone, misses follow-up, has run out of his prescriptions, and has lost food and electricity needs assertive community treatment and housing support: the option that brings the service to the patient rather than asking the patient to come to the service. "ACT" here is Assertive Community Treatment, not acceptance and commitment therapy. For a refugee claimant the same principle runs through settlement agencies, refugee lawyers and legal aid, social work, Ontario Works and housing services, primary care and newcomer clinics, affirming LGBTQ+ organizations and culturally appropriate mental-health services, and a physician's advocacy runs up a ladder from the individual patient to the institution, the community and policy.

Cultural and spiritual considerations

  • Explanatory models: ask "What do you think is happening?" rather than assuming one's own mental model applies. A refugee who attributes hypervigilance and nightmares to ancestral spirits is engaged by exploring that model and booking follow-up.
  • Language barriers: trained interpreters, not family.
  • Social context: racism, migration stress and poverty worsen illness, and interventions should address them.
  • Spirituality: ask "Do you have spiritual or religious beliefs? Do they help you cope?" Positive effects are community, meaning and lower suicide risk; religious affiliation is strongly protective against suicide, and many patients will not raise it unless asked. Negative effects are guilt, feeling punished and conflict with medical advice. Practical issues: Ramadan fasting and medication timing; halal, kosher or vegetarian diet and pill ingredients. First Nations, Inuit and Métis patients may want traditional healing, Elders, ceremony and land-based practice, with or without Western care; an inpatient unit may have Indigenous healers attending.
  • Approach with cultural humility: be respectful, ask, and collaborate.

Trauma therapies, mindfulness and identifying the modality

Questions from the review lecture filled two gaps. Post-traumatic stress disorder has several evidence-based psychotherapies, and nearly all share memory work: avoidance perpetuates PTSD, not wanting to think about or remember what happened is part of what keeps it alive, so the therapies bring the memory into the present in a systematic way and help the person face and reprocess it. EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) does this while the patient makes horizontal saccadic eye movements and is listed in the Canadian anxiety guidelines, which have not been updated since 2014; prolonged exposure has the patient tell the trauma story repeatedly until it loses its charge; trauma-focused CBT and cognitive processing therapy are the other named forms. Mindfulness is fundamental to any psychotherapy: a person has to be aware of a thought or a behaviour before it can be examined or changed, which is why teaching awareness of experience comes first.

The modality is identified from what the sessions do. Exploration of defence mechanisms and of the patient's feelings toward the therapist (transference), and attention to how a critical parent shaped self-image, are psychodynamic; CBT stays in the present with thoughts and behaviours and would not go there; DBT is present-focused and skills-based, the therapy of borderline personality disorder and emotional dysregulation; acceptance and commitment therapy teaches a person their values and how those drive behaviour. A stem that describes long-standing insecurity and relationship conflict without naming a disorder is another clue away from CBT.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • PTSD therapies share memory work because avoidance perpetuates PTSD; EMDR, prolonged exposure, trauma-focused CBT and cognitive processing therapy.
  • Defence mechanisms plus transference = psychodynamic; mindfulness underlies every modality.
  • Childhood focus = psychodynamic; worksheets and thought-testing = CBT; skills and mindfulness = third wave.
  • Panic disorder is treated with CBT (interoceptive exposure) plus an SSRI; DBT is for BPD.
  • Five defences, six distortions; mind reading and fortune telling are both jumping to conclusions.
  • Slow exhale lowers heart rate and blood pressure, then the prefrontal cortex returns; at least ten seconds out; syncope is possible.
  • TIPP: temperature via the diving reflex, intense exercise, progressive muscle relaxation, paced breathing.
  • Four social interventions: case management, supportive housing, income support, peer support; the answer brings the service to the patient.
  • Interpreters, not family; ask about spirituality; fasting and diet change prescribing.
  • Psychotherapy changes the brain, in a pattern that differs from medication.
Psychological treatment starts with validation and then follows one of three models: uncovering early relational patterns, testing and restructuring thoughts, or changing the relationship with thoughts through acceptance and skills. Its physical tools, the sigh, TIPP and the body scan, work by lowering arousal so that thinking can resume. Social, cultural and spiritual interventions are not adjuncts: housing, income, case management, peer support, the patient's own explanatory model and their beliefs shape recovery as much as any prescription.

guides.title: Week 40 · 14 CBL 40: Stanley, a Refugee Claimant with Trauma
guides.html:
CBL 40 · all fifteen questions

CBL 40: Stanley, a Refugee Claimant with Trauma

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The whole case and its questions in one place: engaging across language and culture, the history, risk, investigations, the four-column formulation, the label question, and the supports and advocacy that are the treatment.

The case

Stanley is a refugee claimant who fled his country after a violent attack in which he was injured and his mother died, in the context of persecution for same-sex relationships. He has a shoulder injury with persistent pain, poor sleep, trauma reminders, guilt and self-blame, fear of being returned, unstable housing, financial insecurity, disrupted work, a language barrier, and a refugee hearing ahead. He has a supportive cousin, employment and education, and he is future-oriented and help-seeking. The case is built around fifteen questions, several individual and most for the group; the group's draft answers are partial and the case is completed later in the block. This guide gathers the whole case and its answers in one place; each answer's full teaching sits in the topic guide named beside it.

Before the encounter

1. Facts about his refugee status

Support networks and resources; health coverage (Interim Federal Health Program before provincial coverage); the stage of the claim and the hearing date; legal representation; work-permit status; family in Canada and abroad; and safety if returned. Identifying data in psychiatry is the social context of the illness, and for a claimant it includes the legal process itself.

2. Special considerations for communication

A possible language barrier, met with a trained interpreter, never a family member; trauma-informed care, safety and control for a patient who may disclose horror; and cultural difference without assumptions, eliciting his explanatory model with "what do you think is happening?" rather than assuming one's own applies. The six strategies against bias apply: cultural humility, the Cultural Formulation Interview, eliciting the patient's perspective, collaborating with interpreters and cultural liaisons, learning idioms of distress, and separating pathology from accepted practice.

During the interview

3. A closed-off patient

Reassurance; confidentiality reviewed up front with its three exceptions; a safe, comfortable environment; attention to one's own body language, tone and attitude; and time. The interview should not feel like an interrogation, and a patient who feels judged clams up. Resistance is a phenomenon to notice and name gently, not to steamroll: "I notice this is hard to talk about; what's going on for you right now?"

4. Responding empathically to trauma

Thank him for sharing and trusting you; acknowledge and validate: "I'm very sorry. You went through something terrifying, and you lost your mother in the middle of it. Thank you for trusting me enough to tell me. How are you feeling talking about this now? Is there anything you need from me right now before we continue?" Empathy is feeling with the person while keeping objectivity; sympathy stays outside; no response begins with "at least". Validate, and keep validating.

7. History-taking with a refugee

The approach is the same: a full history of present illness, symptom by symptom, the four screens, substances, past history, family and personal history, risk. What is added is the refugee-specific context: the persecution, the journey, the loss, the claim, the hearing, coverage and supports. What is easily missed: the developmental and personal history taken to the depth the case needs, and the questions about safety on return.

Making sense of it

8. The formulation

BiologicalPsychologicalSocialCultural
PredisposingNo clear biological vulnerability identifiedLongstanding fear from concealing his sexualityLongstanding threat of discovery and persecutionPersecution of same-sex relationships in his country of origin
PrecipitatingShoulder injury and pain after the attackGrief after his mother's death; guilt and self-blame; fear of returnViolent attack; forced migration; loss of home and occupation; the upcoming hearingDisplacement from his community and its norms
PerpetuatingPoor sleep; persistent painTrauma reminders; guilt; anticipatory fear about returnHousing instability; financial insecurity; occupational disruption; limited supportsLanguage barrier; isolation from a cultural community
ProtectiveNo significant medical comorbidity or substance useFuture orientation; help-seeking; perseverance; capacity to work and planSupportive cousin; employment; educationConnection to an affirming community where available

In one sentence: Stanley experienced severe interpersonal violence, the death of his mother and forced migration in the context of persecution for his sexual orientation, and his distress now is the reactivation of years of concealed fear by an attack and a bereavement, maintained by pain, poor sleep, insecurity and the hearing ahead, and protected against by his own perseverance, his cousin and his work. The template marks the psychological column as advanced; the cultural column is the CBL's addition to the formulation grid, where culture is otherwise folded into social.

9. Investigations while the diagnosis is uncertain

Whether he meets full criteria for PTSD or for adjustment disorder is a question for psychiatry, and Week 41's trauma material is where the criteria live. Meanwhile, medical contributors are excluded: at minimum a CBC and TSH, and for a newcomer as indicated electrolytes, glucose, B12, HIV and hepatitis or STI screening, with imaging if there was head injury. A medical condition can produce a psychiatric picture, hypothyroidism among them, and the diagnostic hierarchy puts physical causes at the top.

13. Making sense of the symptoms; next steps

Hypervigilance, nightmares, avoidance, poor sleep and guilt after a trauma are the norm in the months that follow; most people's symptoms resolve within a year, and persistence beyond a month with impairment is the territory of PTSD, with adjustment disorder and depression as the alternatives. Next steps: complete the risk assessment, the medical work-up, the formulation and the supports below, and refer to psychiatry for the diagnostic question.

14. Does trauma require a diagnosis, and what does a label cost?

Trauma does not go hand in hand with a DSM diagnosis; many exposed people never meet criteria. A label such as PTSD, or "other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder" for the subthreshold case, gains reliable communication, access to treatment and services, evidence-based pathways and, for a hearing, documentation; it costs the arbitrary threshold, heterogeneity, the risk of stigma, and the fact that it says what without saying why. The formulation, not the label, guides care.

15. Trauma, identity and relationships

With or without a diagnosis, trauma alters beliefs about self, others and the world, and about trust, intimacy, anger and self-esteem, the themes the personal history looks for. Stanley's identity was formed under concealment and threat; the attack confirmed the world as dangerous and made the loss of his mother his fault in his own account; relationships are shaped by whether trust is possible again. Attachment cascades and the effects of invalidation describe the same path.

Risk

6. When a patient reveals suicidal ideation

The most important next step is the assessment itself, not disposition. Understand what drives the thoughts and when they come and go; then the ladder: method, means and access, intent, past attempts; classify acute versus chronic and active versus passive; check hope and protective factors; and assess safety. The draft's questions about drivers, plan, certainty and hope are a start; intent, means, past attempts, protective factors and safety complete it. Asking does not increase risk, and previous attempts are among the strongest predictors.

Supports and advocacy

10. Community and interdisciplinary supports

NeedSupport
SettlementNewcomer and settlement agencies
LegalRefugee lawyer; legal aid
Housing and incomeSocial work; Ontario Works; housing services
HealthPrimary care; refugee and newcomer clinics
IdentityAffirming LGBTQ+ community organizations
Mental healthCulturally appropriate services when indicated

These are the four social interventions of psychiatry, case management, housing, income and peer support, applied to a newcomer, and they are essential components of care, not adjuncts. What to document in a letter for the hearing is left open in the draft: a factual account of the symptoms and findings, their consistency with the reported events, their course and impact on function, and the treatment plan, written within the limits of what was observed.

11 and 12. Support in this session, and advocacy

Even in one visit a physician can validate, provide an interpreter, explain the process, connect him to a settlement agency and a newcomer clinic, and begin the letter. Advocacy runs up a ladder from the individual (this patient's coverage and letter) to the institution (interpreter access, refugee clinics) to the community to policy and systems. Organizations named for the Greater Toronto Area: Health Providers Against Poverty (poverty and health equity), the Decent Work and Health Network (employment conditions as determinants of health), Canadian Doctors for Medicare (equitable public health care), Homes First (housing and homelessness), Progress Toronto (municipal advocacy), SURJ Toronto (racial justice).

The history question

5. The DSM and homosexuality

Homosexuality was listed as a disorder in DSM-I (1952) and DSM-II (1968). Evelyn Hooker's early-1950s comparison of thirty gay men and thirty matched controls on projective tests found no difference; a gay psychiatrist addressed the 1972 APA meeting in disguise; it was removed by APA vote in 1973, replaced by "sexual orientation disturbance" and then "ego-dystonic homosexuality" in DSM-III, dropped in 1987. For Stanley the point is direct: the persecution he fled once had a place in the diagnostic manual of the profession now treating him.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Trained interpreter, never family; explore the explanatory model; trauma-informed and assumption-free.
  • Validate before anything else; no "at least".
  • The history is the same history, plus the refugee context.
  • Suicidal ideation: assess, do not dispose; method, means, intent, attempts, protective factors.
