  • CBC and TSH before assuming the picture is purely psychiatric.
  • Four-column formulation; persecution is predisposing, the attack precipitating, the hearing and housing perpetuating, the cousin protective.
  • Trauma does not require a diagnosis; the label has costs and gains; the formulation guides care.
  • Advocacy ladder: individual, institution, community, policy.
Stanley's case runs the whole week: engaging a frightened patient across language and culture, taking the same history with the refugee context added, assessing risk, excluding medical causes, formulating across four columns, and mobilizing the social, legal and community supports that are the treatment as much as any referral. The case is completed later in the block, and this guide is updated when it is.

guides.title: Week 40 · 15 Dermatomes, Myotomes & the Neuro Primer: Lesion Localization
guides.html:
PW02 · NeuroPrimer · Neuro

Dermatomes, Myotomes & the Neuro Primer: Lesion Localization

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The course's own dermatome, myotome and reflex standard, and the primer that turns it into a localization method: root vs cord, UMN vs LMN, and why the imaging you order depends on getting it right.

Definitions, and why the tables differ between books

  • Dermatome — the area of skin supplied by the cutaneous sensory fibres of a single spinal nerve, and therefore arising from a single spinal level.
  • Myotome — the group of muscle cells controlled by the somatic motor fibres of a single spinal nerve. Those cells may be distributed across several different muscles, so one myotome can control more than one movement.
  • Radiculopathy — a lesion of a nerve root. Myelopathy — a lesion of the spinal cord. Every localization answer in this week resolves to one or the other.

Anatomy textbooks and clinical textbooks give different root lists, the anatomy books typically being more inclusive. The clinical resolution is that most muscles are supplied predominantly by one root, or at most two, and it is that predominance that makes precise localization possible. The tables below are the ones used throughout this course, including assessments — they were built from clinical electromyography and neuromuscular texts plus consensus among several neuromuscular neurologists. Where another textbook disagrees, these tables take precedence.

Localization is an intersection
The lesion is the single root shared by every weak muscle. Biceps is predominantly C5 and C6; pronator teres is predominantly C6 and C7. Weakness in both therefore points to a single C6 lesion — (C5, C6) ∩ (C6, C7) = C6. Triceps is a predominantly C7 muscle, so triceps weakness with an intact biceps moves the lesion down a level. The intersection comes before the root is named.
Do not confuse a root lesion with a peripheral nerve lesion. Peripheral nerves form by overlapping of fibres within a plexus, so the cutaneous territory of one peripheral nerve spans portions of several dermatomes. The pad of the thumb is C6 and the pad of the middle finger is C7, yet both are reached by the same peripheral nerve, the median nerve. Numbness in thumb and middle finger together is a median nerve pattern; numbness confined to one of them is a root pattern.

Myotomes

Upper limb movementRoot(s)Lower limb movementRoot(s)
Abduction of shoulderC5Flexion of hipL2, L3
Flexion of elbowC5, C6Extension of hipS1
Extension of elbowC7Abduction and medial rotation of hipL5
Pronation of forearmC6, C7Adduction of hipL3, L4
Supination of forearmC6Extension of kneeL3, L4
Extension of wristC7Flexion of kneeL5, S1
Flexion of wristC7Dorsiflexion of ankleL5
Extension of digitsC7Plantarflexion of ankleS1
Flexion of digitsC8Inversion of ankleL5
Flexion of thumb at IP jointC8Eversion of ankleL5
Abduction and adduction of digitsC8, T1——

Two details of the table are easily missed. Wrist flexion and wrist extension are both C7, opposed movements sharing one root. And the course assigns both ankle inversion and ankle eversion to L5; many clinical texts split them into eversion L5–S1 and inversion L4–L5, but L5 for both is the course standard and the expected answer.

Dermatome test points

One test point per level, the points touched when a limb is screened.

RootUpper limb test pointRootLower limb test point
C5Lateral upper armL1Groin / inguinal
C6ThumbL2Anterior mid-thigh
C7Middle fingerL3Medial knee
C8Little finger and medial border of the handL4Medial malleolus
T1Medial arm and medial forearmL5Dorsum of foot
——S1Lateral foot
——S2Posterior thigh
——S2–S4Saddle / perineal, in concentric rings around the anus

The medial forearm band is T1, not C8 — C8 is the medial border of the hand running into the little finger. Posteriorly there is an axial line separating S2 from L5 and L4: a boundary where dermatomes that sit next to each other on the skin are not neighbouring spinal segments. Because the perineal dermatomes are concentric rings, saddle anaesthesia maps cleanly onto S2–S4, which is what makes it a discrete, testable red-flag finding rather than a vague complaint.

Root, movement, reflex and dermatome in one table

RootKey movement(s)ReflexDermatome
C5Shoulder abductionBiceps (C5, C6); brachioradialis (C5, C6)Lateral upper arm
C6Elbow flexion (C5, C6); supination; pronation (C6, C7)Biceps; brachioradialisThumb
C7Elbow extension, finger extension; wrist flexion and extensionTricepsMiddle finger
C8Finger flexion; thumb flexion at IP; finger abduction (C8, T1)—Little finger
T1Abduction and adduction of digits (C8, T1)—Medial arm
L1——Groin
L2Hip flexion (L2, L3)—Anterior mid-thigh
L3Hip flexion; hip adduction; knee extension (L3, L4)Knee (L3, L4)Medial knee
L4Knee extension, hip adduction (L3, L4)Knee (L3, L4)Medial malleolus
L5Ankle dorsiflexion, big toe extension, ankle inversion, hip abduction; eversion; knee flexion (L5, S1)—Dorsum of foot
S1Ankle plantarflexion, hip extension; knee flexion (L5, S1)AnkleLateral foot
S2–S4——Saddle / perineal

Note the empty reflex cells: there is no routinely tested reflex for C8, T1 or L5. An L5 radiculopathy therefore has to be caught on power and sensation — dorsiflexion, big toe extension, inversion, hip abduction, and the dorsum of the foot — because the reflexes will be normal.

The anatomy that drives localization

  • The cervical canal contains both the spinal cord and the exiting nerve roots, so a cervical disc can compress a nerve root (most common), the cord, or both, depending on its direction (central versus lateral) and size.
  • The spinal cord ends at L1. Below that the canal contains only the lumbosacral nerve roots, so a lumbar disc almost never affects the cord and involves roots alone.
  • Commonest degenerative levels: cervical C5–C6 and C6–C7, then C4–C5; lumbar L4–L5 and L5–S1, then L3–L4. These are also the levels whose radiculopathies are seen most often.
  • The anatomy and the syndrome are distinct: the lumbosacral nerve roots are the structure; cauda equina syndrome is a clinical syndrome caused by compression of those roots.
Cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency
(a) Low back pain plus (b) saddle (perineal) anaesthesia plus (c) bladder and/or bowel dysfunction — urinary retention with overflow, or unrecognized faecal incontinence — with or without leg pain, sensory loss or weakness. It is a CORE Back Tool red flag. The same threshold applies above the conus: compressive myelopathy and cauda equina syndrome are both surgical emergencies once bladder and bowel function are compromised.

Radiculopathy on history is any one or more of: radicular pain, described as shooting or sharp and shock-like; numbness or tingling; weakness; and impaired bladder or bowel control. On examination a root lesion gives sensory loss in a dermatomal distribution and weakness in a myotomal distribution — which is why the two tables above are the examinable core.

Acute mechanism: the nucleus pulposus herniates. In the lumbar spine a lateral herniation impinges a single nerve root and produces a discrete radiculopathy; a central herniation can catch a whole group of roots and is the one that threatens cauda equina syndrome. Chronic mechanism: degenerative change narrows the canal and foramina over years — lumbar spinal stenosis. Three structures crowd the canal at once: thickened ligamentum flavum, hypertrophied facet joints, and a bulging disc. It presents as neurogenic claudication: pain, numbness and/or weakness and fatigue in the legs brought on by prolonged walking, worsened by extension of the back, and relieved by forward flexion or sitting down. That flexion-relief pattern is the discriminator from vascular claudication.

The neurological examination

ComponentWhat to do and what to look for
ToneRule out spasticity
BulkLook for atrophy in muscles sharing a myotome — triceps for C7, gastrocnemius for S1
Power, upper limbShoulder abduction (C5) · elbow flexion (C5, C6) · elbow extension and finger extension (C7) · finger flexion and abduction (C8)
Power, lower limbKnee extension and hip adduction (L3, L4) · ankle dorsiflexion, big toe extension, ankle inversion, hip abduction (L5) · ankle plantarflexion and hip extension (S1)
ReflexesBiceps (C5, C6) · brachioradialis (C5, C6) · triceps (C7) · knee (L3, L4) · ankle (S1) · rule out ankle clonus
Functional testsWalking on the heels for dorsiflexion · walking on the toes and single-leg toe raises for plantarflexion · tandem gait for balance
Plantar responseRule out an extensor response — the big toe extends, with or without fanning of the other toes: the Babinski sign
SensationReduced pinprick in a dermatomal distribution · rule out saddle anaesthesia (S2–S4) · rule out a sensory level
Provocative testsLumbar: straight leg raise (L4–S1) and femoral stretch test (L2–L4) · cervical: Spurling's test
A sensory level is not a dermatomal sensory loss. Dermatomal loss — one band, one level — means a root. A sensory level, a dermatomal level below which all sensation is lost, suggests a spinal cord lesion and changes both the urgency and the region imaged. Testing proceeds upward until the level where sensation becomes normal, and the finding is named as one or the other.

Worked example, S1 radiculopathy, one of the commonest radiculopathies: tone normal; atrophy of the gastrocnemius; weakness of ankle plantarflexion and hip extension; reduced or absent ankle reflex; flexor (normal) plantar response; reduced sensation over the lateral foot. Every element of that constellation is a lower motor neuron sign, and together they name both the level and the compartment.

Upper versus lower motor neuron

The motor pathway is a two-neuron chain spanning the CNS and the PNS. The upper motor neuron has its cell body in the primary motor cortex and descends to synapse on the lower motor neuron, whose cell body sits in the ventral horn and whose axon travels in a peripheral nerve to the neuromuscular junction. The CNS/PNS boundary falls between the lower motor neuron cell body and its axon, at the root exit — which is why a root lesion gives pure LMN signs.

ComponentUpper motor neuron lesionLower motor neuron lesion at a root
ToneIncreased — spasticityNormal or reduced
BulkNormalReduced — atrophy
PowerDiffuse, in an UMN pattern: extensors weaker than flexors in the upper limb, flexors weaker than extensors in the lower limbMyotomal
ReflexesIncreased, with ankle clonusReduced or absent, no clonus
Plantar responseExtensor — pathologicalFlexor — normal

Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in tone — a sudden resistance to quick passive movement of the limb, absent on slow movement. Ankle clonus is elicited with the hip and knee flexed together and the ankle quickly dorsiflexed. The primer introduced this table in the musculoskeletal block as background; it defers the detail to the Neuro block, and this is that block.

Leg weakness: lumbar spine or cervical spine?
Two things make the obvious answer unsafe. Back and neck pain often co-exist, and both a cervical cord lesion and a lumbar root lesion can produce lower limb symptoms alone. A cervical cord lesion strikes the UMN segment of the pathway to the leg; a lumbar root lesion strikes the LMN segment. So a cervical cord lesion can cause leg weakness — while a cervical nerve root lesion cannot. The discriminator is tone, reflexes and plantar response, and it is why the CORE Neck Tool asks about changes in walking and gait.

Why localization changes management

Correct localization is what allows the correct region to be imaged. A wrong localization leads to false reassurance from a normal scan and a missed culprit. The worked error: a cervical disc compressing the cord causes progressive bilateral leg weakness and difficulty walking and needs urgent surgery; the examiner misses the UMN signs, assumes a lumbar cause, orders a lumbar MRI, and the pathology goes unfound — a delay that can end in permanent disability.

Why not simply image the whole spine? Three reasons. Resource stewardship. Time and tolerability — whole-spine imaging takes double to triple as long, and a claustrophobic patient who manages a single region in about 15–20 minutes will not manage close to an hour. And specificity — two-thirds of asymptomatic people show degenerative disc change on imaging, so an unlocalized scan generates findings that cannot be interpreted.

Three questions close every back or neck pain assessment: (1) are there signs of a specific nerve root, and if so which one? (2) are there signs of the spinal cord rather than the roots? (3) are there signs of a surgical emergency — compressive myelopathy or cauda equina syndrome?

Discriminators and exam traps

  • C7 carries the most: elbow extension, wrist flexion and extension, digit extension, the triceps reflex, the middle finger. C8 is digit flexion and the little finger.
  • Elbow flexion is C5, C6 but supination is C6 alone; pronation is C6, C7.
  • Dorsiflexion L5, plantarflexion S1. Hip flexion L2, L3 but hip extension S1. Hip abduction L5 but hip adduction L3, L4.
  • Knee reflex L3–L4, ankle reflex S1, and nothing for C8, T1 or L5.
  • L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot — the three most often swapped.
  • Straight leg raise L4–S1, femoral stretch L2–L4, Spurling's for the cervical roots.
  • The cord ends at L1, so lumbar disc disease hits roots only, while cervical disc disease can hit root, cord or both.
  • In an LMN lesion tone is normal or reduced — normal tone does not exclude a radiculopathy, and the reflex and plantar findings carry the weight.
Localize before imaging: the single root shared by every weak muscle names the level, and tone, reflexes and the plantar response separate root (LMN) from cord (UMN) — a cervical cord lesion and a lumbar root lesion can look identical from the legs, and only one of them appears on a lumbar scan.

guides.title: Week 40 · 16 Imaging of the Nervous System I: Basics of CT and MR
guides.html:
SLM02 · Neuroimaging

Imaging of the Nervous System I: Basics of CT and MR

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How CT and MR generate image contrast, what every sequence shows, and when to order which.

Attenuation: how x-rays make contrast

Imaging modalities divide by whether or not they use x-rays. X-ray based, with a radiation dose: plain films, cerebral angiography, myelography and CT. Not x-ray based: MRI. A heated cathode (−) produces electrons that accelerate to the anode (+) and strike a tungsten target — the x-rays arise at the target, not at the cathode.

The image depends entirely on attenuation: the degree to which x-rays are absorbed, which depends on the density of the material traversed. The rule:

  • High density → high attenuation → white on the image.
  • Low density → low attenuation → black on the image.

The reference materials, in order of decreasing density: lead → bone → muscle → water → fat → air. Every density question in this material — the quizzes, the Hounsfield table, the contrast agents — is that one ordering applied.

CT acquisition and Hounsfield units

CT is still x-ray attenuation, but sampled from many angles: a rotating x-ray source, rotating detectors and a moving table combine into a composite three-dimensional image. Hounsfield units (HU) convert those attenuation values into a visual greyscale, on a scale from −1000 to +1000.

MaterialHU rangeOn brain CT
Bone+400 to +10001000
Soft tissue+40 to +80muscle 60
Grey / white matter—80 / 50
Water, CSF00
Fat−60 to −100−100
Lung−400 to −600—
Air−1000−1000

The exact numbers are not examinable; the ordering is. Two consequences are heavily testable. First, grey matter (80 HU) is denser, and therefore brighter on CT, than white matter (50 HU) — the opposite of their relationship on T1. Second, ranked densest first: iodinated contrast > clotted blood > liquid blood > grey matter > white matter > CSF > fat. Clotted blood is denser than unclotted blood, which is exactly why acute hemorrhage looks hyperdense.

Windowing

Whiter pixels mean higher HU. A monitor cannot display the whole HU range at once, so the window/level settings select which slice of the range is spread across the available greys. Windowing changes nothing about the underlying data — the same acquisition viewed two ways looks like two different scans. Narrow window = high contrast, which amplifies the few-HU loss of grey–white differentiation in early stroke; wide window = lower contrast but a much wider range shown, giving headroom for dense blood alongside normal brain.

Two naming points matter for the exam. One passage calls the centre point the "window" and the range the "level", which is the reverse of standard usage and of the summary — conventionally W = window width = the range and L = level = the centre. And the brain window is printed twice with different numbers: once as a centre of 40 with a range of 100, and once as W80 L40; the centre of 40 agrees, the width does not, so expect either 80 or 100 for the width.

WindowSettingWhat it is for
BrainW80 L40routine parenchymal review
StrokeW30 L30subtle early ischemic hypodensity
BleedW200 L100hyperdense acute blood
Bonecentre 100, range 2000skull, trabecular detail, fractures

Blood on CT by age

Density falls as a clot ages and its protein breaks down, so the same collection changes colour over weeks:

  • Acute — hyperdense, roughly 50–70 HU, brighter than brain. This is the appearance the bleed window is designed to show.
  • Subacute — isodense with brain over days to a couple of weeks. This is the dangerous phase: a subdural collection can be nearly invisible, betrayed only by mass effect or a displaced grey–white junction.
  • Chronic — hypodense, approaching CSF density.

MR signal of blood by age is a separate, more complicated scheme and is not covered here; the working rule to carry is the blanket one — most pathology is bright on T2 and dark on T1 — plus GRE/SWI, where blood products are dark at every age.

Contrast, the blood–brain barrier and safety

All x-ray-based contrast, CT included, is iodine-based: high density → high attenuation → easily seen, and generally non-toxic. MR contrast is gadolinium, visible because it is bright on T1.

Iodinated (CT)Gadolinium (MR)
Why it is visiblehigh density → high attenuationbright on T1
Allergyyes — mild rash through to anaphylaxisyes, but rare
Renal harmcontrast-induced nephropathy; pre-existing renal insufficiency is the single most important risk factornephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure
Otherfluid overload—
Vessels without contrast?no — CTA and CTV both need IV contrastyes — time-of-flight for arteries, phase-contrast for veins

A contrast-enhanced CT head shows three things: cerebral arteries (CTA), cerebral veins (CTV), and regions of blood–brain barrier breakdown — tumour, infection, active inflammation. The mechanism is the single most examinable line here: the integrity of the vessel wall is compromised, so contrast leaks out of the intravascular space. Gadolinium enhancement on MR works by the identical mechanism, and adds the meninges, which is how meningitis enhances.

CTA versus CTV is purely a matter of timing — same injection, same scanner, early acquisition for arteries and late for veins. The MR-specific advantage is that vessels can be imaged with no contrast at all, at a quality described as similar to contrast-enhanced angiography or venography. In practice the non-contrast time-of-flight arterial images can be the crisper of the two; treat the two approaches as comparable rather than assuming contrast always wins.

Renal function matters for both agents, but the injuries are different and are commonly swapped. Iodinated contrast causes contrast-induced nephropathy — renal insufficiency is the risk factor, the kidney is the target. Gadolinium in established renal failure causes nephrogenic systemic fibrosis — renal failure is the risk factor, the skin and connective tissue are the target. Fluid overload is a third, separate iodinated-contrast effect. Screen for ferromagnetic implants and retained metallic foreign bodies before any MR: the static field can move or heat them.

The other x-ray-based modalities

  • Plain films — the best way to screen bone anatomy quickly, and give minimal information about the CNS.
  • Cerebral angiography — images intracranial vessels dynamically, but needs vascular access, usually a femoral puncture, and is therefore invasive; it also needs fluoroscopy and injected contrast.
  • Myelography — lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or lower, to stay below the conus, which ends at L1–L2. Contrast opacifies the CSF around the cord and cauda equina, so a mass or a stenosis appears as an indentation or a block in the white contrast column.

Invasive is the pivot word. CTA/CTV and MRA/MRV are the non-invasive counterparts of catheter angiography, and are the initial tests of choice for a suspected cerebral vascular abnormality.

How MR makes an image

The patient is placed in a strong magnetic field and spinning hydrogen protons align with it. A radiofrequency pulse tips that alignment away; when the pulse stops the protons relax back, releasing energy that is detected and reconstructed into an image. Two relaxation processes are measured, T1 and T2, and every tissue has its own characteristic T1 and T2 relaxation rates — that is the whole basis of MR contrast. The signal from a voxel, a three-dimensional volume of tissue, depends on the number of protons in it plus its T1 and T2. Images are produced by pulse sequences: gradients and RF pulses switched on and off in a choreographed pattern, each designed to interrogate a specific tissue attribute.

Ordering an MRI
A brain MRI automatically includes all of the standard sequences and they need not be specified — except MR angiogram and venogram, which must be requested by name. The requisition must still state the diagnoses to be confirmed or ruled out, because that is what determines the protocol.

The sequences and what each one shows

T1 versus T2: CSF is dark on T1 and bright on T2; white matter is whiter than grey on T1, and darker than grey on T2.

The one-second discriminator
Look at the CSF. Dark CSF = T1. Bright CSF = T2. Then apply the blanket rule: most pathology is bright on T2 and dark on T1.
  • FLAIR — T2-weighted, but with the CSF signal suppressed. It is the sequence for edema and demyelination, because a T2-bright lesion sitting next to a T2-bright ventricle is camouflaged until the CSF is turned off. Periventricular MS plaques are the classic demonstration: invisible-ish on plain T2, conspicuous on FLAIR.
  • DWI with ADC — DWI measures the random Brownian motion of water; the apparent diffusion coefficient, in mm²/s, quantifies it. Low ADC means restricted diffusion, which appears bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map. The two are always acquired and read together, because T2 signal alone can make a lesion look bright on DWI. Causes of restricted diffusion, in order of frequency: acute ischemia or stroke, most commonly, through cellular swelling; densely cellular tumours, typically malignant; and abscess. The stroke mechanism is worth stating precisely — cell death produces cytotoxic edema, water accumulates inside cells, and free movement of water between intracellular and extracellular space is restricted.
  • GRE / SWI — identifies hemorrhage and calcification, both of which appear dark, because both distort the local field: blood products are paramagnetic, calcium and bone are diamagnetic. Multiple small round black dots scattered through the cortex of an older patient are the microhemorrhages of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, a cause of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage.
  • T1 with gadolinium — shows where the blood–brain barrier has broken down. Two enhancement patterns can coexist in a single lesion: a blush (diffuse, hazy) and a ring (bright rim around a non-enhancing centre).
  • MRA / MRV — arteries and veins, obtainable without contrast, and the only sequences that must be requested by name.

Signal cheat sheet

Tissue or findingCTT1 / T2FLAIR · DWI-ADC · GRE
CSF / water0 HU, darkdark / brightFLAIR dark (suppressed); ADC bright
Grey matter80 HU, brighter than whiterelatively dark / relatively brightFLAIR keeps T2-type contrast
White matter50 HU, darker than greyrelatively bright / relatively dark—
Bone / air / fat+400 to +1000 / −1000 / −60 to −100air black; fat bright on T1GRE: bone dark, diamagnetic
Iodinated contrast / gadoliniumdensest thing on the scalegadolinium bright on T1—
Acute blood, clottedhyperdense, denser than liquid blood; bleed windowbright on T2, dark on T1 as a first approximationGRE dark (paramagnetic)
Chronic microhemorrhageoften invisible—GRE: black dots — amyloid angiopathy
Edemahypodensedark / brightFLAIR bright
Demyelination—dark / bright, but camouflaged next to CSFFLAIR bright and conspicuous
Acute infarctsubtle hypodensity; stroke window—DWI bright / ADC dark
Malignant tumour / abscessenhances — barrier broken; ring enhancementblush and/or ring after gadoliniumcan restrict diffusion
Calcificationdense, bright—GRE dark (diamagnetic)

CT versus MR: when to order which

AxisCTMR
Basis and radiationx-ray attenuation and density, in Hounsfield units, viewed through a chosen window; iodine contrast; radiation doseproton relaxation (T1, T2) and proton number per voxel, via pulse sequences; gadolinium; no radiation
Availabilityfar more available, much easier to obtain urgently in the EDslower and scarcer; typically the planned or outpatient study
Subtle abnormalitylower sensitivityhigher sensitivity
Typical usesbone pathology — fractures, dislocations, metastases; acute hemorrhage; trauma; acute strokebrain parenchymal pathology, using sequence-specific information
Urgent vessel questionpreferred — CTA or CTV, e.g. large-vessel occlusion in acute strokenot preferred when the answer is needed now
Contrast allergy or pregnancyavoidpreferred — and can be done with no contrast at all
Ordering mechanicsspecify contrast and phaseall sequences automatic except MRA and MRV
The four deciders
For most vascular questions the information from CT and MR is comparable, so diagnostic yield is rarely what decides. What decides: urgency and availability → CT; already getting an MRI, or needing higher sensitivity for a subtle lesion → MR; prior iodinated-contrast allergy → MR; pregnancy or any reason to avoid radiation → MR.

Practice questions, worked

Lateral skull film, two arrows on the cranial vault — is attenuation high or low? Keyed high. Both arrows sit on skull bone: high density → high attenuation → white. Low is wrong because low attenuation appears black, and the arrowed regions are white.

Lateral cervical spine, one arrow on the dark band anterior to the vertebral bodies — keyed low. The arrow is on the air-filled airway: low density → low attenuation → black. The pair test a single skill — map the greyscale value under the arrow back onto the density ladder.

Worked case: a 36-year-old man presents to the ER after a seizure, and a CT is shown before and after contrast, each asked "is this normal?" Non-contrast: no — there is subtle hyperdensity in the right occipital lobe, which is not expected to be detected at this stage of training. Post-contrast: no, and the abnormality is no longer subtle once intravenous contrast is given — it is a right occipital arteriovenous malformation. The expectation is recognition that the study is abnormal and that contrast unmasked the lesion, not the specific diagnosis from the images alone.

DWI/ADC self-test. Two panels are shown with three questions — which is the DWI and which the ADC, where is the restricted diffusion, and what is the differential. There is no keyed answer available for this one, so no specific diagnosis should be treated as the intended answer. Reasoned through: the panel with dark CSF and bright parenchyma is the DWI and the one with bright CSF is the ADC map; restricted diffusion is the area that is bright on DWI and dark on ADC; and the defensible differential is the standard three — acute ischemia or stroke, densely cellular malignant tumour, abscess.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Grey/white brightness flips between modalities — grey matter is brighter on CT, white matter is brighter on T1. Getting this backwards misreads both.
  • Clotted blood is denser than liquid blood, which is why acute hemorrhage is bright on CT and why a subacute collection fades to isodense.
  • Enhancement is leakage, not uptake. Contrast appears where the vessel wall has lost integrity, not where a tissue has taken the agent up.
  • GRE does not distinguish hemorrhage from calcification — both are dark; only the adjective (paramagnetic versus diamagnetic) differs. Correlate with CT, where calcium is bright and old blood often is not.
  • MR can image vessels with no contrast at all; CT cannot. CTA and CTV always require an injection.
  • Window settings change the picture, never the data — a "negative" CT read on the wrong window is not a negative CT.
Dark CSF is not uniquely T1. FLAIR also shows dark CSF, but keeps T2-type parenchymal contrast, so a lesion that is bright on FLAIR next to dark CSF is not a T1-bright lesion. Whether the periventricular white matter carries T2-type contrast settles it before a sequence is called T1.
Density decides CT — high density → high attenuation → white, measured in Hounsfield units and displayed through a chosen window; proton relaxation decides MR — dark CSF = T1, bright CSF = T2, FLAIR = T2 with CSF suppressed, DWI bright with ADC dark = restricted diffusion, GRE dark = blood or calcium, gadolinium bright on T1; and on either modality, enhancement means contrast has leaked through a broken blood–brain barrier.

guides.title: Week 40 · 17 Development of the Brain
guides.html:
SLM06 · Embryology

Development of the Brain

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Neurulation, neural tube defects, the five vesicles and their cavities, and how grey matter ends up on the outside.

Where the nervous system comes from

The CNS has a single embryological source — the neural tube. The PNS has two — the neural tube and the neural crest. The brain is part of the CNS, so the whole story of brain development begins with the tube.

The neural tube is built twice

The neural tube forms from two separate tissue sources, by two distinctly different morphogenetic mechanisms. In primary neurulation the tube forms by folding of ectoderm. In secondary neurulation it forms by condensation and cavitation of mesoderm left over from the primitive streak. The two lumens then join, and the result is one continuous cavity.

Primary neurulationSecondary neurulation
SourceEctoderm, induced over the notochordMesoderm of the remains of the primitive streak
Mechanismfolding: plate → folds → groove → fusion → tube, then delaminationcondensation into a solid medullary cord, cavitation, and mesenchymal-to-epithelial transformation
Productprimary neural tube — brain and most of the spinal cordsecondary neural tube — the most caudal spinal cord
Timingclosure complete in the 4th week; rostral neuropore ~25 days, caudal ~28 daysafter the caudal neuropore has closed

Ectoderm versus mesoderm is the cleanest discriminator, and the sequencing rule — secondary neurulation only begins once the caudal neuropore is shut — is the second.

Primary neurulation, step by step

Induction occurs in the ectoderm overlying the notochord and is organized by the notochord. It converts that ectoderm into neuroectoderm, forming the neural plate — a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, also called the neuroepithelium. The switch is visible at the molecular level: surface (epidermal) ectoderm expresses L-CAM and E-cadherin, while induced neuroectoderm switches to N-CAM and N-cadherin.

Three named stages follow:

  1. Elevation of the neural folds. The edges of the neural plate lift, bordering a midline neural groove.
  2. Apposition, contact and fusion. The folds move together, touch, and fuse across the midline to form the neural tube.
  3. Delamination. The tube separates from the overlying surface ectoderm.

At about 22 days the dorsal view shows somites flanking the groove and neural crest arising at the crest of the folds, going on to become the dorsal root ganglion.

Why delamination matters
Separation of the tube from the surface does two things at once. It lets the surface ectoderm fuse across the midline, giving the skin over the CNS. And it opens a space for mesoderm to migrate in between tube and ectoderm, giving the bone and the other connective-tissue coverings. The coverings of the CNS exist because the tube let go of the surface.

Closure timing. Closure begins at what will become the cervical spinal cord and proceeds rostrally and caudally at the same time, finishing in the 4th week — often before the pregnancy is recognized. The last two points to close are the rostral and caudal neuropores: the rostral at about 25 days after fertilization, the caudal at about 28 days. Those day numbers are the hard timing data.

Secondary neurulation

The remnant of the primitive streak lies just caudal to the caudal neuropore. Once that neuropore has closed, this mesoderm condenses into a rod-like medullary cord. Its cells lose their unpolarized, stellate mesenchymal appearance and take on a polarized epithelial one — mesenchymal-to-epithelial transformation — becoming a pseudostratified columnar neuroepithelium arranged radially around a cavity. That secondary cavity then becomes continuous with the lumen of the primary neural tube, completing neural tube development.

Sources differ: the slides put the epithelial transformation of the caudal cell mass before the cavity appears; the narration has the lumen develop first and the surrounding cells transform around it. Standard embryology (Langman's; Sadler) describes secondary neurulation as condensation of the caudal eminence mesenchyme into a solid cord that then canalises, so the slide order is the one to give: condense and transform first, cavitate second.

Open neural tube defects

When the neural folds fail to come together, the result is an open neural tube defect. These defects cluster around the rostral and caudal neuropores, for a simple mechanical reason: the neuropores are the last regions to close, so they have the longest window in which to fail.

  • Incidence 1 in 1000 pregnancies.
  • Risk factors: family history, diabetes mellitus, obesity, anticonvulsant use.
  • Most cases have unknown etiology.
  • Folic acid supplementation reduces risk.
Neuropore that failsShould closeResulting defectRegion
Rostral (anterior)~25 daysAnencephalycranial — brain and vault; incompatible with life
Caudal (posterior)~28 daysMyeloschisisspinal cord — an open mid- to lower-back lesion
Anencephaly is not a failure of the brain to form. The brain tissue does form. Because the rostral neuropore stays open, the neural plate remains exposed to amniotic fluid and the tissue progressively deteriorates. It is destruction of tissue that was made, not absence of tissue that was never made — the commonest way this is asked, and the commonest way it is answered wrongly.

Note how the folate point and the timing point fit together. Closure is finished by about 28 days, which for most patients is before a pregnancy is even suspected. That is why folic acid has to be in place before and around conception to do anything — a supplement started at the first antenatal visit is already too late for neurulation. Folic acid supplementation reduces risk; no dose is specified.

Flexures

Once the tube has closed, its rostral end undergoes a series of bends and dilatations. The bends are flexures; the dilatations are vesicles. Three flexures are named:

  • Cervical flexure — where the future spinal cord meets the future brain; a ventral bend.
  • Cephalic (mesencephalic) flexure — at the future midbrain; also a ventral bend.
  • Pontine flexure — in the region of the developing pons, a very acute, sharp bend.

Only the pontine flexure is given a histogenetic consequence, and it is a big one: it everts the alar plates, rearranging the sensory and motor columns of the brainstem. The consequence is described under the alar and basal plates below.

Vesicles, derivatives and cavities

The rostral dilatations first form three primary vesicles — prosencephalon, mesencephalon and rhombencephalon — which then subdivide into five secondary vesicles: the prosencephalon into telencephalon and diencephalon, the mesencephalon staying as it is, and the rhombencephalon into metencephalon and myelencephalon. Those five, plus the rest of the tube, give the whole adult CNS and the whole ventricular system.

VesicleAdult derivativeCavity
TelencephalonCerebral hemisphereLateral ventricles
DiencephalonDiencephalonThird ventricle
MesencephalonMidbrainCerebral aqueduct
MetencephalonPons and cerebellumFourth ventricle
MyelencephalonMedullaFourth ventricle
Rest of the neural tubeSpinal cordCentral canal
Three "only" facts in that table
The diencephalon is the only vesicle whose name does not change on the way to the adult. The metencephalon is the only vesicle with two derivatives (pons and cerebellum). The fourth ventricle is the only cavity supplied by two vesicles (metencephalon and myelencephalon). And the table's real message, in one line: the ventricular system is simply the lumen of the neural tube, regionally dilated.

Expansion of the hemispheres. Fetal brains at 5, 6, 7 and 8 months and at term show a surface that is essentially smooth until about the 5th to 6th month, gyrifying through the last trimester. The mechanism is mechanical: the telencephalic vesicles grow back over most of the other vesicles, then keep expanding while constrained by the developing skull, so the surface folds. The insula folds in first, then the rest of the gyri and sulci appear. The optic vesicle buds from the diencephalon early, but the eye is not followed further here.

Histogenesis: the three zones of the tube wall

Cells born at the lumen migrate outward, and the wall sorts itself into three concentric zones. This is the single scheme that explains grey and white matter.

ZonePositionCells and fateAdult identity
Ventricularinnermost, against the lumenproliferating neuroectoderm that stays putEpendyma
Intermediate (mantle)middleneuroblasts → neurons, glioblasts → glia; neuroblast cell bodies stop hereGrey matter
Marginaloutermostaxons extended outward from those neuroblasts; glioblasts follow and become oligodendrogliaWhite matter

The marginal zone starts as a layer of bare axons. It becomes white matter because some glioblasts migrate out into it, differentiate into oligodendroglia, and myelinate those fibres. Myelin is what converts the marginal zone into white matter.

Alar and basal plates

Within the intermediate zone, neuroblasts accumulate in two columns. Dorsal accumulation creates the alar plates, whose neurons become interneurons receiving input from the fibres of primary sensory neurons in the periphery. Ventral accumulation creates the basal plates, giving motor neurons that grow their axons out into the periphery — both somatic motor and preganglionic autonomic.

Alar plateBasal plate
Position in the spinal cordDorsal; midline partner the roof plateVentral; midline partner the floor plate
Neurons producedInterneurons receiving primary sensory inputMotor — somatic and preganglionic autonomic
At the fourth ventricle, after eversionLateralMedial
Boundary between themSulcus limitansSulcus limitans

At the level of the fourth ventricle — that is, the metencephalon and myelencephalon — the pontine flexure everts the alar plates, swinging them laterally as the roof plate is stretched thin. So the arrangement flips from sensory dorsal, motor ventral in the spinal cord to sensory lateral, motor medial in the floor of the fourth ventricle, with the sulcus limitans still marking the boundary in both.

The alar plate does not contain the sensory neuron. The primary sensory neuron cell body sits in the spinal ganglion and is neural-crest-derived, outside the cord entirely. What the alar plate holds is the interneuron that receives that fibre's input. Saying "the alar plate becomes the sensory neurons" is the classic error.
Alar plate, displaced laterally
Three brainstem nuclei are alar-plate derivatives forced laterally by the pontine flexure: the vestibular nucleus, the spinal nucleus of CN V, and the solitary nucleus. All three are sensory, and all three sit lateral precisely because of the eversion.

The cerebellum

The cerebellum develops at the dorsal edges of the metencephalon — at the rhombic lip, the dorsolateral tip of the everted alar column — and grows to cover the fourth ventricle. The two hemispheres begin dorsally, merge with each other in the midline, and enlarge until the cerebellum roofs the ventricle it grew beside. The same alar column also sends cells migrating ventrally to form the pontine nuclei and the olivary nucleus.

Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus

The Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari) malformation often accompanies open neural tube defects of the spinal cord. The chain is mechanical, in order:

  1. An open spinal NTD tethers the cord and pulls the hindbrain down.
  2. Parts of the cerebellum and medulla are displaced inferiorly into the foramen magnum.
  3. The displaced cerebellum compresses the foramen of Magendie — the median aperture of the fourth ventricle — against the medulla.
  4. CSF produced in the ventricles cannot escape into the subarachnoid space.
  5. It accumulates within the ventricles → hydrocephalus.
  6. Relief is a shunt placed into the ventricles and tunneled under the skin into a body cavity, usually draining to the abdomen, in some cases to the heart.

Hydrocephalus itself is taken up in week 41; what belongs here is the embryological chain from spinal defect to blocked outflow.

Radial glia and the migration disorders

The three-zone plan puts grey matter inside and white matter outside — exactly what the spinal cord looks like. But the cerebral and cerebellar cortices are grey and outermost, the reverse. Grey matter reaches the outside by way of radial glial cells, which conduct migrating neuroblasts out to the cortex in both cerebrum and cerebellum. A radial glial cell spans the full width of the tube wall, from the ventricular surface all the way to the marginal zone. Neurons born in the ventricular zone climb along it until they can go no further, and settle there — which is why the cortex builds up from the inside out. In the cortical wall the three basic zones are refined to five: from the ventricle outward, ventricular → subventricular → intermediate → cortical plate → marginal.

When that migration fails, the grey matter stops short, and the clinical presentation is epilepsy and developmental delay.

DisorderWhat the MRI showsGene
Subcortical band heterotopia ("double cortex")bands of grey matter interposed in the white matter between the cortex and the lateral ventriclesDCX
Periventricular nodular heterotopiagrey matter fails to migrate and remains along the lateral ventriclesFLNA

The position of the ectopic grey matter shows how far the migration got. Grey still lining the ventricle means migration never really started — periventricular nodular heterotopia, FLNA. Grey stranded part-way out means migration arrested in transit — subcortical band heterotopia, DCX. Both are recognized on the grey/white signal pattern, not on the gyral pattern.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • CNS = neural tube only; PNS = neural tube + neural crest.
  • Primary = ectoderm by folding; secondary = primitive-streak mesoderm by condensation and cavitation, and secondary begins only after the caudal neuropore closes.
  • Rostral neuropore ~25 days → anencephaly; caudal ~28 days → myeloschisis — both within week 4, at the last regions to close.
  • Anencephaly is degeneration of tissue that did form after exposure to amniotic fluid, not failure to form.
  • Ventricular → ependyma, intermediate → grey, marginal → white; myelination by oligodendroglia is what makes the marginal zone white.
  • Sensory dorsal / motor ventral in the cord becomes sensory lateral / motor medial at the fourth ventricle, sulcus limitans the boundary at both levels, pontine flexure the cause.
  • Grey is inside in the cord but outside in the cortex — radial glia are the whole reason, and their failure is the heterotopias.
The neural tube is built twice — ectoderm by folding, primitive-streak mesoderm by condensation and cavitation — yet ends as one lumen. Its rostral dilatations become the five vesicles whose cavities are the ventricular system, and its wall is three zones: ventricular to ependyma, intermediate to grey, marginal to white. Every clinical item follows from that plan — the neuropores close last so defects cluster there, the pontine flexure everts alar into lateral, and radial glia are what carry grey matter to the outside.

Night-Before High-Yield

Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders

Week 40 · Psych I — Introduction, Assessment & Treatment, Personality Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite
★ Do-not-miss · first-step reflexes
Suicidal ideation disclosed → direct risk assessment now — ideation, method, means, intent, past attempts, protective factors. Never refer or dispose first.
Overdose or self-harm, medically cleared → assess current mental state and suicidality before admitting, discharging, or declaring that admission won't help. An attempt while intoxicated still gets the full assessment.
Self-harm ≠ suicide → deliberate self-harm is tissue damage without suicidal intent, but 1-year suicide risk after self-harm is 37× — believe the stated intent and assess.
Delusions plus confusion → move UP the diagnostic hierarchy: physical or drug-induced cause, not primary psychosis. Always ask about substances and symptoms when abstinent.
Every depressed patient is screened for mania before an antidepressant, and for psychotic depression when severe; most time spent ill in bipolar disorder is spent depressed.
MDE needs 5 of 9 in one 2-week period, gated on depressed mood or anhedonia — 4 of 9 is not an MDE; adversity does not exclude an episode when the extent and the loss of function say otherwise.
Psychotic depression, refusing food and drink, actively suicidal, medications failed → ECT is standard of care; DBS is experimental.
Open NTD → 1:1000 pregnancies; risk factors family history, diabetes, obesity, anticonvulsants; most idiopathic; folic acid supplementation reduces risk.
Imaging safety → iodinated contrast: allergy, contrast-induced nephropathy (renal insufficiency the key risk factor), fluid overload. Gadolinium: nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure. MR images vessels with no contrast at all.

Burden, stigma and the media Guide 1

Global burden 1 in 8 people have a mental disorder; 1 in 6 years lived with disability
Treatment gap Only about a third of depressed patients in high-income countries are treated
Comorbid mental illness Worsens physical outcomes — admissions, readmissions, cancer mortality
Canada suicide ~12 deaths/day, ~3× higher in men, second leading cause ages 15–34
Youth 1 in 5 meet criteria; anxiety disorders the commonest
Three levels of stigma Individual · interpersonal · structural (racism, no leave)
Papageno vs Werther P = protective (recovery stories lower suicide); W = worse (sensationalized coverage raises it)
Contagion vs the named effect Pick the specific effect over the generic word
Social media Awareness up; misinformation and self-diagnosis common

History of psychiatry and the DSM Guide 2

DSM-III (1980) Paradigm shift: operationalized criteria, atheoretical and descriptive
DSM-I and DSM-II Narrative, not criterion-based; DSM-IV an update, not a shift
DSM-III's three rules Distress/impairment; validated checklist; reliably identifiable only
Inter-rater reliability before DSM-III As low as 30%
Degeneration theory Inherited defects make people "unfit"; endpoint therapeutic nihilism
Shell shock Dr. Charles Myers, WW1; talk therapy and hypnosis; military aim = return to duty
Why the hysteria explanation collapsed Male soldiers presented with a "feminine" disease
Evelyn Hooker, early 1950s 30 gay men vs 30 matched controls — no difference
Only 1930s somatic therapy that survived ECT — built for psychosis, best for mood

Mental disorder and classification Guide 3

What makes a disorder Clinically significant impairment — not the stressor, not the duration
Expectable response Lives in the definition of disorder, not in the depression criteria
Categorical DSM-5-TR (APA), ICD-11 (WHO); discrete, threshold-based
Dimensional HiTOP, RDoC; continuum; research, not practice
Four limitations Arbitrary thresholds, comorbidity, heterogeneity, subthreshold illness
5 of 9 vs 4 of 9 The arbitrary-threshold trap; over 250 combinations = heterogeneity
Panic criterion A Abrupt surge peaking within minutes, ≥ 4 of 13 symptoms
Panic criterion B ≥ 1 month of worry or maladaptive behaviour change
Grief vs depression Any moments of enjoyment? All day, most days? Libido probes anhedonia
Chronic adversity Depression still counts when the extent and the lost function exceed the normative response

Vulnerability: diathesis, stress, attachment Guide 4

Diathesis–stress Illness = predisposition + stressor, both continuous; protective factors buffer
Two sisters, one ill The one with childhood trauma has the higher diathesis
ACEs 10 items before age 18; ~64% have ≥ 1, ~12% have ≥ 4; ≥ 4 = high risk
At ≥ 4 ACEs Depression ~4.4×, drug use > 10×, suicide attempt up to 12×
Each positive childhood experience Lowers adult depression risk 26%
Attachment styles Anxious · avoidant · disorganized; about a third of adults insecure
Attachment to phenotype Anxious → GAD/panic; avoidant → substance, restricting; disorganized → BPD
Evolutionary psychology Once-adaptive traits (anxiety) maladaptive when overshooting
Bias to know Same vignette, Black patient → more schizophrenia; answer = cultural humility, Cultural Formulation Interview, interpreters
Biosocial theory of BPD Emotionally sensitive temperament × invalidating environment

The interview: process Guide 5

Four goals Understand the concern, alliance, diagnosis and safety, shared plan
Four safety items Suicide, violence, driving, children
Confidentiality exceptions Threat to life, child safety, driving — stated before disclosure
Empathy, operationalized Paying attention, then showing it; "that must have been very difficult"
Never begins with "At least…"
Language rule "Die by suicide" not "commit"; "drug use" not "abuse"
Sensitive topics Raise them in the middle — never save them for the end
Resistance · acting out Blocks · discharges; the process comment is the response
Transference · countertransference Patient's past onto clinician · clinician's own reaction; identification = lost objectivity
Unknown medication mentioned Say you don't know, gather details, review with the supervisor
Losing the thread Signpost or summarize, then pivot; one question at a time
Two quick screens Seen or heard things others couldn't? Ever no sleep with tons of energy?
Impression as a student Name what was missed; there is almost always another chance to ask

History content and screens Guide 6

Psychiatric ROS Mood, mania, psychosis, anxiety, cognition, eating, sexual; substances by type, route, frequency, last use
MDE mnemonic MSIGECAPS — nine letters for nine criteria
Mania mnemonic GST PAID — decreased need for sleep, not insomnia
Collateral Psychosis without insight; suicidal presentations in the ED
Bigger in psychiatry Developmental and social history; ask allergies too
Six risk headings Suicide, other self-harm, violence, inability to self-care, self-neglect, dependents

Mental status examination Guide 7

Mnemonic ASEPTIC — the psychiatric physical exam; observed, not asked
Mood vs affect Subjective, in quotation marks vs observed quality, range, stability, congruence
Restricted vs incongruent No variation in expression vs a stated mood that clashes with the affect
Flat vs restricted Flat is the quality; restricted is the range
Hallucination vs illusion No stimulus vs distorted real stimulus
Depersonalization vs derealization Self unreal vs world unreal; non-psychotic dissociation
Modality clues Auditory psychiatric; visual delirium; olfactory neurological/TLE; tactile (formication) substances; hypnagogic benign
Delusion Fixed false belief — thought content, not perception
Thought form ladder Linear → circumstantial → tangential → disorganized; over-inclusive = anxiety; clang and neologisms = severe
Pressured speech Fast and hard to interrupt; its opposite is latency
Prosody Flat in depression; stereotyped in ID/autism; sing-song in mania
Antipsychotic movement signs Parkinsonian shuffle and tremor, tardive dyskinesia, catatonia
Insight vs judgement Recognizing illness (be specific) vs behaviour; both needed for capacity
Depression · mania · psychosis on the MSE Slowed speech and latency · pressured speech · flat affect, internal preoccupation

Diagnosis, formulation, case report Guide 8

Three components of sickness Illness (signs), predicament (context), disease (pathophysiology)
Diagnostic ladder Confusion at the top, impaired reality-testing in the middle, affective symptoms at the bottom
Diagnosis vs formulation What vs why now — a formulation must contain a "because"
The grid 4 P's × bio/psycho/social; the CBL adds a cultural column
The four P's Vulnerability, trigger, maintainer, strengths
Placing a factor Insecure attachment = psychological predisposing; unemployment precipitating; avoidance perpetuating; a symptom is not a factor
Type 1 diabetes Predisposes to depression via inflammation; the mother's depression is heritability in one column, absence in another
The plan's three requirements Biopsychosocial, feasible, mitigates safety concerns
Case write-up History, MSE, diagnostic impression, management plan; summary of 2–3 sentences
Impression shape ID line → course and medical exclusion → diagnosis with criteria → safety negatives and what was missed → plan
OSCE scope Interview technique assessed in every station, not just psychiatry

Personality disorders Guide 9

Trait becomes disorder when It causes distress or functional impairment
General criterion A ≥ 2 of 4: cognition, affectivity, interpersonal, impulse control
Antisocial PD's unique requirement Age ≥ 18 plus conduct disorder before age 15; lowest threshold, 3 of 7
Psychopathy Not a DSM diagnosis — Hare PCL-R
Cluster A mapping Schizotypal ≈ positive, schizoid ≈ negative, paranoid ≈ paranoia
Schizoid vs avoidant Doesn't want relationships vs wants but fears rejection
Schizotypal vs avoidant anxiety Paranoid, doesn't fade with familiarity
OCPD vs OCD Ego-syntonic, no true obsessions or compulsions
5-of-9 disorders Schizotypal, narcissistic, borderline
Temperament Innate, biologically based, foundational to personality

Borderline personality disorder Guide 10

Threshold 5 of 9 → 256 possible combinations
The nine, in short Affective instability, suicidality, anger, relationships, self-image, abandonment, impulsivity, dissociation/paranoia, emptiness
Idealization and devaluation The unstable-relationships criterion — about others, not self
Criterion 4 trap Impulsivity needs ≥ 2 areas and excludes self-harm
Criterion 7 Transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation — not a psychotic disorder
Epidemiology string 2–6% / 6% / 10% / 20% — population, primary care, outpatient, inpatient
Lifetime completed suicide 8–10%; about three quarters self-harm
The temperament's three features Low threshold, high intensity, slow return to baseline
Childhood sexual abuse 10–20% general population vs 40–70% inpatient BPD
Medication for BPD None treats it; psychotherapy first line; polypharmacy the classic error
DBT in numbers 6–12 months, 1 h individual + 2 h group, ~75% response; fourth mode = phone coaching
Distress in the office Validate → both-and → offer help → suggest a skill → another

Self-harm and suicide risk Guide 11

Deliberate self-harm defined Tissue damage without suicidal intent
Suicide rate after self-harm 439.1 vs 11.8 per 100,000 person-years — 37×
Self-harm alone Never establishes BPD
First step on disclosure Direct risk assessment, before any disposition decision
Screen order Ideation → method → means → intent → past attempts; then acute/chronic, active/passive, protective factors
Means restriction 1–2 week prescriptions; firearms locked, ammunition separate
Avoid reinforcing self-harm Neutral acutely, warm when not self-harming; say "for emergencies"
Suicide without illness Rational suicide, MAID, intoxication-driven impulsive attempts — still assess
Lithium Uniquely anti-suicidal among the psychotropics

Biological treatments Guide 12

Antidepressant targets Serotonin and/or norepinephrine — monoamines
Serotonin · noradrenaline sources Raphe nuclei · locus coeruleus
Dopamine, both directions ↑ psychosis; ↓ amotivation and anhedonia
The sufficient list Fluoxetine, venlafaxine, bupropion, mirtazapine · lithium, valproate, lamotrigine · haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine · benzodiazepines short-term, propranolol · methylphenidate/amphetamines, atomoxetine, guanfacine · naltrexone/acamprosate, methadone/buprenorphine
Stems carry clues Class is inferred from the vignette; trade names not required
Lithium · valproate · lamotrigine Suicide prevention · acute mania · bipolar depression
Clozapine Treatment-resistant schizophrenia
Memantine · donepezil NMDA antagonist · cholinesterase inhibitor
Methadone · buprenorphine Full agonist · partial agonist; naltrexone and acamprosate anti-craving
Benzodiazepine for panic Not a treatment; antidepressant daily and standing + CBT
ECT Most effective antidepressant; 8–12 seizures, 3/week; standard of care for resistant depression, acute suicidality, catatonia
ECT risks Anaesthetic (~1 in 100,000), post-ictal confusion, rare memory problems, sore jaw; DBS experimental
Psychedelics 5-HT2A agonism → default mode network disruption, ↑ plasticity; research or special access only; ketamine = prescribable NMDA antagonist
CAM 30–50% use it, often undisclosed

Psychological, social, spiritual treatments Guide 13

Identify the modality Childhood, defences, transference = psychodynamic; worksheets = CBT; skills and mindfulness = third wave; values = ACT
Validation The first move in every psychotherapy; cannot be overdone
DBT's four skill modules Emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, mindfulness
TIPP Temperature (diving reflex), intense exercise, progressive muscle relaxation, paced breathing
Physiological sigh Double inhale, long exhale ≥ 10 s; heart rate and pressure fall, prefrontal cortex returns
Five defences · six distortions Denial, projection, sublimation, displacement, regression · all-or-nothing, over-generalizing, mental filter, disqualifying the positive, jumping to conclusions, magnification
PTSD therapies EMDR, prolonged exposure, trauma-focused CBT, cognitive processing therapy — all memory work, because avoidance perpetuates PTSD
Mindfulness Fundamental to any psychotherapy: awareness before change
Four social interventions Case management (ACT), supportive housing, income support, peer support
Cultural rules Trained interpreters not family; explore the explanatory model; ask about spirituality
Medication hesitancy Explore the concerns — not escalation to neurostimulation or admission
Psychotherapy changes the brain In a pattern that differs from medication

CBL: Stanley Guide 14

Before the meeting Language barrier, trauma-informed care, no assumptions
Closed off Reassurance, confidentiality, safe environment, body language and tone
After disclosure Thank, acknowledge, validate; "is there anything you need from me before we continue?"
Refugee-specific facts Claim stage and hearing, legal representation, coverage, work status, family, safety if returned
Suicidal ideation Direct risk assessment now
Formulation grid Bio/psycho/social/cultural × 4 P's; the cultural column is the addition
Work-up while awaiting psychiatry CBC, TSH at minimum
Supports and advocacy Settlement, legal aid, social work, OW, housing, newcomer clinics, affirming organizations; individual → institution → community → policy

Localization — dermatomes and myotomes Guide 15

Which list wins on assessments The course handout, over any textbook
The localization method Intersection of the weak muscles' root lists
Biceps (C5,C6) + pronator teres (C6,C7) weak C6; triceps predominantly C7
C5 · C6 · C7 sensory points Lateral upper arm · thumb · middle finger
C8 · T1 sensory points Little finger · medial arm
L3 · L4 · L5 · S1 sensory points Medial knee · medial malleolus · dorsum of foot · lateral foot
Ankle inversion and eversion Both labelled L5 in the course figure
Reflex roots Biceps C5–C6, triceps C7, knee L3–L4, ankle S1
Cauda equina syndrome Back pain + saddle anaesthesia + bladder/bowel dysfunction — surgical emergency

Imaging — CT and MR basics Guide 16

Attenuation rule High density → high attenuation → white
Density order Lead > bone > muscle > water > fat > air
Hounsfield anchors Air −1000, fat −60 to −100, water 0, bone +400 to +1000
Grey vs white matter CT: grey (80 HU) brighter than white (50 HU); T1: white brighter — flips
Dark CSF · bright CSF T1 · T2; FLAIR = T2 with CSF suppressed
Most pathology Dark on T1, bright on T2
Restricted diffusion Low ADC, bright DWI — usually acute ischaemia
GRE/SWI finds Haemorrhage and calcification — both dark; multiple black dots = amyloid angiopathy
Enhancement means Blood–brain barrier broken — tumour, infection, inflammation
Request by name MRA and MRV; CT urgent/bone/acute blood; MR parenchyma

Development of the brain Guide 17

CNS vs PNS origin CNS neural tube only; PNS neural tube plus neural crest
Primary · secondary neurulation Ectoderm by folding · mesoderm by cavitation
Inducer and product Notochord induces ectoderm → neural plate
Neuropore closure Rostral ~25 days, caudal ~28 days — the 4th week
Rostral failure · caudal failure Anencephaly · myeloschisis
Three zones, inside out Ventricular → ependyma; intermediate → grey; marginal → white
Alar vs basal Alar dorsal sensory; basal ventral motor; sulcus limitans divides; pontine flexure everts the alar plates
Only vesicle with two derivatives Metencephalon → pons and cerebellum
Chiari II chain Open NTD → foramen magnum herniation → hydrocephalus → shunt
Migration disorders Band heterotopia = DCX; periventricular nodular = FLNA

Scope statements Lecturers

Pharmacology The medication slide is sufficient; stems carry clues; trade names not needed
Out of scope by statement Culturally specific/spiritual experiences; CAM detail; the attachment-prevalence number; ECT side effects; the nosology module
"You don't need to memorize" Means clues will be given, not that it's off the exam
Case report Described by the preceptor as not a high-stakes assessment; satisfactory needed to pass
Interview skills Assessed in every OSCE station
